📖 Worked example — a challenge-level proof, start to finish

WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: if n² is even, then n is even (contrapositive)
Step 1 — choose the method. Direct is awkward (starting from n² tells you little about n). Take the contrapositive: “if n is odd, then n² is odd” — equivalent, and easier.
Step 2 — prove it. Let n be odd: n = 2k + 1. Then n² = (2k+1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1 — an odd number. ✓
Step 3 — conclude. The contrapositive is proved, so the original holds. ∎

Challenge questions grade the METHOD choice as much as the algebra: contradiction for √2/primes, contrapositive when the conclusion is easier to negate, induction for “for all n” sums.

Logic, Proofs, Sets & Relations Reference

A conditional p → q equals ¬p ∨ q. Its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p is logically equivalent; its converse and inverse are not.

⚙ FORMULAS
  • Distribute implication: (p → q) ∧ (p → r) ≡ p → (q ∧ r).
  • De Morgan: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q; ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q.
  • Inclusion-exclusion: |A∪B∪C| = Σ|A| − Σ|A∩B| + |A∩B∩C|.
💡 KEY RESULTS
  • Negating quantifiers flips each and negates the core: ¬∀x∃y P ≡ ∃x∀y ¬P.
  • An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, transitive; its classes partition the set.
    🔎 Partition

    A split of a set into non-overlapping, non-empty blocks that cover everything — each element in exactly one block.

    Example: Integers split into evens and odds.
    🔎 Equivalence relation

    Reflexive + symmetric + transitive. It carves the set into equivalence classes — disjoint groups of \"equivalent\" elements.

    Example: \"Same birthday month\" groups everyone into 12 classes.
  • A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive.
    🔎 Partial order

    Reflexive + antisymmetric + transitive — a \"less-than-or-equal\" style ranking where some pairs may be incomparable.

    Example: \"Is a subset of\": {1} ⊆ {1,2}, but {1} and {2} are incomparable.
  • The number of equivalence relations on an n-set equals the Bell number: B₃=5, B₄=15.
📝 TECHNIQUE

To prove √2 irrational by contradiction, assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms; derive that a and b are both even, contradicting lowest terms. Induction proves ∀n P(n) via a base case plus P(k) → P(k+1).

⚠ SUBTLETY

Reflexive relations on an n-set number 2^(n²−n); antisymmetric relations number 2ⁿ · 3^(n(n−1)/2). A relation can be both symmetric and antisymmetric (only the diagonal), and one that is neither is common.

📖 Worked example — a challenge-level computation, start to finish

WORKED EXAMPLE — Boolean matrix product (paths in a graph)
A = [ 0 1 ; 1 0 ] (edge 1↔2), B = [ 1 0 ; 1 1 ]. Compute the Boolean product A ⊙ B (∧ for multiply, ∨ to combine):
• entry (1,1): (0∧1) ∨ (1∧1) = 0 ∨ 1 = 1
• entry (1,2): (0∧0) ∨ (1∧1) = 1
• entry (2,1): (1∧1) ∨ (0∧1) = 1
• entry (2,2): (1∧0) ∨ (0∧1) = 0
Result: [ 1 1 ; 1 0 ]. Each 1 answers “is there a path?” — never a count. Any sum that would exceed 1 stays 1.

Boolean Algebra, Matrices & Graphs Reference

Boolean algebra uses + (OR), · (AND), and complement. Simplify with identities before drawing conclusions.

⚙ FORMULAS
  • Absorption: x + xy = x; complement: xy + xy' = x.
  • XNOR: x'y' + xy = (x ⊕ y)' — the two diagonal K-map corners.
  • Handshake theorem: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|.
  • Euler's formula (connected planar): v − e + f = 2.
  • Complete graph edges: |E(Kₙ)| = n(n−1)/2.
💡 KEY RESULTS
  • A connected graph has an Euler circuit iff every vertex has even degree.
  • A tree with n vertices has exactly n−1 edges and is acyclic and connected.
    🔎 Tree

    A connected graph with NO cycles. Always has exactly n − 1 edges, and exactly one path between any two vertices.

    Example: A family tree or a folder hierarchy — one way to get anywhere.
  • K₅ and K₃,₃ are the minimal non-planar graphs (Kuratowski).
📝 TECHNIQUE

The Boolean (zero-one) product A ⊙ B uses ∨ for the outer sum and ∧ for the inner product: (A⊙B)ₓ₣ = ∨ₖ (aₓₖ ∧ bₖ₣). It records reachability, not counts.

⚠ SUBTLETY

An Euler path traverses every edge once; a Hamilton path visits every vertex once — a graph can have one without the other. There is no simple degree test for Hamilton circuits. Also, all even degrees only guarantees an Euler circuit when the graph is connected.

📖 Worked examples — do one of each kind before the problems

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — inclusion-exclusion
|A| = 20, |B| = 15, |A ∩ B| = 5. Then |A ∪ B| = 20 + 15 − 5 = 30 — subtract the overlap once because the plain sum counted it twice.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — evaluate a proposition
p = T, q = F: evaluate (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬q. Inner first: p ∨ q = T; ¬q = T; then T ∧ T = T. Work inside-out, one connective at a time.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — simplify a Boolean expression
ab + ab′ = a(b + b′) (factor) = a·1 (complement) = a. Name the law at each step — that’s where partial credit and speed both live.

Formulas & method

These problems mix counting with logic. Keep the core formulas handy.

  • Inclusion-exclusion (two sets): |A∪B| = |A| + |B| − |A∩B|. For three sets, |A∪B∪C| = |A|+|B|+|C| − |A∩B| − |A∩C| − |B∩C| + |A∩B∩C|.
  • Power set: a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, so |P(A)| = 2ⁿ.
    🔎 Power set P(A)

    The set of ALL subsets of A — including ∅ and A itself. Size 2ⁿ.

    Example: P({a,b}) = { ∅, {a}, {b}, {a,b} } — 4 subsets.
  • Truth table: a formula with k distinct variables needs 2ᵏ rows.
  • Connectives: ¬ flips a truth value; ∧ (AND) is T only if both are T; ∨ (OR) is F only if both are F; p→q is F only when p=T, q=F.

Worked example

Let |A|=12, |B|=9, |A∩B|=4. Then |A∪B| = 12 + 9 − 4 = 17. To evaluate (p∨q)∧¬r at p=F, q=T, r=F: p∨q = T, ¬r = T, so the whole expression is T∧T = T (true). For Boolean algebra, simplify first when you can: A·B + A·B̄ = A·(B + B̄) = A·1 = A, then substitute the value of A.

The toolkit these problems assume

📘 DEFINITION
a mod n is the remainder when a is divided by n. 17 mod 5 = 2, because 17 = 3 × 5 + 2. The result is always in 0 … n − 1.

Modular arithmetic is done term by term: (5 mod 3) + (8 mod 3) = 2 + 2 = 4. Note the answer is not reduced again unless the question asks for the total mod 3.

📘 DEFINITION
⌊x⌋ (floor) is the greatest integer ≤ x; ⌈x⌉ (ceiling) is the least integer ≥ x. For positives these feel like rounding down and up. For negatives they still mean the same thing, which is where mistakes happen: ⌊−2.3⌋ = −3, not −2, because −3 is the greatest integer that is still ≤ −2.3. And ⌊2.5⌋ + ⌈2.5⌉ = 2 + 3 = 5.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The Euclidean algorithm — gcd(48, 36)

Repeatedly replace the pair by (smaller, remainder) until the remainder is 0. The last non-zero remainder is the gcd.

  1. 48 = 1 × 36 + 12
  2. 36 = 3 × 12 + 0
  3. The remainder has hit 0, so the answer is the previous one: gcd(48, 36) = 12.
📘 DEFINITION
Arrangements with repeated items. n items with repeats give n! ÷ (the factorial of each repeat count). \"BOOK\" has 4 letters with O appearing twice: 4! / 2! = 24 / 2 = 12 distinct arrangements. Dividing by 2! removes the orderings that only swap the two identical Os.
📘 DEFINITION
A recurrence defines each term from the previous one. For a(n) = a(n−1) + 3 with a(1) = 2, just walk it: a(2) = 5, a(3) = 8, a(4) = 11. (Adding a constant each time makes it arithmetic, so a(n) = 2 + 3(n − 1) gives the same answer directly.)
📘 DEFINITION
The pigeonhole principle: if n items go into m containers and n > m, some container holds at least two. With 13 people and 12 months, two must share a birth month — no matter how the birthdays fall.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Spot the shape of the question: \"remainder\" → mod · \"greatest integer ≤\" → floor · \"more items than categories\" → pigeonhole · \"repeated letters\" → divide by the repeat factorials · \"each term from the last\" → recurrence.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — one matrix-product entry
A = 1234, B = 5678. Entry (1,2) of AB = row 1 · column 2 = 1·6 + 2·8 = 22. Row across, column down — one dot product per entry.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — geometric series sum
2 + 6 + 18 + 54 (a = 2, r = 3, n = 4): S = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) = 2(81 − 1)/2 = 80. Check: 2+6+18+54 = 80 ✓.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — graph counting
K₆: edges = n(n−1)/2 = 6·5/2 = 15. A tree on 6 vertices: always n − 1 = 5 edges. Degree sum with 15 edges: 2·15 = 30 (handshake).

Formulas & method

This section computes results from matrices, relations, and sequences.

  • Matrix product: entry (i,j) of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B: Σ aᵢₖ·bₖⱼ. For a Boolean product replace + with OR and · with AND.
  • Relations on a set of n elements: there are 2^(n²) relations total, 2^(n²−n) reflexive relations, and 2^(n(n+1)/2) symmetric relations.
    🔎 Relation

    Any set of ordered pairs from a set — which elements are \"related\" to which. Drawn as a digraph with arrows.

    Example: \"Divides\" on {1,2,4}: pairs (1,2),(1,4),(2,4),(1,1),(2,2),(4,4).
  • Functions A→B: there are |B|^|A| of them.
  • Arithmetic series: Sₙ = n/2·(a₁ + aₙ) = n/2·(2a + (n−1)d).
    🔎 Series

    The SUM of a sequence’s terms: a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + …

    Example: The sequence 1, ½, ¼ … gives the series 1 + ½ + ¼ + … = 2.
  • Geometric series: Sₙ = a·(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) for r ≠ 1.
  • Modular arithmetic: a mod m is the remainder after dividing a by m.

Worked example

Number of functions from a 3-element set to a 4-element set: 4³ = 64. Sum 2 + 5 + 8 + 11 (4 terms, a = 2, d = 3): S = 4/2·(2 + 11) = 2·13 = 26.

Counting: permutations, combinations, and repetition

QuestionFormulaExample
Order matters, no repeats — permutationP(n, r) = n! / (n − r)!arrange 3 of 5 books: P(5,3) = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60
Order does not matter — combinationC(n, r) = n! / (r!(n − r)!)2-person committee from 6: C(6,2) = 15
Order matters, repeats allowednr3-letter strings from 26 letters: 26³ = 17,576

Permutations count ordered selections; combinations count unordered ones; and permutations with repetition allow an item to be reused. The two questions to ask, in this order: does order matter, and may an item be used twice. Those two answers pick the formula every time.

A committee is the classic combination — swapping who was chosen first does not make a different committee. A shelf of books is the classic permutation, because rearranging them plainly gives a different shelf.

🎯 EXAM TIP
C(n, r) is always smaller than P(n, r) by exactly a factor of r!, because each unordered choice corresponds to r! ordered ones. If your answer is too big, you probably used a permutation where order did not matter.

📖 Worked examples — do one of each kind before the problems

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — count truth-table rows
A formula with 4 distinct variables has 2⁴ = 16 rows — each variable doubles the combinations. Rows where p ∧ q ∧ r is true: exactly 1 (all true).
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — bitwise operations, column by column
1011 AND 1101: columns give 1·1, 0·1, 1·0, 1·1 → 1001. 1011 XOR 1101 → differs in the middle two → 0110. Line the bits up and work one column at a time.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — check a quantifier over a finite domain
Domain {1, 2, 3}, P(x): x² < 9. P(1) ✓, P(2) ✓, P(3): 9 < 9 ✗ → ∀x P(x) is false (one counterexample kills a universal); ∃x P(x) is true.

Formulas & method

A truth table for a formula with n distinct variables has 2^n rows, one per combination of values. To evaluate a compound proposition, substitute the given values and apply the connective rules.

  • Negation ¬p: flips the value.
  • Conjunction p ∧ q: true only when both are true.
  • Disjunction p ∨ q: false only when both are false.
  • Conditional p → q: false only when p is true and q is false.
  • Biconditional p ↔ q: true when p and q have the same value.
    🔎 Biconditional (p ↔ q)

    \"p if and only if q\" — true when p and q MATCH (both true or both false).

    Example: \"You pass iff you score ≥ 60\" — passing and scoring ≥60 always agree.

Two propositions are logically equivalent when they have identical columns in every row. For example p → q equals its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p. To count how many of the 2^n rows make a formula true, build the table and tally the true rows.

Quantifiers

Over a finite domain, ∀x P(x) is true only if P holds for every element; ∃x P(x) is true if P holds for at least one. Check each element in turn.

Bit operations

Bitwise AND keeps a 1 only where both bits are 1; OR gives 1 where either bit is 1; XOR gives 1 where the bits differ. Operate column by column.

Mini-example

With p=T, q=F evaluate (p ∧ q) ∨ p: p ∧ q = F, then F ∨ T = T.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Parity: n² + n is always even
  1. Factor it: n² + n = n(n + 1).
  2. n and n + 1 are consecutive integers, so exactly one of them is even.
  3. A product with an even factor is even.
  4. So n² + n is always even, for every integer n.

Factoring first avoids splitting into odd and even cases.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Using Σ2i = n(n + 1)

Compute 2 + 4 + 6 + … + 12.

  1. The terms are 2i for i = 1 … 6, since the last term 12 = 2 × 6.
  2. Apply the formula with n = 6: n(n + 1) = 6 × 7.
  3. = 42.

Finding n from the last term is the step to be careful with: n is 6, not 12.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — count the functions
|A| = 3, |B| = 4: functions A → B number |B|^|A| = 4³ = 64 (each of 3 inputs freely picks one of 4 outputs). Injections: 4·3·2 = 24 (no reuse allowed).
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — power set and products
A set with 6 elements has 2⁶ = 64 subsets; C(6,2) = 15 of them have exactly two elements. |A × B| with |A| = 4, |B| = 7: 4 · 7 = 28 ordered pairs.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — symmetric difference
|A| = 7, |B| = 6, |A ∩ B| = 4: |A △ B| = |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B| = 13 − 8 = 5 — subtract the overlap TWICE because it belongs to neither “only-A” nor “only-B.”

Formulas & method

Inclusion-exclusion relates union and intersection sizes: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. Rearranging gives |A ∩ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∪ B|.

  • Power set: a set with n elements has 2^n subsets, so |P(A)| = 2^n.
  • Subsets of a fixed size: the number of k-element subsets of an n-set is the binomial coefficient C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!).
    🔎 Subset (⊆)

    A ⊆ B when everything in A is also in B. Every set is a subset of itself; ∅ is a subset of everything.

    Example: {1,2} ⊆ {1,2,3} ✓.
  • Cartesian product: |A × B| = |A| · |B|.
  • Symmetric difference: |A △ B| = |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B|.

Counting functions

The number of functions from A to B is |B|^|A| (each of the |A| inputs independently chooses one of |B| outputs). The number of injections from A to B (with |A| = k, |B| = m and k ≤ m) is the falling factorial m · (m − 1) · … · (m − k + 1). When A and B have the same finite size n, the injections are exactly the bijections, and there are n! of them.

Set-builder counts

To count a set defined by a condition, list or count the elements of the domain that satisfy it. For example, |{ x ∈ ℤ : 1 ≤ x ≤ 10 and x is even }| = 5.

Mini-example

If |A| = 3 and |B| = 2, the number of functions A → B is 2^3 = 8.

Floor and ceiling together. ⌊2.5⌋ = 2 and ⌈2.5⌉ = 3, so ⌊2.5⌋ + ⌈2.5⌉ = 5. For any non-integer x, ⌊x⌋ + ⌈x⌉ = 2⌊x⌋ + 1; for an integer they are equal and the sum is 2x.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Finding an inverse value without finding the inverse function

f(x) = 3x − 2. Compute f⁻¹(7).

  1. f⁻¹(7) asks: which input gives an output of 7?
  2. Solve 3x − 2 = 7 → 3x = 9 → x = 3.
  3. Check: f(3) = 3(3) − 2 = 7 ✓.

Solving the equation is quicker than deriving f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3 and then substituting, though both give 3.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — evaluate a Boolean expression
(A ∨ B) ∧ ¬B at A = 1, B = 0: inner first: A ∨ B = 1; ¬B = 1; then 1 ∧ 1 = 1.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — one matrix-product entry
A = 1234, B = 5678. Entry (2,1) of AB = row 2 of A · column 1 of B = 3·5 + 4·7 = 15 + 28 = 43. (Row across, column down — every entry is one dot product.)
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — a 2×2 determinant
det −2341 = ad − bc = (−2)(1) − (3)(4) = −2 − 12 = −14. Nonzero → invertible.

Boolean algebra

Use ∧ (AND, the product), ∨ (OR, the sum) and ¬ (NOT, complement). Rules: x∧1=x, x∧0=0, x∨0=x, x∨1=1. Absorption gives A∨(A∧B)=A and A∧(A∨B)=A. To evaluate, substitute the 0/1 inputs and reduce inner brackets first.

Minterms

A function of n variables has 2ⁿ input rows. The number of minterms is how many rows output 1. For F=A∨B over three variables A,B,C, only the rows with A=0 and B=0 give 0 (two such rows, C=0 or 1), so 8−2=6 minterms.

Matrices

Entry (i,j) of a product AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B: (AB)ᵢⱼ = Σₖ AᵢₖBₖⱼ. For a Boolean product use ∧ for the products and ∨ to combine, so each entry is 0 or 1. The sum A+B adds entrywise; the transpose Aᵀ swaps rows and columns so (Aᵀ)ᵢⱼ=Aⱼᵢ.

Determinants

For 2×2, detabcd = ad − bc. For 3×3, expand along the first row with alternating signs: a·det(minor) − b·det(minor) + c·det(minor).

DNF size. A DNF has one minterm per row where the function is true. If a 3-variable function is true in exactly 3 of its 8 rows, its DNF has 3 minterms. (The CNF would correspondingly have one maxterm per false row — 5 of them.)

Dimensions. (m × n)(n × p) = m × p: the inner numbers must match and they vanish, leaving the outer two. A is 3×2 and B is 2×5, the inner 2s match, so AB is 3×5.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — arithmetic series
First term 3, difference 5, 10 terms: S = n/2 · (2a + (n−1)d) = 5 · (6 + 45) = 5 · 51 = 255.
WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — count relations
Reflexive relations on a 3-element set: the 3 diagonal pairs are forced; the other 9 − 3 = 6 pairs are free choices → 2⁶ = 64.
WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — handshake lemma
15 edges → degree sum = 2 · 15 = 30. (Every edge contributes 2 to the total degree — one per end.)

Relations

A relation on a set with n elements is a subset of A×A, which has n² ordered pairs. The number of reflexive relations is 2^(n²−n) (the diagonal is forced, the other n²−n pairs are free). The number of symmetric relations is 2^(n(n+1)/2).

🔎 Reflexive

Every element relates to ITSELF — every vertex has a self-loop; the matrix diagonal is all 1s.

Example: \"≤\" is reflexive (x ≤ x always); \"<\" is not.

Series

Arithmetic sum of n terms with first term a and common difference d: S = n/2·(2a + (n−1)d). Geometric sum with ratio r ≠ 1: S = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1). A summation like Σ (2k+1) splits as 2Σk + Σ1.

Graphs

The complete graph Kₙ has n(n−1)/2 edges. The handshake lemma says the sum of all vertex degrees equals 2·|E|. A tree with n vertices always has n−1 edges. The number of walks of length k between two vertices equals the matching entry of the k-th power of the adjacency matrix: (Aᵏ)ᵢⱼ.

Modular arithmetic

Reduce after combining: (a + b) mod m or (a·b) mod m is the remainder after dividing by m.

\n

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

\n
THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
\n
THE 3-STEP LOOP
\n\n\n\n
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
\n
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
\n\n\n\n\n
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
\nStart the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
\n
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
\n
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
\n
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers \"learn it in 25 minutes\" instead of hours.

Discrete mathematics starts with logic because every later topic is built on it: a set is defined by a condition, a proof is a chain of implications, and a Boolean circuit is a truth table in hardware. A proposition is the atom of all that — a declarative statement with a definite truth value, true or false, but not both.

The test is whether it can be judged. \"7 is prime\" is a proposition, and so is \"7 is even\" — false propositions are still propositions. \"What time is it?\" is a question, \"Close the door\" is a command, and \"x > 5\" contains a free variable, so none of the three is a proposition until the variable is pinned down.

The five operators

OperatorSymbolRead asTrue when
Negation¬pnot pp is false
Conjunctionp ∧ qp and qboth are true
Disjunctionp ∨ qp or qat least one is true — false only when both are false
Exclusive orp ⊕ qp xor qexactly one is true — they differ
Conditionalp → qif p then qalways, except when p is true and q is false

The one that trips people is ∨. In everyday speech \"or\" usually means one or the other but not both — \"you can have soup or salad\". In logic ∨ is inclusive: it is true when both are true. The exclusive version has its own symbol, ⊕, and it is the one that means \"exactly one\".

Truth tables

A truth table lists every combination of truth values for the variables and the resulting value of the expression. With n variables it has 2n rows — two variables give four, three give eight — and that count is asked directly.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — building the table for p ∧ ¬q
  p     q  |  ¬q  |  p ∧ ¬q\n--------+------+---------\n  T     T  |  F   |    F\n  T     F  |  T   |    T     <- the only true row\n  F     T  |  F   |    F\n  F     F  |  T   |    F

Fill the variable columns in a fixed pattern so you never miss a row: the first column alternates in blocks of half the rows, the next in blocks of a quarter, and so on. Then build the expression up one operator at a time, innermost first.

Order of evaluation matters as much as it does in arithmetic. Work through parentheses first, then ¬, then ∧, then ∨, and finally → and ↔. So ¬p ∨ q means (¬p) ∨ q, not ¬(p ∨ q) — and those two are genuinely different statements.

Three names for whole expressions

Once a table is built, the last column has one of three characters. A tautology is true in every row — p ∨ ¬p. A contradiction is false in every row — p ∧ ¬p. A contingency is anything else, true in some rows and false in others. Most expressions are contingencies; the exam asks about the other two.

📘 DEFINITION

Proposition: a declarative statement with exactly one truth value, true or false

Negation (¬): reverses the truth value

Conjunction (∧): true only when both operands are true

Disjunction (∨): inclusive or — true when at least one operand is true

Exclusive or (⊕): true when exactly one operand is true

Truth table: a table of every truth-value combination and the resulting value; 2ⁿ rows for n variables

Tautology: an expression true under every assignment

Contradiction: an expression false under every assignment

Contingency: an expression that is true in some rows and false in others

Compound proposition: propositions joined by one or more operators

★ ON THE OA

A proposition is a declarative statement with a definite truth value — a question or a command is not one. Operators: ¬ NOT, ∧ AND (true only when both are true), ∨ OR (inclusive — false only when both are false), ⊕ XOR (true when they differ). A table with n variables has 2ⁿ rows.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Do not read ∨ as everyday \"or\". T ∨ T is true. If a question wants exactly one, it will use ⊕ — and if it says \"or\" in English, check which one it means before answering.

The six connectives at a glance

Everything in this unit is built from these. The one that costs marks is the conditional: p → q is FALSE in exactly one row — when the promise is made and broken, p true and q false. In every other row, including both rows where p is false, it is true.

📊 FIGURE — every connective, with the rows that define it
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

\"p → q is true when p is false\" feels wrong the first ten times you meet it. The reading that fixes it: a conditional is a promise. \"If it rains, I bring an umbrella.\" On a dry day you have broken no promise whatever you carry, so the statement stands. It is only falsified by rain plus no umbrella.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — is (p ∧ ¬q) → p a tautology?

Build every row. Two variables means 2² = 4 rows.

pq¬qp ∧ ¬q(p ∧ ¬q) → p
TTFFT
TFTTT
FTFFT
FFTFT

The last column is T in every row, so yes — it is a tautology. A column of all Fs would make it a contradiction; a mixture makes it a contingency. Those three words are the vocabulary the question will use.

A support desk writes its escalation rule in English: a ticket is escalated when it is marked urgent and is not yet assigned, or when it has been open for more than five days. Three conditions carry the whole rule, so give each one a letter: u = marked urgent, a = already assigned, d = open more than five days. The rule is then E = (u ∧ ¬a) ∨ d.

A truth table is built one column at a time, never in one leap. The figure shows the four stages: fill the input columns in the fixed pattern, then the innermost negation, then the AND, then the OR.

📊 FIGURE — a truth-table walk — one column per stage
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — reading one ticket off the table
1.
Ticket 4187 is marked urgent, has already been assigned to an agent, and has been open six days. So u = T, a = T, d = T.
2.
Column ②: ¬a. The ticket is assigned, so a = T and ¬a = F.
3.
Column ③: u ∧ ¬a = T ∧ F = F. The urgent-and-unassigned reason does not apply.
4.
Column ④: (u ∧ ¬a) ∨ d = F ∨ T = T.
5.
The ticket is escalated — not because it is urgent, but because of the five-day clause. One true disjunct is enough for ∨.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an OR that is not the logical ∨ — the checkout coupon
1.
A shop offers: you may apply a free-shipping code or a 10% code, but not both. Let s stand for the free-shipping code and d for the 10% code.
2.
Write the two candidate tables side by side:
3.
 s  d | s ∨ d | s ⊕ d\n------+-------+-------\n T  T |   T   |   F   <- the rows disagree here\n T  F |   T   |   T\n F  T |   T   |   T\n F  F |   F   |   F
4.
The last three rows agree. In the first row — the customer applies both codes — inclusive ∨ says \"allowed\" and ⊕ says \"not allowed\".
5.
The shop means f ⊕ t. Everyday \"or\" is usually exclusive; the logical ∨ is not, and the difference is exactly one row.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Two things go wrong in the same place. First, ∨ is inclusive — p ∨ q is true when both are true, so \"at least one\" is the right reading, never \"exactly one\". Second, precedence: ¬p ∨ q means (¬p) ∨ q. Reading it as ¬(p ∨ q) changes the answer in two of the four rows. Negation binds tightest, then ∧, then ∨, then → and ↔.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Three facts pay for themselves. A table over n variables has 2ⁿ rows — 3 sensors give 8, 5 give 32. Fill the inputs in the canonical pattern (leftmost column: T for the top half, F for the bottom half; each column after that alternates twice as fast) so a question about \"row 5\" means the same row for you as for the examiner. And learn the shortcut rows: ∧ is true in one row only, ∨ is false in one row only, ⊕ is true when the two differ.

Two things these questions expect

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Counting bit strings with fixed positions

How many bit strings of length 5 begin with 1 and end with 0?

  1. Position 1 is forced to 1 — one choice.
  2. Position 5 is forced to 0 — one choice.
  3. The middle three positions are free: 2 × 2 × 2.
  4. Total = 2³ = 8.

Fixing a position multiplies by 1; each free position multiplies by 2.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Translating a policy into a formula

\"Unlocks when the badge is valid AND the time is within office hours, OR when the fire panel signals evacuation.\" Let b, h, e be those three.

  1. \"badge valid AND within office hours\" → (b ∧ h).
  2. \"OR when evacuation\" attaches to that whole condition → (b ∧ h) ∨ e.
  3. The brackets carry the meaning: b ∧ (h ∨ e) would wrongly require a badge during an evacuation.

Translate the comma. It marks where the OR splits the sentence.

The conditional p → q is the operator the whole course runs on — every theorem, every proof and every definition is an implication — and it is also the one whose truth table looks wrong the first time you see it.

Read p → q as a promise: \"if p happens, I guarantee q\". The only way to break a promise is for p to happen and q not to. That is the single false row.

  p     q  |  p → q\n--------+---------\n  T     T  |    T\n  T     F  |    F     <- the ONLY false case\n  F     T  |    T     \\  promise never tested,\n  F     F  |    T     /  so it was not broken

The two bottom rows are called vacuously true. \"If I win the lottery I will buy you a car\" — if I do not win, I have not lied, whatever happens next. A false hypothesis makes the whole conditional true, and exam questions exploit that constantly.

The four related conditionals

From any p → q you can build three relatives, and knowing which are equivalent is worth several marks.

NameFormEquivalent to the original?
Conditionalp → q—
Converseq → pNo
Inverse¬p → ¬qNo
Contrapositive¬q → ¬pYes — always

Test it with a real sentence. \"If it is a dog, it is a mammal\" is true. Its converse — \"if it is a mammal, it is a dog\" — is false. Its inverse — \"if it is not a dog, it is not a mammal\" — is also false. Its contrapositive — \"if it is not a mammal, it is not a dog\" — is true, and always will be. The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other, and neither is equivalent to the original.

The contrapositive being equivalent is not a curiosity: it is the engine of contrapositive proof in 7.2, where proving ¬q → ¬p is often far easier than proving p → q directly.

The biconditional

p ↔ q, read \"p if and only if q\", is true exactly when p and q have the same truth value. It is equivalent to (p → q) ∧ (q → p) — both directions — which is why proving an \"if and only if\" theorem means proving two separate implications.

📐 Equivalences worth memorising
Conditional as ∨
p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q
Contrapositive
p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p
Negated conditional
¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q
Biconditional
p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p)
Double negation
¬(¬p) ≡ p

The third line is the one people get wrong. The negation of \"if p then q\" is not another conditional — it is the single case that breaks the promise: p is true and q is false.

📘 DEFINITION

Conditional (p → q): false only when p is true and q is false

Hypothesis / antecedent: the p in p → q

Conclusion / consequent: the q in p → q

Vacuously true: a conditional made true by a false hypothesis

Converse: q → p — not equivalent to the original

Inverse: ¬p → ¬q — not equivalent to the original

Contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p — always equivalent to the original

Biconditional (p ↔ q): true when p and q have the same truth value

Logically equivalent (≡): two expressions with identical truth tables

★ ON THE OA

p → q is FALSE in exactly one case: p true, q false. Everything else, including a false premise, is true. The key equivalences are p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q ≡ ¬q → ¬p. The converse and inverse are equivalent to each other and not to the original.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Two expressions are logically equivalent when their truth tables match column for column. If you are unsure whether a claimed equivalence holds, build both tables — four rows settles it and no reasoning can talk you out of it.

Converse, inverse, contrapositive

From one conditional you can form three others, and the exam tests whether you know which of them you are allowed to use.

📊 FIGURE — the conditional square
NameFormEquivalent to the original?
Originalp → q—
Converseq → pNo
Inverse¬p → ¬qNo
Contrapositive¬q → ¬pYes — always
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the sentence that makes it obvious

Original: \"If it is a dog, then it is a mammal.\" True.

Converse — \"If it is a mammal, then it is a dog.\" False: a cat is a counterexample.
Inverse — \"If it is not a dog, then it is not a mammal.\" False: the same cat.
Contrapositive — \"If it is not a mammal, then it is not a dog.\" True, and it has to be — it says exactly what the original says.

Notice the converse and the inverse are false together. That is not a coincidence: they are each other's contrapositive.

📘 DEFINITION

p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q. Rewriting a conditional as a disjunction is the single most useful move in this unit — it lets you push a negation in with De Morgan, and it turns \"prove the implication\" into \"prove the OR\".

Consequently ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q: the negation of an implication is not another implication, it is an AND.

An SLA says: if an outage runs past four hours, the customer receives a service credit. That is a conditional, and reading it as a promise makes its odd truth table obvious. The only way to break the promise is for the outage to run long and no credit to appear. Every other combination leaves the promise intact — including the two rows where the outage never ran long, which are the vacuously true ones.

📊 FIGURE — one table settles which relatives of p → q are equivalent
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a prerequisite rule and its three relatives
1.
The catalogue states: if a student is enrolled in Discrete Math II, then they have passed Discrete Math I. Let p = enrolled in II, q = passed I. The rule is p → q, and it is true.
2.
Converse (q → p): if a student has passed Discrete Math I, then they are enrolled in II. False — plenty of students pass I and stop there.
3.
Inverse (¬p → ¬q): if a student is not enrolled in II, then they have not passed I. False, for the same reason, and notice it says the same thing as the converse.
4.
Contrapositive (¬q → ¬p): if a student has not passed Discrete Math I, then they are not enrolled in II. True — and it must be, because it is equivalent to the rule itself.
5.
So of the four sentences, two are true (the rule and its contrapositive) and two are false (converse and inverse). That pairing is the whole examinable point.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what it takes to break the promise — negating a conditional
1.
A vendor promises: if the device fails within 12 months, we replace it. Symbolically p → q.
2.
A customer wants to claim the promise was broken. That claim is ¬(p → q).
3.
Rewrite the conditional first: p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q.
4.
Negate with De Morgan: ¬(¬p ∨ q) ≡ ¬(¬p) ∧ ¬q ≡ p ∧ ¬q.
5.
In English: the device failed within 12 months AND it was not replaced. The negation of a conditional is not another conditional — it is the single row that breaks it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
The converse feels like a restatement and is not one. \"If it is a dog, it is a mammal\" is true; \"if it is a mammal, it is a dog\" is false. Swapping the two halves is converse; negating both halves is inverse; doing both — swap and negate — is the contrapositive, and only that one is safe to substitute for the original.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Two lines close most conditional questions. p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q turns any conditional into a disjunction you can evaluate at a glance, and ¬(p → q) ≡ p ∧ ¬q handles every \"when is this promise broken\" item. Remember also that a false hypothesis makes the whole conditional true: \"if 2 + 2 = 5 then the sky is green\" is a true statement.

Apply the three related forms to \"if a number is divisible by 4, then it is even\": only the contrapositive (\"if it is not even, it is not divisible by 4\") is guaranteed true along with the original. The converse (\"if even, then divisible by 4\") is false — 6 is even and not divisible by 4 — and the inverse is false for the same reason. When a question offers converse, inverse and contrapositive, the contrapositive is the only one that must hold.

📘 DEFINITION
Necessary vs sufficient. In p → q, the hypothesis p is sufficient for q (p happening guarantees q), and q is necessary for p (without q, p cannot have happened — that is the contrapositive speaking). \"Scoring 90+ is sufficient for an A; an A is necessary for having scored 90+.\"

Negation is easy for a single proposition and needs a rule once operators are involved. De Morgan's Laws are that rule, and they are the most reused identities in the course — they reappear for sets in Unit 2 and for circuits in Unit 3, in exactly the same shape.

📐 De Morgan's Laws
Negated AND
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
Negated OR
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q
For sets
(A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′ and (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′

The rule of thumb is break the bar, flip the connective: distribute the negation onto both parts and swap ∧ for ∨. In English: the opposite of \"both\" is \"at least one is not\", and the opposite of \"at least one\" is \"neither\".

Checking it against a sentence makes it stick. The negation of \"it is raining and cold\" is not \"it is not raining and not cold\" — it is \"either it is not raining, or it is not cold\". Only one of them has to fail for the conjunction to fail.

Predicates and quantifiers

A predicate is a statement containing a variable, like P(x): x > 5. It is not a proposition, because it has no truth value until x is supplied. Quantifiers are what turn one into a proposition by saying how much of the domain it must hold for.

QuantifierSymbolReadsTrue whenFalse when
Universal∀x P(x)for all x, P(x)P(x) holds for every xone counterexample exists
Existential∃x P(x)there exists an x with P(x)at least one x worksno x works at all

The asymmetry in the last two columns is the point. To prove ∀ you must cover the whole domain; to disprove it you need a single counterexample. To prove ∃ one example is enough; to disprove it you must rule out everything.

Negating a quantifier

Negation swaps the quantifier and negates the inside — the same \"flip it\" pattern as De Morgan, which is not a coincidence, since ∀ is a long conjunction and ∃ is a long disjunction.

📐 Quantifier negation
Negated universal
¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x)
Negated existential
¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x)
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — negate \"every student passed\"
1.
Write it symbolically: ∀x P(x), where P(x) is \"student x passed\".
2.
Apply the rule: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x).
3.
Read it back: some student did not pass — not \"every student failed\", which is a much stronger claim.

With two quantifiers, order matters. ∀x ∃y (y > x) says every number has something bigger, which is true. Swap them and ∃y ∀x (y > x) says one number is bigger than everything, which is false. Same symbols, different claim.

📘 DEFINITION

De Morgan's Laws: negating a conjunction gives a disjunction of negations, and vice versa

Predicate: a statement containing a variable, with no truth value until the variable is supplied

Domain (universe of discourse): the set of values a quantified variable ranges over

Universal quantifier (∀): asserts the predicate holds for every element of the domain

Existential quantifier (∃): asserts the predicate holds for at least one element

Counterexample: a single case that makes a universal statement false

Free vs bound variable: a variable not governed by a quantifier, versus one that is

★ ON THE OA

De Morgan: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q — break the bar, flip the connective. The same shape works for sets: (A ∩ B)′ = A′ ∪ B′. Negating a quantifier swaps ∀ and ∃ and negates the predicate.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The negation of \"all birds fly\" is \"some bird does not fly\", not \"no bird flies\". Flipping ∀ to ∃ is the whole rule; do not over-negate into the opposite extreme.

Negating a quantifier

Two rules, and they are the same shape as De Morgan's laws for ∧ and ∨ — because \"for all\" is a long AND and \"there exists\" is a long OR.

📘 DEFINITION

¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x) — \"not everything is P\" means \"something is not P\".
¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x) — \"nothing is P\" means \"everything is not P\".

📊 FIGURE — what the quantifiers claim about a five-element domain

Read the middle row carefully. One failure — one object that is not P — is enough to kill a ∀ claim. That is why a single counterexample disproves a universal statement, and why no number of examples proves one.

StatementProved byDisproved by
∀x P(x)A general argument covering every xOne counterexample
∃x P(x)One exampleA general argument that no x works
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — negate \"every student passed every exam\"

Symbolically: ∀s ∀e Passed(s, e). Negate it by walking left to right, flipping each quantifier and carrying the ¬ inward:

¬∀s ∀e Passed(s,e) ≡ ∃s ¬∀e Passed(s,e) ≡ ∃s ∃e ¬Passed(s,e)

In English: \"some student failed some exam.\" Not \"no student passed any exam\" — that is a much stronger claim, and it is the distractor.

Negation is the operation policies are written around: a rule says what is accepted, and the system has to work out what is rejected. De Morgan is how that is done safely.

📊 FIGURE — negating a policy, and negating a quantifier — the same move
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — negating an access policy with three clauses
1.
The policy: access is granted when the account is active AND the device is enrolled AND the request comes from a managed network. Write it as a ∧ e ∧ m.
2.
Access is denied exactly when the policy fails: ¬(a ∧ e ∧ m).
3.
Apply De Morgan across all three: ¬(a ∧ e ∧ m) ≡ ¬a ∨ ¬e ∨ ¬m.
4.
Read it back: the account is inactive, or the device is not enrolled, or the network is unmanaged. Any one of the three is enough to deny.
5.
Sanity-check with a case. An active account on an enrolled device over a coffee-shop network: a = T, e = T, m = F. The original is T ∧ T ∧ F = F (denied), and the expanded form is F ∨ F ∨ T = T (denied). They agree. ✓
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — negating a nested quantified claim about a course catalogue
1.
The claim: every student has at least one course they are eligible to enrol in. With S(x) the students and E(x, y) \"student x is eligible for course y\", that is ∀x ∃y E(x, y).
2.
Negate the whole thing: ¬∀x ∃y E(x, y).
3.
Push the negation past the first quantifier — ∀ becomes ∃: ∃x ¬∃y E(x, y).
4.
Push it past the second — ∃ becomes ∀: ∃x ∀y ¬E(x, y).
5.
Read it back: there is a student who is eligible for no course at all. Each quantifier flips as the negation moves inward, and the predicate ends up negated.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
\"Not all servers are patched\" does not mean \"no server is patched\". ¬∀x P(x) is ∃x ¬P(x) — at least one fails — whereas \"none are patched\" is ∀x ¬P(x), a far stronger claim. The same error in De Morgan form is negating a conjunction into a conjunction: ¬(a ∧ e) is ¬a ∨ ¬e, never ¬a ∧ ¬e.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Negation is mechanical if you work outside in: every ∧ becomes ∨, every ∨ becomes ∧, every ∀ becomes ∃, every ∃ becomes ∀, and the innermost predicate is negated last. Order matters too: ∀x ∃y lets y depend on x (\"every ticket has some agent\"), while ∃y ∀x demands one y that works for all x (\"one agent handles every ticket\") and is the stronger claim.
📘 DEFINITION
The logical equivalence asked for most often is p → q ≡ ¬p ∨ q. A conditional is false only when p is true and q is false, and \"not p, or q\" fails in exactly that one case. Every implication can be rewritten as a disjunction this way, which is how conditionals are removed before converting a formula to CNF.

Equivalences tell you when two statements say the same thing. Rules of inference tell you when one statement legitimately follows from others — and that is the step from logic to proof, because a proof is nothing but a chain of these applied in order.

An argument is a list of premises followed by a conclusion. It is valid when the conclusion must be true whenever all the premises are true. Note what that does not say: validity is about the form, not about whether the premises are actually true. An argument can be valid and have a false conclusion, if it was fed false premises. It is sound only when it is both valid and its premises are genuinely true.

The rules you are expected to name

RulePremisesConclusion
Modus ponensp → q, and pq
Modus tollensp → q, and ¬q¬p
Hypothetical syllogismp → q, and q → rp → r
Disjunctive syllogismp ∨ q, and ¬pq
Additionpp ∨ q
Simplificationp ∧ qp
Conjunctionp, and qp ∧ q
Resolutionp ∨ q, and ¬p ∨ rq ∨ r

Two of these carry most of the exam weight. Modus ponens — \"the mode that affirms\" — takes a conditional and its hypothesis and concludes the consequent: if it rains the ground gets wet; it is raining; therefore the ground is wet. Modus tollens — \"the mode that denies\" — takes the conditional and the denial of the consequent: the ground is not wet, therefore it is not raining. That one works because it is the contrapositive from the previous lesson in action.

The two fallacies

Each of those two has an invalid look-alike, and questions are built on the pair.

FallacyLooks likeWhy it fails
Affirming the consequentp → q, and q, therefore pq could have another cause — the ground may be wet from a sprinkler
Denying the antecedentp → q, and ¬p, therefore ¬qsame reason — no rain does not mean dry ground

The way to keep them apart is to notice which part of the conditional the second premise touches. Affirm the hypothesis (p) and you are fine — that is modus ponens. Deny the conclusion (¬q) and you are fine — that is modus tollens. Affirm q or deny p and you have a fallacy.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — is this argument valid?
1.
Premises: \"If the server is down, the site is unreachable.\" The site is unreachable.
2.
Symbolise: p → q, and q. Conclusion offered: p — the server is down.
3.
Match it against the table: affirming q to conclude p is affirming the consequent.
4.
Verdict: invalid. The site could be unreachable for a different reason — a DNS failure, a network cut.

Checking validity with a truth table

When a rule name does not come to mind, validity can always be settled mechanically. Build the truth table for all the premises and the conclusion, then look only at the rows where every premise is true. If the conclusion is true in all of those rows, the argument is valid; a single row where the premises hold and the conclusion fails is a counterexample.

📘 DEFINITION

Argument: a set of premises together with a conclusion

Valid: the conclusion is true whenever all the premises are true — a property of the form

Sound: valid, and the premises are actually true

Modus ponens: from p → q and p, conclude q

Modus tollens: from p → q and ¬q, conclude ¬p

Hypothetical syllogism: from p → q and q → r, conclude p → r

Disjunctive syllogism: from p ∨ q and ¬p, conclude q

Affirming the consequent: the fallacy of concluding p from p → q and q

Denying the antecedent: the fallacy of concluding ¬q from p → q and ¬p

★ ON THE OA

Learn the two valid rules and their two fallacies as a set of four. Modus ponens: affirm p, conclude q. Modus tollens: deny q, conclude ¬p. Affirming q or denying p is a fallacy. Validity is about form only — a valid argument with false premises can have a false conclusion.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

Every proof technique in the next unit is one of these rules made explicit. Direct proof is a chain of modus ponens; contrapositive proof is modus tollens; proof by contradiction is the observation that a valid argument cannot lead from true premises to an absurdity.

The valid rules — and the two that imitate them

An argument is valid when the conclusion must follow from the premises. Validity is about shape, not about whether the statements are true: a valid argument from false premises is still valid.

📊 FIGURE — three rules that work, two that do not

The two red panels are worth memorising as errors, because they are the wrong answers on nearly every question in this section. Both mistake p → q for p ↔ q — they assume the arrow runs both ways, and it does not.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — spot the fallacy

\"If the server is down, the site is slow. The site is slow. Therefore the server is down.\"

Shape: p → q, q, ∴ p. That is affirming the consequent — invalid. The site could be slow for a dozen other reasons; the premise never claimed the server was the only cause.

Change the second premise to \"the site is not slow\" and the shape becomes p → q, ¬q, ∴ ¬p — modus tollens, which is valid.

RulePremisesConclusion
Modus ponensp → q, pq
Modus tollensp → q, ¬q¬p
Hypothetical syllogismp → q, q → rp → r
Disjunctive syllogismp ∨ q, ¬pq
Simplificationp ∧ qp
Conjunctionp, qp ∧ q
Additionpp ∨ q
Resolutionp ∨ q, ¬p ∨ rq ∨ r
🎯 EXAM TIP

To test an argument you are unsure of, build the truth table and look for a row where every premise is T and the conclusion is F. Find one and the argument is invalid; find none and it is valid. That single test replaces all the rule names.

An argument is a list of premises with a conclusion, and it is valid when the conclusion cannot be false while every premise is true. Validity is a property of the shape, not of the facts: an argument can be valid and still reach a false conclusion, if it was handed a false premise. Add true premises to a valid form and the argument is sound.

📊 FIGURE — a proof is a chain of named rules — and two shapes that only look like rules
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — is this incident argument valid?
1.
The premises: if the certificate has expired, the TLS handshake fails (c → h); if the handshake fails, the browser shows a warning (h → w); no warning was shown (¬w).
2.
Chain the first two with hypothetical syllogism: from c → h and h → w, conclude c → w.
3.
Now combine c → w with ¬w using modus tollens: conclude ¬c.
4.
Conclusion: the certificate has not expired. Every step is a named rule, so the argument is valid.
5.
Is it sound? Only if the premises are actually true — if some browsers suppress the warning, premise 2 is false and the conclusion is not supported, even though the form is fine.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — spotting the fallacy, and proving it with one row
1.
The claim: if the disk is full, the nightly backup fails. The backup failed. Therefore the disk is full.
2.
Symbolise: p → q, q, therefore p. The second premise affirms the consequent, not the hypothesis.
3.
To show invalidity, find one row where the premises are true and the conclusion is false. Take p = F, q = T.
4.
Check: p → q is F → T = T ✓. q is T ✓. The conclusion p is F ✗.
5.
That row is a counterexample, so the argument is invalid. Concretely: the backup failed because the network share was unmounted, and the disk had plenty of room.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
The two fallacies are told apart by which half of the conditional the second premise touches. Affirm the hypothesis (p) → modus ponens, valid. Deny the conclusion (¬q) → modus tollens, valid. Affirm the conclusion (q) → affirming the consequent, invalid. Deny the hypothesis (¬p) → denying the antecedent, invalid. Learning the four as a 2 × 2 grid is faster than learning them as sentences.
🎯 EXAM TIP
To show an argument is invalid you need exactly one row of the truth table in which every premise is true and the conclusion is false — you never have to build the whole table. To show it is valid, name the rule at each step instead; that is faster than a table and it is what \"which rule of inference\" questions are testing.
📘 DEFINITION
Reasoning with quantifiers — the four bridge rules. Propositional rules (modus ponens, disjunctive syllogism…) work on plain statements. To use them on quantified statements you first cross the bridge down to a named element, reason there, and cross back up.

UI — Universal Instantiation: from ∀x P(x), conclude P(c) for ANY name c. Always legal.
EI — Existential Instantiation: from ∃x P(x), conclude P(c) — but c must be a fresh name, never one already in use.
EG — Existential Generalization: from P(c), conclude ∃x P(x). Always legal.
UG — Universal Generalization: from P(c), conclude ∀x P(x) — ONLY when c was arbitrary, carrying no special assumptions.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Worked chain: ∀x (A(x) ∨ B(x)) and ∃x ¬B(x) — what follows?
  1. EI on the second premise: pick a fresh name c with ¬B(c).
  2. UI on the first premise at that same c: A(c) ∨ B(c).
  3. Disjunctive syllogism: A(c) ∨ B(c) with ¬B(c) leaves A(c).
  4. EG: from A(c), conclude ∃x A(x).

Why not ∀x A(x)? Take the domain {1, 2} with A = {1}, B = {2}: both premises hold, but A(2) is false. One countermodel kills the universal — checked mechanically over every model with domain size ≤ 4, ∃x A(x) survives all of them and ∀x A(x) does not.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Worked chain: universal modus ponens and tollens

From ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) and P(c): UI gives P(c) → Q(c); modus ponens gives Q(c).

From ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) and ¬Q(c): UI gives P(c) → Q(c); modus tollens gives ¬P(c).

Concrete: \"every prime > 2 is odd\" and \"31 is a prime > 2\" → 31 is odd. The universal supplies the rule; instantiation lets you fire it at a specific case.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Two ways these proofs go wrong. EI with a used name: from ∃x Tall(x) and ∃x Rich(x) you may NOT instantiate both to the same c — that invents one person who is tall and rich. Fresh name each time. UG from a special c: if c came from an EI step or carries any assumption, generalizing to ∀x is invalid — that is how \"one example proves the rule\" sneaks in.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Exam strategy for \"which is a valid conclusion\": instantiate down, reason propositionally, generalize up — and expect the honest answer to be an ∃ statement. A ∀ conclusion needs the premises to hold it for EVERY element, which one existential premise almost never gives you.

A proof is a chain of valid inferences from definitions and known results to a conclusion. What makes discrete maths proofs approachable is that almost all of them start from one of a handful of definitions, applied literally.

📐 The definitions almost every proof uses
Even
n = 2k for some integer k
Odd
n = 2k + 1 for some integer k
Divides (a | b)
b = a·k for some integer k
Rational
n = a/b with a, b integers and b ≠ 0

A direct proof assumes the hypothesis is true and works forward to the conclusion using those definitions and ordinary algebra. Its shape never varies: state what you are assuming, translate it with a definition, do the algebra, and translate back into the language of the conclusion.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: the sum of two even integers is even
1.
Assume m and n are even.
2.
Translate using the definition: m = 2j and n = 2k, for some integers j and k.
3.
Compute: m + n = 2j + 2k = 2(j + k).
4.
Recognise the form: j + k is an integer, so m + n has the form 2 × (an integer).
5.
Translate back: by the definition of even, m + n is even. ∎

Step 4 is the one people skip and the one that carries the proof. It is not enough to reach 2(j + k) — you must say that j + k is an integer, because \"even\" means two times an integer, and that is the condition being satisfied.

Notice also the use of different letters. Writing m = 2k and n = 2k would prove only that a number plus itself is even, which is a much weaker claim. Each arbitrary quantity gets its own name.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: if n is odd then n² is odd
1.
Assume n is odd, so n = 2k + 1 for some integer k.
2.
Square it: n² = (2k + 1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1.
3.
Force the form 2(something) + 1: n² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1.
4.
Conclude: 2k² + 2k is an integer, so n² is odd. ∎

Step 3 is the whole technique: you already have the answer, and the work is rearranging it into the shape the definition demands. When a direct proof stalls, it is nearly always because the target form has not been written down first.

📘 DEFINITION

Theorem: a statement proved true

Proof: a valid chain of reasoning from premises and definitions to a conclusion

Direct proof: assume the hypothesis, derive the conclusion by definitions and algebra

Lemma: a smaller result proved in order to support a larger one

Corollary: a result that follows immediately from a theorem just proved

Conjecture: a statement believed true but not yet proved

∎ / QED: the marker that a proof is complete

★ ON THE OA

A direct proof assumes the hypothesis and derives the conclusion using definitions and algebra. The definitions you must have memorised are: an even integer is 2k, an odd integer is 2k + 1, with k an integer. Most direct-proof questions are testing whether you applied those literally.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Write the target form before you start manipulating. If you must end at \"2 × integer\", you know to aim for a factor of 2 — and that turns the algebra from exploration into a goal you are steering toward.

What a direct proof looks like on the page

A direct proof of p → q assumes p and walks to q. Almost all the difficulty is in one step: replacing a word with its definition, so that algebra becomes possible.

📊 FIGURE — the five moves, on \"if n is even then n + 2 is even\"
WordDefinition you substitute
n is evenn = 2k for some integer k
n is oddn = 2k + 1 for some integer k
a divides bb = a·k for some integer k
n is rationaln = a/b for integers a, b with b ≠ 0
A ⊆ Bevery x ∈ A satisfies x ∈ B
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

\"For some integer k\" is doing real work. When you assume two things are even you must write n = 2k and m = 2j — using k for both secretly asserts they are the same number, and the proof collapses. A grader looks for exactly that.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: the sum of two odd integers is even

Let m and n be odd. By definition m = 2j + 1 and n = 2k + 1 for some integers j and k — different letters.

m + n = (2j + 1) + (2k + 1) = 2j + 2k + 2 = 2(j + k + 1).

j + k + 1 is an integer, so m + n is 2 × (an integer), which is the definition of even. ∎

Almost every direct proof in this course runs on the same five moves, and the reason it feels mechanical is that it is mechanical: a definition converts the hypothesis into algebra, ordinary algebra rearranges it, and the same definition read backwards converts the result into the conclusion.

📊 FIGURE — the shape of a direct proof, with the step everyone skips marked
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a depot ships in multiples of 7 — prove the combined load is too
1.
Claim. If 7 | m and 7 | n, then 7 | (m + n).
2.
Assume the hypothesis: 7 divides m and 7 divides n.
3.
Translate with the definition of \"divides\": m = 7j for some integer j, and n = 7k for some integer k. Two quantities, two letters.
4.
Algebra: m + n = 7j + 7k = 7(j + k).
5.
Recognise the form. j and k are integers, so j + k is an integer, and m + n is 7 × (an integer).
6.
Translate back: by the definition of divisibility, 7 | (m + n). ∎ A 21-crate load and a 35-crate load make 56 = 7 × 8, but that single check is an illustration, not the proof.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: if a file size n is a multiple of 4, then n² is a multiple of 16
1.
Assume n is a multiple of 4. By definition, n = 4k for some integer k.
2.
Square it: n² = (4k)² = 16k².
3.
Force the target form. \"Multiple of 16\" means 16 × (an integer), so write n² = 16 · (k²).
4.
Close the gap: k is an integer, so k² is an integer.
5.
Conclude: n² = 16 × (an integer), so n² is a multiple of 16. ∎ Check with n = 12: n² = 144 = 16 × 9. ✓
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Two habits sink direct proofs. Reusing a letter — writing m = 7k and n = 7k — silently assumes the two quantities are equal, so the proof only covers a special case. And stopping at the algebra: reaching 7(j + k) is not the end, because the definition demands 7 times an integer, and saying \"j + k is an integer\" is the sentence that satisfies it. Testing examples, however many, is never a proof of a \"for all\" claim.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Write the target form down first. If the conclusion is \"is odd\", write 2(?) + 1 at the bottom of the page before you start; the whole proof then becomes the job of manoeuvring your expression into that shape. Nearly every direct proof that stalls has stalled because the goal form was never written down.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Direct proof: divisibility of a memory block

A memory block of size n is a multiple of 4. Show n² is a multiple of 16.

  1. \"n is a multiple of 4\" means n = 4k for some integer k. Introduce the variable rather than arguing about examples.
  2. Square it: n² = (4k)² = 16k².
  3. Write it in the required shape: n² = 16(k²), and k² is an integer.
  4. That is exactly the definition of \"multiple of 16\", so the proof is complete.

The last step is the one graders look for. Producing 16k² is not enough on its own — you must say that k² is an integer, since that is what makes 16k² a multiple of 16.

Some statements resist a direct attack. \"√2 is irrational\" gives you nothing to expand, because it says what something is not. Two indirect techniques handle these, and both work by proving something logically equivalent to what was asked.

Proof by contrapositive

This one rests entirely on the equivalence from 1.2: p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p. So instead of proving \"if p then q\", you prove \"if not q then not p\" — a different-looking statement that is guaranteed to be just as true.

It is worth reaching for whenever the negation of the conclusion is more concrete than the conclusion itself. \"n² is even\" gives you nothing to substitute; \"n is odd\" gives you 2k + 1 immediately.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: if n² is even then n is even
1.
Direct is awkward — \"n² is even\" means n² = 2k, and taking a square root leads nowhere.
2.
Switch to the contrapositive: if n is odd, then n² is odd.
3.
Assume n is odd: n = 2k + 1.
4.
Then n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd.
5.
The contrapositive is proved, so the original statement is proved. ∎

Proof by contradiction

Here you assume the statement is false and show that the assumption forces an absurdity — something that contradicts a known fact or contradicts itself. Since the assumption cannot be true, the statement must be.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: √2 is irrational
1.
Assume the opposite: √2 is rational, so √2 = a/b with a and b integers, b ≠ 0, and the fraction in lowest terms (no common factor).
2.
Square both sides: 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b².
3.
So a² is even, and by the previous result a is even. Write a = 2c.
4.
Substitute: (2c)² = 2b² → 4c² = 2b² → b² = 2c², so b is even too.
5.
But a and b are both even — they share the factor 2, contradicting \"lowest terms\".
6.
The assumption is impossible, so √2 is irrational. ∎

Step 1 does two things and both matter: it negates the claim, and it adds the \"lowest terms\" condition. That condition is what the contradiction eventually violates, so the proof does not work without it.

TechniqueAssumeAim forBest when
Directpqthe hypothesis gives you something to expand
Contrapositive¬q¬pthe negated conclusion is more concrete than the conclusion
Contradictionp ∧ ¬qan absurditythe claim is a negative — irrational, infinite, no solution
Counterexample—one failing caseyou want to disprove a universal claim

The last row is the cheapest technique in mathematics and is examined. To disprove \"every prime is odd\" you do not argue — you produce 2 and stop. One counterexample defeats any ∀ statement.

📘 DEFINITION

Proof by contrapositive: proving ¬q → ¬p, which is logically equivalent to p → q

Proof by contradiction: assuming the statement false and deriving an absurdity

Indirect proof: the umbrella term for both of the above

Counterexample: a single case disproving a universal statement

Rational number: expressible as a/b with a, b integers and b ≠ 0

Irrational number: a real number that is not rational

★ ON THE OA

Contradiction assumes the statement is false and derives an absurdity. Contrapositive proves ¬q → ¬p, which is logically equivalent to p → q and is often easier. To disprove a \"for all\" claim, one counterexample is a complete proof.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Contrapositive and converse are different, and swapping them is the standard error. The contrapositive of p → q is ¬q → ¬p and is always equivalent; the converse is q → p and is not.

Two indirect proofs, and how to tell them apart

📊 FIGURE — contrapositive assumes one thing; contradiction assumes the opposite of the goal

They feel similar and the exam relies on that. The distinction: contrapositive only ever applies to an implication, and you end by deriving ¬p. Contradiction applies to any statement at all, and you end by deriving an absurdity such as \"n is both even and odd\" or \"1 < 0\".

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — contrapositive — if n² is even then n is even

Direct is awkward: knowing n² is even does not immediately factor. Take the contrapositive instead — if n is odd then n² is odd.

Assume n is odd, so n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. Then n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is 2·(integer) + 1 — odd. ✓

Having proved the contrapositive, the original is proved, because the two are equivalent.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — contradiction — √2 is irrational

Assume the opposite: √2 = a/b in lowest terms, so a and b share no common factor.

Then 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b² — a² is even, so a is even, so a = 2m. Substituting: 4m² = 2b², so b² = 2m² — so b is even too.

But a and b were in lowest terms and now both are even. That is impossible, so the assumption fails and √2 is irrational. ∎

Two techniques for the statements a direct attack cannot reach. They are easy to confuse because both begin by negating something — the difference is what gets negated. Contrapositive negates both halves and swaps them, then proves that directly. Contradiction negates the goal itself and hunts for an absurdity.

📊 FIGURE — the two indirect techniques side by side
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — contrapositive — a checksum claim
1.
Claim. If 5n + 3 is even, then n is odd.
2.
Direct is awkward: \"5n + 3 is even\" gives 5n + 3 = 2m, and solving for n produces a fraction.
3.
Switch to the contrapositive: if n is even, then 5n + 3 is odd. (Negate both halves and swap them.)
4.
Assume n is even: n = 2k for some integer k.
5.
Compute: 5n + 3 = 10k + 3 = 2(5k + 1) + 1.
6.
5k + 1 is an integer, so 5n + 3 has the form 2 × (integer) + 1 and is odd. The contrapositive is proved, and by the equivalence p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p, so is the claim. ∎
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — contradiction — a load-balancing claim
1.
Claim. Three servers together handle 60 requests in a minute. Then at least one server handled 20 or more.
2.
Assume the opposite: every server handled 19 or fewer. (The negation of \"at least one is ≥ 20\" is \"all are ≤ 19\".)
3.
Follow it through: the total is at most 19 + 19 + 19 = 57.
4.
Collide with a known fact: the total is 60, and 60 > 57. The assumption forces 60 ≤ 57, which is false.
5.
The assumption cannot hold, so at least one server handled 20 or more. ∎ Note that the proof names no particular server — that is typical of contradiction, which shows something exists without exhibiting it.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Negating the goal is where marks are lost. The negation of \"at least one is ≥ 20\" is \"all are ≤ 19\", not \"one is ≤ 19\". And the contrapositive is not the converse: from \"if p then q\" the contrapositive is \"if not q then not p\" — swap and negate. Swapping without negating gives the converse, which is not equivalent and proves nothing.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Choose by looking at the two negations. If ¬q is more concrete than q — \"n is odd\" gives you 2k + 1 to substitute, while \"n² is even\" gives you nothing — use the contrapositive. If the claim is a negative or a non-existence (\"irrational\", \"no largest\", \"infinitely many\"), use contradiction, because assuming the opposite is the only way to get an equation to work with.

Direct proof handles one statement. Mathematical induction proves infinitely many at once — every statement of the form \"for all integers n ≥ 1, P(n)\". It is the right tool whenever a claim is indexed by n: a summation formula, a divisibility claim, an inequality.

The image that makes it work is a line of dominoes. Knock over the first one, and guarantee that each domino knocks over the next, and every domino falls — however many there are. The proof has exactly those two parts, and both are required.

PartWhat you doDomino
Base caseverify P(1) directlypush the first domino
Inductive stepassume P(k), prove P(k + 1)each one topples the next

The assumption in the second part has a name — the inductive hypothesis — and it is not circular reasoning, which is the objection everyone raises first. You are not assuming what you want to prove. You are proving a conditional: if it holds at k, then it holds at k + 1. Combined with the base case, that chains upward through every integer.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2
1.
Base case, n = 1. Left side = 1. Right side = 1(2)/2 = 1. They match. ✓
2.
Inductive hypothesis. Assume it holds at n = k: 1 + 2 + … + k = k(k + 1)/2.
3.
Goal. Show it holds at k + 1, i.e. that the sum equals (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.
4.
Build from the hypothesis. The sum to k + 1 is [sum to k] + (k + 1) = k(k + 1)/2 + (k + 1).
5.
Algebra. Factor out (k + 1): (k + 1)[k/2 + 1] = (k + 1)(k + 2)/2.
6.
That is exactly the goal, so P(k) → P(k + 1). With the base case, the formula holds for all n ≥ 1. ∎

Step 4 is where every induction proof is won or lost: you must use the inductive hypothesis, substituting it in rather than re-deriving the sum. If your proof never mentions the assumption, it is not an induction proof.

The base case is not a formality either. The claim \"n² + n + 41 is prime for all n ≥ 0\" survives an inductive-step argument that looks plausible and fails at n = 41. Both halves have to hold.

Strong induction

Strong induction changes the hypothesis: instead of assuming only P(k), you assume P(1) through P(k) all hold, and prove P(k + 1) from any of them. It is the version needed when the case you are proving depends on a much earlier case rather than the immediately previous one — proving every integer above 1 has a prime factorisation, for instance, where n = a·b sends you to two smaller factors.

📘 DEFINITION

Mathematical induction: proving P(n) for all n ≥ base by proving P(base) and P(k) → P(k+1)

Base case: the smallest value, verified directly

Inductive step: the proof that P(k) implies P(k + 1)

Inductive hypothesis: the assumption that P(k) holds

Strong induction: assuming P(1) through P(k) rather than P(k) alone

Well-ordering principle: every non-empty set of positive integers has a least element — the principle induction rests on

★ ON THE OA

Induction has exactly two required parts: (1) the base case P(1), and (2) the inductive step — assume P(k), prove P(k + 1). A question showing a proof with one part missing is asking you to spot which. The assumption is called the inductive hypothesis.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Write the k + 1 target on the page before doing any algebra. Induction is a matter of steering the expression toward a form you already wrote down, and it is far harder without the destination in front of you.

Why induction works

📊 FIGURE — the two things you must prove, and why they are enough

You never check infinitely many cases. You check one case and one implication, and the implication does the rest of the work forever.

PartWhat you proveWhat it buys you
Base caseThe statement holds for n = 1 (or whatever the smallest n is)The first domino falls
Inductive hypothesisASSUME it holds for some n = kNot a proof — an assumption you are allowed to make
Inductive stepUsing that assumption, prove it holds for n = k + 1Every domino knocks over the next
ConclusionTherefore it holds for all n ≥ 1They all fall
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — prove 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n+1)/2

Base case, n = 1. Left side = 1. Right side = 1(2)/2 = 1. They match. ✓

Inductive hypothesis. Assume 1 + 2 + … + k = k(k+1)/2 for some k ≥ 1.

Inductive step. Show it for k + 1. Start from the left side and split off the last term — this is the move that makes the assumption usable:

1 + 2 + … + k + (k+1)
  = [k(k+1)/2] + (k+1)   ← the bracket is the hypothesis
  = (k+1)[k/2 + 1]
  = (k+1)(k+2)/2

And (k+1)(k+2)/2 is exactly the formula with n replaced by k+1. ✓

Conclusion. By induction the formula holds for all n ≥ 1.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The inductive step must use the hypothesis. A \"proof\" that reaches the k+1 case without ever substituting the assumed k case has proved nothing — that is the most common way an induction answer is marked wrong. In the worked example the substitution happens on the second line; if you cannot point at that line in your own work, you have not done induction.

Induction proves infinitely many statements at once, and the place it is won or lost is a single line: the point where the inductive hypothesis is substituted in rather than re-derived. Everything else is bookkeeping.

📊 FIGURE — the inductive step, with the substitution marked
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a lecture hall — row i has 2i seats; prove the first n rows hold n(n + 1) seats
1.
Base case, n = 1. Row 1 has 2 seats. The formula gives 1(1 + 1) = 2. They match. ✓
2.
Inductive hypothesis. Assume that for some k ≥ 1 the first k rows hold k(k + 1) seats.
3.
Goal. Show the first k + 1 rows hold (k + 1)(k + 2) seats.
4.
Build from the hypothesis. Seats in the first k + 1 rows = (seats in the first k rows) + (seats in row k + 1) = k(k + 1) + 2(k + 1).
5.
Factor: (k + 1)[k + 2] = (k + 1)(k + 2). That is exactly the goal.
6.
Base case plus inductive step, so the formula holds for every n ≥ 1. ∎ Spot-check n = 4: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20 and 4 × 5 = 20. ✓
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a divisibility claim — prove 3 divides 4ⁿ − 1 for every n ≥ 1
1.
Base case, n = 1. 4¹ − 1 = 3, and 3 | 3. ✓
2.
Inductive hypothesis. Assume 3 | (4ᵏ − 1), i.e. 4ᵏ − 1 = 3m for some integer m.
3.
Goal. Show 3 | (4ᵏ⁺¹ − 1).
4.
Rewrite so the hypothesis appears: 4ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 4 · 4ᵏ − 1 = 4(4ᵏ − 1) + 3.
5.
Substitute: = 4(3m) + 3 = 3(4m + 1), and 4m + 1 is an integer.
6.
So 3 divides 4ᵏ⁺¹ − 1, and the claim holds for all n ≥ 1. ∎ Check n = 3: 4³ − 1 = 63 = 3 × 21. ✓
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Two failures, both fatal. Not using the hypothesis: if you compute the k + 1 case from scratch, you have proved one more case, not the theorem — the tell-tale sign is that the assumed formula never appears in your algebra. And skipping the base case: \"n² + n + 41 is prime\" survives a plausible-sounding step and fails outright at n = 41. Both halves are required, and the base case is not always n = 1 — \"n! > 2ⁿ\" starts at n = 4.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Write the goal for k + 1 before doing any algebra: substitute k + 1 into the formula and simplify it, so you know the target expression you are steering towards. Then start from the k-case, add the next term, and drive it to that target. If a claim at n depends on a much earlier case rather than the previous one — coin or postage problems, for instance — use strong induction, assuming everything from the base up to k.
