A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers, described by its dimensions: an m × n matrix has m rows and n columns, always stated in that order. The entry in row i and column j is written aij, and the row index always comes first.

TypeConditionExample
Squaresame number of rows and columns (n × n)2×2, 3×3
Row matrix / vectora single row (1 × n)[1 2 3]
Column matrix / vectora single column (m × 1)[1; 2; 3]
Zero matrixevery entry 0the additive identity
Identity (I)1s on the main diagonal, 0s elsewhere; squarethe multiplicative identity
Diagonalnon-zero entries only on the main diagonal—
Symmetricequal to its own transpose (aij = aji)—
Upper / lower triangularall zeros below / above the main diagonal—

Addition and subtraction

Both are done entry by entry, and both require the two matrices to have identical dimensions. If the sizes differ, the sum is not merely awkward — it is undefined, and that is a favourite exam trap.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — addition

Both matrices are 2 × 3 (two branches, three products), so they add entry by entry:

12894478613062+143885110211758=27118298188247120

But a 2 × 3 and a 3 × 2 cannot be added at all — no entry has a partner in the same position:

128944786130622 × 3+128869413047623 × 2=UNDEFINED

Scalar multiplication

Multiplying by a single number multiplies every entry by it, and it has no dimension restriction at all.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — scalar multiplication

Hours worked, multiplied by an £18 hourly rate — the scalar reaches every entry:

18 ·34274122=612486738396

And it reaches negative entries too: −4 · 25−13−817 = −1005232−68

The transpose

The transpose AT swaps rows and columns: row 1 becomes column 1. An m × n matrix transposes to an n × m matrix, so a 2×3 becomes a 3×2. A matrix equal to its own transpose is symmetric, which requires it to be square.

Addition obeys the rules you would expect — it is commutative and associative, the zero matrix is the identity, and (A + B)T = AT + BT. Multiplication, in the next lesson, is where the surprises are.

Why dimensions dominate this chapter

Almost every matrix question begins with a dimension check, and a surprising number end there. Addition requires identical dimensions; multiplication requires the inner dimensions to match; only square matrices can have a determinant or an inverse; and the transpose swaps the dimensions round. Writing the dimensions above each matrix before starting is the single most effective habit in this chapter.

The habit also catches questions designed to be answered \"undefined\". An exam that offers a numeric answer for (2×3) + (3×2) is testing whether you checked, and the numbers in the options exist only to look plausible.

Where matrices come from

A matrix is a compact way of writing a table of related numbers, and the three uses in this course are worth naming. As a system of equations — the coefficients of several linear equations, which is 4. As a relation or graph — the adjacency matrices of Units 6 and 7, where entries are 0 or 1. And as a transformation — a rule mapping vectors to vectors, which is what makes the inverse meaningful as \"undo\".

The main diagonal

The main diagonal of a matrix runs from the top-left to the bottom-right — the entries where the row index equals the column index. It is the diagonal every other definition in this chapter refers to: the identity matrix has 1s on it, a diagonal matrix has non-zeros only on it, a symmetric matrix mirrors across it, and triangular matrices are defined by which side of it is zero.

📘 DEFINITION

Matrix: a rectangular array of numbers

Dimensions (m × n): rows by columns, always in that order

Entry aᵢⱼ: the value in row i, column j

Square matrix: equal numbers of rows and columns

Identity matrix (I): 1s on the main diagonal, 0s elsewhere

Zero matrix: every entry zero

Transpose (Aᵀ): rows and columns interchanged

Symmetric matrix: equal to its own transpose

Scalar multiplication: multiplying every entry by a single number

★ ON THE OA

Matrix addition requires identical dimensions and is done entry by entry. If the sizes differ the sum is undefined — that is the trap. Scalar multiplication has no such restriction and touches every entry.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Dimensions are always rows × columns. A 2×3 matrix has two rows and three columns, and reading it the other way makes every subsequent multiplication check come out wrong.

Naming a matrix by its shape

📊 FIGURE — the named matrix types
NameConditionNote
Squarerows = columnsonly square matrices have inverses or determinants
Identity I1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhereAI = IA = A — the multiplicative identity
Zero matrixevery entry 0A + 0 = A
Diagonalnon-zeros only on the main diagonalmultiplying diagonals just multiplies entrywise
Upper/lower triangularzeros below / above the diagonalthe determinant is the product of the diagonal
Transpose Aᵀrows and columns swapped(m×n) becomes (n×m)
SymmetricA = Aᵀmust be square; mirrors across the diagonal

Addition and scalar multiplication work entrywise and require identical dimensions — you cannot add a 2×3 to a 3×2. Multiplication is the only operation with the awkward rule, needing the inner dimensions to agree.

Anatomy of a matrix — rows first, then columns

A matrix is just a table with the words stripped off. Keep the words in your head while you learn to read one. The Riverside and Hillcrest branches of a bakery each sold sourdough loaves, bagels and croissants on Monday:

C₁C₂C₃R₁R₂12894478613062R₁ = Riverside, R₂ = Hillcrest · C₁ = sourdough, C₂ = bagels, C₃ = croissants

Two branches means two rows. Three products means three columns. So this is a 2 × 3 matrix — and the dimensions are quoted rows-first, every single time. A 2 × 3 matrix is short and wide; a 3 × 2 matrix is tall and narrow. They are different shapes and they are not interchangeable.

📊 FIGURE — anatomy of a matrix — where aᵢⱼ lives
📘 DEFINITION

Dimensions (m × n): m rows by n columns. Rows first — the same order as the subscripts.

Entry aᵢⱼ: the value where row i crosses column j. Row index first, column index second.

How to say it aloud: “a-two-three” means “go down to row 2, then across to column 3.”

You are asked for…Where you lookValue here
a₁₁row 1, column 1 — Riverside sourdough128
a₁₃row 1, column 3 — Riverside croissants47
a₂₁row 2, column 1 — Hillcrest sourdough86
a₂₂row 2, column 2 — Hillcrest bagels130
a₃₁row 3 — there is no row 3does not exist

Notice that a₁₃ = 47 and a₂₁ = 86 are wildly different numbers. That is on purpose. If a matrix is filled with 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 then reading the wrong way round still gives you a plausible answer and you never find out you were confused. Real data tells you immediately.

Adding matrices — same shape, entry by entry

Addition is the easy operation: line the two tables up and add each pair of numbers that sit in the same position. Both matrices must have identical dimensions, because otherwise some entry has nothing to pair with.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Monday sales + Tuesday sales

Tuesday’s figures came in for the same two branches and the same three products:

12894478613062Monday+143885110211758Tuesday=27118298188247120two-day total

Position by position:

a₁₁: 128 + 143 = 271    a₁₂: 94 + 88 = 182    a₁₃: 47 + 51 = 98
a₂₁: 86 + 102 = 188    a₂₂: 130 + 117 = 247    a₂₃: 62 + 58 = 120

The answer is still 2 × 3, because addition never changes the shape. And the numbers mean something: Hillcrest sold 247 bagels over the two days.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — subtraction — what is left on the shelf

The bakery opened Monday with this much stock, and sold Monday’s figures out of it. Subtraction is the same rule with a minus sign:

310240150295280165opening stock−12894478613062sold Monday=182146103209150103left on the shelf

Riverside bagels: 240 − 94 = 146  (row 1, column 2)
Hillcrest sourdough: 295 − 86 = 209  (row 2, column 1)

Note how the two calculations use different rows and different columns. Saying “row 1, column 2” out loud before you reach for a number is the habit that fixes this whole chapter.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — when addition is undefined

The bakery matrix is 2 × 3. A supplier sends a delivery note laid out the other way round — three products down the side, two branches across — which is 3 × 2:

128944786130622 × 3+128869413047623 × 2=UNDEFINED

These hold the same information, but they are not the same shape, so there is no entry-by-entry pairing to do. 2 × 3 plus 3 × 2 is not zero, not an error in the numbers — it simply does not exist.

Scalar multiplication — one number touches every entry

Multiplying a matrix by a single number (a scalar) multiplies every entry by it. There is no dimension rule at all, because nothing has to pair up.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — hours worked × hourly rate

Two shop assistants, two weeks, hours worked. Everyone is paid £18 an hour, so the wage bill is 18 times the hours matrix:

18 ·C₁C₂R₁R₂34274122hours: R = assistant, C = week=C₁C₂R₁R₂612486738396pay in £

18 × 34 = 612    18 × 27 = 486
18 × 41 = 738    18 × 22 = 396

Assistant 2 in week 1 worked 41 hours — row 2, column 1 — and earned £738.

The transpose — the table turned on its side

The transpose Aᵀ writes each row as a column. Row 1 becomes column 1, row 2 becomes column 2, and an m × n matrix becomes n × m.

A =128944786130622 × 3 — row 1 tinted→ Aᵀ =128869413047623 × 2 — that row is now column 1

Read it as a table and it makes sense: the bakery data has branches down the side and products across the top; the transpose has products down the side and branches across the top. Same numbers, axes swapped. A matrix that equals its own transpose is symmetric — a driving-distance table between towns is the classic example, because the distance from Ashford to Belton equals the distance back.

Named typeWhat makes it thatA realistic instance
Square (n × n)as many rows as columnsa 4 × 4 table of drive times between 4 depots
Row matrix (1 × n)a single rowone branch’s sales across 3 products
Column matrix (m × 1)a single columnone product’s sales across 3 branches
Zero matrixevery entry 0a closed branch: sold nothing all week — A + 0 = A
Identity I1s down the main diagonal, 0s elsewherethe “leave it alone” matrix — A·I = A
Diagonalnon-zeros only on the main diagonala price list applied product-by-product, no mixing
SymmetricA = Aᵀ, so aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢa distance table — always square
Upper triangularall zeros below the main diagonalthe shape row-reduction drives a system into

The main diagonal runs top-left to bottom-right: the entries a₁₁, a₂₂, a₃₃ … where the row number and the column number are the same. It is the only place a row index and a column index agree, which is why so many definitions are phrased around it.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Rows are horizontal; columns are vertical. Dimensions are rows × columns. A 2 × 3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns — it is wider than it is tall. Reading it as “2 columns, 3 rows” makes every later dimension check come out backwards, so a multiplication that is genuinely undefined will look fine to you and one that works will look impossible.

The second half of the same mistake is aᵢⱼ. The row index always comes first: a₃₂ is row 3, column 2 — not column 3, row 2. If a question offers you both numbers as options, it is testing exactly this.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Before doing any arithmetic, write the dimensions above each matrix — “2×3” and “2×3”. For addition and subtraction they must match exactly; if they do not, the answer is “undefined” and you are already finished. Several exam items are pure dimension checks with plausible numeric options attached purely to tempt you into computing something.

Scalar multiplication has no such restriction and never changes the shape, so 5 · (a 2 × 7 matrix) is a 2 × 7 matrix. Transposing does change the shape: m × n becomes n × m.

📘 DEFINITION
Equality of matrices is stricter than it looks: A = B requires the same dimensions and every corresponding entry equal. Two matrices holding the same numbers in a different shape — 2×3 against 3×2 — are not equal, and are not even comparable.

Matrix multiplication is not entry by entry, and that is the first thing to unlearn. Each entry of the product is a dot product — a row of the first matrix combined with a column of the second.

Before computing anything, check that the product is defined. A · B requires the number of columns of A to equal the number of rows of B. Writing the dimensions side by side makes it visible: the inner numbers must match, and the outer numbers give the result's size.

(m × n) · (n × p) → m × p

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — checking dimensions

Only the inner pair has to match. The outer pair is the answer’s shape:

ProductInner numbersDefined?Shape of the answer
(2 × 3) · (3 × 4)3 and 3 — matchYes2 × 4
(2 × 3) · (2 × 3)3 and 2 — differNo — undefined—
(3 × 1) · (1 × 3)1 and 1 — matchYes3 × 3
(1 × 3) · (3 × 1)3 and 3 — matchYes1 × 1 — a single number
(4 × 4) · (4 × 4)4 and 4 — matchYes4 × 4

Notice rows 3 and 4: the same two matrices in the other order give a 3 × 3 and a 1 × 1. Order is not a detail.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — compute a 2×2 product
1.
A = 1234 and B = 5678. Both 2×2, so the product is 2×2.
2.
Entry (1,1) = row 1 of A · column 1 of B = 1·5 + 2·7 = 19.
3.
Entry (1,2) = row 1 · column 2 = 1·6 + 2·8 = 22.
4.
Entry (2,1) = row 2 · column 1 = 3·5 + 4·7 = 43.
5.
Entry (2,2) = row 2 · column 2 = 3·6 + 4·8 = 50.
6.
A·B = 19224350.

The rhythm is always \"row of the first, column of the second\", and the position of the entry tells you which: entry (i, j) uses row i and column j. Saying that aloud while computing prevents the most common slip.

What matrix multiplication does not do

Non-commutativity is the property the exam tests most. Multiplying the same two matrices in the other order usually gives a different answer, and when the matrices are not square it often gives no answer at all, because the inner dimensions no longer match.

Multiplication by the identity matrix leaves a matrix unchanged, which is what makes I the multiplicative identity and sets up the definition of an inverse in the next lesson.

📘 DEFINITION

Matrix product: defined when the columns of the first equal the rows of the second

Dot product: the sum of the pairwise products of a row and a column

Inner / outer dimensions: the inner pair must match; the outer pair gives the result size

Non-commutative: A·B and B·A are generally different

Identity matrix: A · I = I · A = A

★ ON THE OA

A·B is defined only when A's columns = B's rows: (m×n)(n×p) → m×p. Each entry is a row-by-column dot product. It is not commutative — A·B ≠ B·A in general.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Write the two dimension pairs next to each other before computing anything. If the inner numbers differ, the answer is \"undefined\" and no arithmetic is needed — that alone is a complete answer to several exam items.

Row times column

📊 FIGURE — Matrix multiplication = rows · columns
Entry (1,1) of the product comes from row 1 of A (indigo) paired with column 1 of B (green): multiply matching positions and add. Inner dimensions must match — (2×3)·(3×2) works and yields a 2×2 result.
📘 DEFINITION

To multiply A (m×n) by B (n×p) the inner dimensions must match. The result is m×p. Entry (i, j) of the product is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — multiply a 2×3 by a 3×2

A courier’s two vans, carrying small / medium / large parcels; B gives each parcel size’s weight in kg and its handling fee in £.

A =14922617112 × 3B =32751293 × 2

Shapes: (2 × 3)(3 × 2) → the 3s match, so the product is 2 × 2.

(1,1) = 14·3 + 9·7 + 22·12 = 369    total kg in van 1
(1,2) = 14·2 + 9·5 + 22·9  = 271    total fee for van 1
(2,1) = 6·3 + 17·7 + 11·12 = 269    total kg in van 2
(2,2) = 6·2 + 17·5 + 11·9  = 196    total fee for van 2

AB ≠ BA in general — matrix multiplication is not commutative, and often BA is not even defined. Here BA would be (3×2)(2×3) = 3×3, a different size entirely. Assuming you can swap them is the fastest way to lose the mark.

Where each entry of the product comes from

Matrix multiplication is the one operation that is not done entry by entry, and that is the thing to unlearn first. Each entry of the product is a whole dot product: you take a row of the left matrix, a column of the right matrix, multiply them position by position, and add.

The position of the answer tells you which row and which column to use: entry (i, j) of the product is row i of the first matrix dotted with column j of the second. Say that out loud as you compute and the row/column confusion disappears.

📊 FIGURE — one entry of the product = one row · one column
📘 DEFINITION

When it is defined: A·B needs the number of columns of A to equal the number of rows of B. Write (m × n) · (n × p): the inner numbers must match, and the outer numbers give the answer’s size, m × p.

Entry (i, j): aᵢ₁b₁ⱼ + aᵢ₂b₂ⱼ + … — row i across, column j down.

Worked example 1 — parcels, weight and handling fees

A courier runs two vans. Matrix A counts how many small, medium and large parcels each van is carrying. Matrix B holds, for each parcel size, its weight in kilograms and its handling fee in pounds.

A =C₁C₂C₃R₁R₂1492261711R = van, C = small / medium / largeB =C₁C₂R₁R₂R₃3275129R = small / medium / large, C = kg / fee

Shape check first. A is 2 × 3 and B is 3 × 2. The inner numbers are 3 and 3, so the product exists, and the outer numbers say it is 2 × 2 — one row per van, one column per quantity (total kilograms, total fee). That interpretation is a useful sanity check on its own.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — all four entries of A·B

Entry (1,1) — van 1’s total weight. Row 1 of A, column 1 of B:

1492261711·3275129→14·2 + 9·5 + 22·9 = 28 + 45 + 198 = 271

Entry (2,1) — van 2’s total weight. Row 2 now:

1492261711·3275129→6·3 + 17·7 + 11·12 = 18 + 119 + 132 = 269

Entry (2,2) — van 2’s total fee.

Van 1 is carrying 369 kg and will be billed £271. Every number in the answer is a plausible weight or price, which is a further check that you walked the right row and the right column.

Worked example 2 — three shops, three lines, two money columns

A retailer with three shops sold jackets, boots and gloves last week. A second matrix holds the retail price and the wholesale cost of each line.

Shop 2 took £6,636 and the stock it sold cost £4,024 — a gross margin of £2,612. The whole trading summary came out of one multiplication.

Order matters: A·B is not B·A

With ordinary numbers 7 × 4 and 4 × 7 are the same. With matrices they are usually different, and often only one of them is even defined. Two 2 × 2 matrices where both products exist:

A =6215B =4372

(1,1) = 6·4 + 2·7 = 24 + 14 = 38    (1,2) = 6·3 + 2·2 = 18 + 4 = 22
(2,1) = 1·4 + 5·7 = 4 + 35 = 39    (2,2) = 1·3 + 5·2 = 3 + 10 = 13

Same two matrices, same sizes, completely different answers. There is not a single entry in common.

With the courier matrices it is worse still: A·B is (2 × 3)(3 × 2) = 2 × 2, but B·A is (3 × 2)(2 × 3) = 3 × 3 — not merely a different answer, a different shape.

The identity leaves things alone

The identity matrix I has 1s on the main diagonal and 0s everywhere else, and A·I = I·A = A. Check one entry to see why: row 1 of A dotted with column 1 of I is 6·1 + 2·0 = 6, the entry you started with.

6215·1001=6215

Entry (2, 2) = 3 counts the out-and-back trips from Belton: to Ashford and back, to Corley and back, to Denham and back. That diagonal entry is Belton’s number of roads.

Numbers have reciprocals: 5 × 1/5 = 1. Matrices have inverses: A · A−1 = A−1 · A = I. Only square matrices can have one, and not all of them do — which is the whole content of the determinant.

The determinant

For a 2×2 matrix the determinant is a single number that decides invertibility.

det abcd = ad − bc

If det ≠ 0 the matrix is invertible (also called non-singular). If det = 0 it is singular and has no inverse at all — the analogue of dividing by zero.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two determinants

A print shop’s machine-time matrix — press and cutter minutes per poster and per banner:

det8532= 8·2 − 5·3 = 16 − 15 =1→ invertible

A second shop whose two machines use time in the same proportion:

det1525915= 15·15 − 25·9 = 225 − 225 =0→ SINGULAR

Row 2 is 0.6 × row 1, so the second row carries no new information and the matrix cannot be undone.

The second case is not a coincidence: a determinant of zero always means the rows are linearly dependent — one is a multiple or combination of the others — so the matrix squashes space flat and cannot be undone.

The 2×2 inverse

A−1 = (1/det) · d−b−ca

The pattern is worth saying in words because that is how it is remembered: swap the diagonal entries, negate the other two, divide by the determinant.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — invert 4726
1.
Determinant: 4·6 − 7·2 = 24 − 14 = 10. Non-zero, so an inverse exists.
2.
Swap a and d: 6724.
3.
Negate b and c: 6−7−24.
4.
Divide by 10: A⁻¹ = 0.6−0.7−0.20.4.
5.
Check: A · A⁻¹ should give 1001. ✓

Solving a linear system

This is what inverses are for. A system of linear equations can be written as A·x = b, with A the coefficient matrix, x the unknowns and b the constants. Multiplying both sides on the left by A−1 isolates x.

A·x = b ⟹ x = A−1·b

The side matters — you must multiply on the left in both cases, because multiplication is not commutative. And the determinant answers the solvability question before any work is done: det ≠ 0 means exactly one solution, while det = 0 means either no solution or infinitely many, and further work is needed to tell which.

📘 DEFINITION

Inverse (A⁻¹): the matrix satisfying A·A⁻¹ = A⁻¹·A = I; only square matrices can have one

Determinant: a scalar deciding invertibility; ad − bc for a 2×2

Singular: determinant zero — no inverse exists

Non-singular / invertible: determinant non-zero — an inverse exists

Coefficient matrix: the matrix A in A·x = b

Unique solution: guaranteed when det ≠ 0

★ ON THE OA

For a 2×2 matrix abcd, the determinant is ad − bc. If det = 0 the matrix is singular and has no inverse; det ≠ 0 means invertible. The inverse is (1/det)·d−b−ca.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The inverse formula swaps a and d and negates b and c — not the other way round. Swapping the wrong pair produces a matrix that fails the A·A⁻¹ = I check, which is why that check is worth the ten seconds.

The inverse, and when there is not one

📘 DEFINITION

A⁻¹ is the matrix with A·A⁻¹ = A⁻¹·A = I. Only square matrices can have one, and a square matrix has one exactly when its determinant is non-zero.

📊 FIGURE — a 2×2 inverse, verified
For a 2×2 abcdValue
Determinantad − bc
Inverse(1/(ad − bc)) × d−b−ca
Invertible whenad − bc ≠ 0
Called singular whenad − bc = 0 — no inverse exists

The pattern is worth saying aloud: swap a and d, negate b and c, divide by the determinant. Forgetting to divide is the most common slip, and the resulting matrix fails the A·A⁻¹ = I check immediately — which is why you should always run that check.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — solve Ax = b with A = 3423 and b = [10, 7]

det A = 1, so A⁻¹ = 3−4−23.

x = A⁻¹b = [3(10) + (−4)(7), (−2)(10) + 3(7)] = [30 − 28, −20 + 21] = [2, 1].

Check in the original: 3(2) + 4(1) = 10 ✓ and 2(2) + 3(1) = 7 ✓.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

x = A⁻¹b, not bA⁻¹ — the inverse goes on the left, because that is the side you multiplied from to cancel A. Matrix multiplication does not commute, so the sides are not interchangeable.

The determinant is a crossing

For a 2 × 2 matrix the determinant is one number that answers one question: can this matrix be undone? You get it by multiplying along the two diagonals and subtracting. The diagonal that runs down to the right is added; the one that runs down to the left is subtracted.

📊 FIGURE — det = ad − bc, drawn as two crossing diagonals
📘 DEFINITION

For A = abcd    det A = ad − bc.

det A ≠ 0 → A is invertible (also called non-singular): A⁻¹ exists and is unique.

det A = 0 → A is singular: no inverse exists at all. This is the matrix version of dividing by zero.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two determinants from a real setting

A print shop makes posters and banners. Each poster needs 8 minutes on the press and 3 on the cutter; each banner needs 5 minutes on the press and 2 on the cutter. That is the machine-time matrix:

A =C₁C₂R₁R₂8532R₁ = press, R₂ = cutter · C₁ = poster, C₂ = banner

det A = 8·2 − 5·3 = 16 − 15 = 1

Non-zero, so the machine hours can be worked backwards into a production count — which is exactly the question solved further down.

Now a second shop whose two products use time in the same proportion:

S =C₁C₂R₁R₂1525915

det S = 15·15 − 25·9 = 225 − 225 = 0

Zero, so S is singular. Look at why: row 2 is exactly ⅗ of row 1 (9 = 0.6 × 15, 15 = 0.6 × 25). The second machine tells you nothing the first did not, so no total of machine hours can pin down how many of each product were made. A zero determinant always means one row is a multiple or a combination of the others.

The 2 × 2 inverse — swap, negate, divide

A⁻¹ = (1 / det A) · d−b−ca  — swap the two main-diagonal entries a and d, negate the other two, then divide everything by the determinant.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — inverse 1 — the print shop matrix, det = 1
A =8532det A = 8·2 − 5·3 = 1

Swap 8 and 2, negate 5 and 3, divide by 1 (which changes nothing):

A⁻¹ =2−5−38

Verify it. A·A⁻¹ must be the identity. Row 1 of A with column 1 of A⁻¹, and so on:

(1,1) = 8·2 + 5·(−3) = 16 − 15 = 1
(1,2) = 8·(−5) + 5·8  = −40 + 40 = 0
(2,1) = 3·2 + 2·(−3) = 6 − 6   = 0
(2,2) = 3·(−5) + 2·8 = −15 + 16 = 1

8532·2−5−38=1001I — verified

Four dot products and you know the inverse is right. It is worth the ten seconds every time.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — inverse 2 — det ≠ 1, so the division matters

A joinery workshop: each bookshelf uses 12 board-feet of oak and 9 minutes of sanding; each side table uses 8 board-feet and 7 minutes.

B =C₁C₂R₁R₂12897R₁ = oak (board-feet), R₂ = sanding (min) · C₁ = bookshelf, C₂ = side table

det B = 12·7 − 8·9 = 84 − 72 = 12

Swap 12 and 7, negate 8 and 9, then divide by 12:

B⁻¹ =(1/12) ·7−8−912=7/12−2/3−3/41as exact fractions

Verify it. Keep the 1/12 outside and multiply B by the bracketed matrix first:

12897·(1/12)7−8−912=(1/12)120012=1001I — verified

(1,1) = 12·7 + 8·(−9) = 84 − 72 = 12  → 12/12 = 1
(1,2) = 12·(−8) + 8·12  = −96 + 96 = 0
(2,1) = 9·7 + 7·(−9)   = 63 − 63 = 0
(2,2) = 9·(−8) + 7·12   = −72 + 84 = 12 → 12/12 = 1

Forgetting the ÷12 is the standard error, and this check catches it instantly: you would get 12s down the diagonal instead of 1s.

Solving A·x = b — the point of all this

A system of linear equations packs into one matrix equation. The coefficients become A, the unknowns become the column x, the constants become the column b. Then multiply both sides on the left by A⁻¹:

A·x = b  ⟹  A⁻¹·A·x = A⁻¹·b  ⟹  I·x = A⁻¹·b  ⟹  x = A⁻¹·b

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — how many posters and how many banners?

The press ran for 470 minutes and the cutter for 180 minutes. Each poster: 8 press, 3 cutter. Each banner: 5 press, 2 cutter. With p posters and n banners:

8p + 5n = 470   (press minutes)
3p + 2n = 180   (cutter minutes)

A =8532x =pnb =470180

det A = 1, so A⁻¹ = 2−5−38 and x = A⁻¹·b. Row 1 of A⁻¹ with the single column of b, then row 2:

2−5−38·470180→2·470 + (−5)·180 = 940 − 900 = 40
2−5−38·470180→(−3)·470 + 8·180 = −1410 + 1440 = 30
x =403040 posters, 30 banners

Check in the original equations: 8(40) + 5(30) = 320 + 150 = 470 ✓ and 3(40) + 2(30) = 120 + 60 = 180 ✓.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the joinery workshop, using B⁻¹

The workshop used 1,200 board-feet of oak and 915 minutes of sanding. With s bookshelves and t side tables:

12s + 8t = 1200   (board-feet)
 9s + 7t =  915   (sanding minutes)

det B = 12, B⁻¹ = (1/12)·7−8−912, so:

s = (1/12)[ 7·1200 + (−8)·915 ] = (1/12)(8400 − 7320) = 1080/12 = 90
t = (1/12)[ (−9)·1200 + 12·915 ] = (1/12)(−10800 + 10980) = 180/12 = 15

x =901590 bookshelves, 15 side tables

Check: 12(90) + 8(15) = 1080 + 120 = 1200 ✓ and 9(90) + 7(15) = 810 + 105 = 915 ✓.

What the determinant tells youAbout A·x = b
det A ≠ 0exactly one solution, for every possible b
det A = 0either no solution or infinitely many — the determinant alone cannot say which; row-reduce to find out
det A = 0 and b = 0infinitely many (the all-zero solution always works, plus others)

Determinants of bigger matrices: for a triangular matrix (all zeros on one side of the main diagonal) the determinant is simply the product of the diagonal entries. 735028006 has determinant 7 · 2 · 6 = 84. That is why row-reduction to triangular form is a practical way to get a determinant by hand.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

x = A⁻¹·b, never b·A⁻¹. The inverse goes on the left, because the left is the side you multiplied from in order to cancel A. Multiplication does not commute, so the sides are not interchangeable — and with b a column, b·A⁻¹ is not even a defined product.

Compute the determinant first, always. If it is zero you can answer “singular / no unique solution” without inverting anything, and several exam items ask nothing more than that. If it is non-zero, keep the 1/det outside the brackets while you work — the arithmetic stays in whole numbers and you cannot forget the division.

Only square matrices have determinants or inverses. If a question hands you a 2 × 3 and asks for its inverse, the answer is that it does not have one, no matter what the entries are.

Inverting a matrix works for 2×2 and becomes unpleasant beyond it. Gaussian elimination is the general method, and it solves systems of any size by systematically clearing entries to zero.

It rests on three elementary row operations, and the reason it is valid is that each one produces a system with the same solutions as the one before.

OperationNotationWhy it is safe
Swap two rowsRi ↔ Rjthe order of equations never mattered
Multiply a row by a non-zero constantkRiscaling an equation does not change its solutions
Add a multiple of one row to anotherRi + kRjadding equal quantities to both sides

The constant in the second operation must be non-zero. Multiplying a row by 0 destroys the equation, and that restriction is examined directly.

The augmented matrix

A system is written as an augmented matrix — the coefficients, a vertical bar, then the constants — so that row operations act on everything at once.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — setting it up

Each row is one equation; each column is one unknown; the bar separates the coefficients from the constants.

  a +   s +  t =  240    (tickets sold)
22a + 14s + 9t = 3920    (takings, £)
       s +  t =  120    (non-adult tickets)

becomesR₁R₂R₃111│24022149│3920011│120columns: a   s   t  │  constants

A missing term is a 0, never a blank — the third equation has no a in it, so its first entry is 0. Losing that zero is how columns get misaligned.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — solve it by elimination
1.
Swap rows so the leading entry is 1: [1 −1 | 1], [2 1 | 5].
2.
Clear below the leading 1: R₂ − 2R₁ gives [0 3 | 3].
3.
Scale: (1/3)R₂ gives [0 1 | 1], so y = 1.
4.
Back-substitute into row 1: x − 1 = 1, so x = 2.
5.
Check both original equations: 2(2) + 1 = 5 ✓ and 2 − 1 = 1 ✓.

Echelon form and reading the answer

The target is row-echelon form: each leading entry (the pivot) is to the right of the one above it, and everything below a pivot is zero. Continue to reduced row-echelon form — pivots equal to 1 with zeros above as well as below — and the solution can be read straight off with no back-substitution.

The final shape also tells you how many solutions there are, which is the question exams most often ask.

Final row looks likeMeans
a pivot in every variable columnexactly one solution
a row of all zerosa redundant equation — infinitely many solutions (a free variable)
[0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0no solution — the system is inconsistent

That last row says 0 = c, which is false, so nothing can satisfy the system. Recognising it immediately saves you from hunting for a solution that does not exist.

📘 DEFINITION

Elementary row operations: swap, scale by a non-zero constant, add a multiple of another row

Augmented matrix: coefficients and constants written together, separated by a bar

Pivot: the leading non-zero entry of a row

Row-echelon form: pivots stepping right, zeros below each pivot

Reduced row-echelon form: pivots equal to 1 with zeros above and below

Back-substitution: working upward from the last equation to find the remaining unknowns

Inconsistent system: a system with no solution

Free variable: a variable with no pivot; its presence gives infinitely many solutions

★ ON THE OA

Gaussian elimination uses exactly three row operations — swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero constant, and add a multiple of one row to another — to reach row-echelon form. A row [0 0 | c] with c ≠ 0 means no solution; a row of all zeros means infinitely many.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Work one column at a time, top to bottom, and never move on until every entry below the current pivot is zero. Skipping ahead is what turns a mechanical procedure into an unrecoverable mess.

Row reduction, one column at a time

Gaussian elimination drives the augmented matrix to row echelon form — a staircase of leading entries with zeros beneath — then back-substitutes.

📊 FIGURE — three steps of elimination on a 3×3 system
Elementary row operationEffect on the solution set
Swap two rowsNone
Multiply a row by a non-zero scalarNone
Add a multiple of one row to anotherNone

All three are reversible, which is exactly why the solution set never changes. The \"non-zero\" in the second one matters: multiplying a row by 0 destroys information and is not allowed.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — finish the system above

The last row reads −4z = −12, so z = 3.

The middle row reads y + z = 2, so y = 2 − 3 = −1.

The top row reads x + 2y + 3z = 9, so x = 9 − 2(−1) − 3(3) = 9 + 2 − 9 = 2.

Solution (2, −1, 3). Substituting into the original second equation checks it: 2(2) − (−1) + 3 = 4 + 1 + 3 = 8 ✓.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A row that reduces to 0 0 0 | 5 says 0 = 5, so the system is inconsistent — no solution. A row of 0 0 0 | 0 is a redundant equation, leaving a free variable and infinitely many solutions. Reading those two rows the wrong way round is the standard error.

Row operations, and why they are safe

Every row of an augmented matrix is an equation. That is the idea the whole method rests on. Anything you are allowed to do to a system of equations, you are allowed to do to the rows — and there are exactly three such moves.

Row operationWrittenThe equation-level reason it is safe
Swap two rowsRᵢ ↔ Rⱼthe order you list equations in never mattered
Multiply a row by a non-zero constantkRᵢdoubling both sides of an equation does not change its solutions
Add a multiple of one row to anotherRᵢ + kRⱼadding equal quantities to both sides of an equation is always valid

The word non-zero in the second one is examined directly. Multiplying a row by 0 turns an equation into 0 = 0, destroying information you cannot get back — so it is not an elementary row operation. All three legal moves are reversible, and that reversibility is precisely why the solution set never changes.

📊 FIGURE — row echelon form: the staircase of pivots

A full elimination, one operation per line

A school fundraiser sold adult tickets at £22, senior tickets at £14 and student tickets at £9. Three facts were recorded:

240 tickets were sold altogether  →  a + s + t = 240
takings were £3,920               →  22a + 14s + 9t = 3920
seniors and students together: 120  →  s + t = 120

Write the coefficients on the left of the bar and the constants on the right. Each column belongs to one unknown: column 1 is a, column 2 is s, column 3 is t.

augmented matrix:R₁R₂R₃111│24022149│3920011│120columns: a   s   t  │  constants

R₂ ↔ R₃R₁R₂R₃111│240011│1200−8−13│−1360put the tidy row with the leading 1 up next

Swapping is free and it saves fractions: row 3 already had a 1 in column 2.

R₃ + 8R₂R₁R₂R₃111│240011│12000−5│−400clears column 2 below the new pivot

Row 3 was [0, −8, −13 │ −1360]. Add 8 × row 2 = [0, 8, 8 │ 960] to get [0, 0, −5 │ −400].

(−1/5)R₃R₁R₂R₃111│240011│120001│80scale the last pivot to 1 — row echelon form

The last row now reads 0a + 0s + 1t = 80, so t = 80 student tickets.

R₂ − R₃R₁R₂R₃111│240010│40001│80clears above the third pivot
R₁ − R₃R₁R₂R₃110│160010│40001│80clears above it in row 1 too
R₁ − R₂R₁R₂R₃100│120010│40001│80reduced row echelon form

Read the last matrix off row by row: a = 120, s = 40, t = 80 — 120 adult, 40 senior and 80 student tickets.

Check all three original equations:
120 + 40 + 80 = 240 ✓    22(120) + 14(40) + 9(80) = 2640 + 560 + 720 = 3920 ✓    40 + 80 = 120 ✓

You could have stopped at the fourth matrix. That is row echelon form — the staircase with zeros beneath — and from there you back-substitute: the bottom row gives t = 80; the middle row says s + t = 120, so s = 40; the top row says a + s + t = 240, so a = 120. Carrying on to reduced row echelon form (1s on the diagonal, zeros above and below) means the answers are simply written in the last column with no back-substitution at all.

Reading the final shape: one, none, or infinitely many

The elimination does more than find a solution — its final shape tells you how many solutions exist, which is what exams ask most often.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a system with no solution

A depot claims that its two van types together made 45 runs, and also that three times as many runs of each type came to 150. With x and y runs:

 x +  y =  45
3x + 3y = 150

startR₁R₂11│4533│150
R₂ − 3R₁R₁R₂11│4500│15the last row says 0 = 15

Row 2 now reads 0x + 0y = 15, which is false for every x and y. The system is inconsistent: no solution. The two claims contradict each other — 3 × 45 is 135, not 150.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a system with infinitely many solutions

Same first claim, but the second is now consistent with it — four times as many runs came to 180:

 x +  y =  45
4x + 4y = 180

startR₁R₂11│4544│180
R₂ − 4R₁R₁R₂11│4500│0a row of all zeros

Row 2 reads 0 = 0 — true, but empty. The second equation was just the first one restated, so there is only one real constraint on two unknowns. y is a free variable: pick any value, set x = 45 − y, and you have a solution. Infinitely many solutions.

A row in the final matrixWhat it meansHow many solutions
a pivot in every variable columnevery unknown is pinned downexactly one
[ 0 0 0 │ 0 ] — all zerosa redundant equation, leaving a free variableinfinitely many
[ 0 0 0 │ 15 ] — zeros then non-zerothe row asserts 0 = 15, which is falsenone — inconsistent
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Confusing the two zero rows. [0 0 0 │ 0] and [0 0 0 │ 15] look almost identical and mean opposite things. Zeros all the way across, constant included = a redundant equation = infinitely many solutions. Zeros on the left with anything non-zero on the right = 0 = 15 = no solution at all. Reading these the wrong way round is the standard error in this section.

Changing two rows in one step. Rᵢ + kRⱼ changes row i only. Row j is the donor and comes through untouched. If both rows changed, you have done two operations at once and lost track of the system.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Work strictly one column at a time, left to right, and do not move on until every entry below the current pivot is zero. Write the operation next to each new matrix exactly as you did it — “R₂ − 22R₁” — because when the arithmetic goes wrong (and it will) you can find the step instead of restarting.

Use a swap to avoid fractions. If the pivot position holds an awkward number and a row below it starts with 1, swap them first: swapping is free and it keeps every later step in whole numbers.

Row echelon form and reduced row echelon form

RequirementREFRREF
Zero rows sit at the bottom✓✓
Each pivot is to the right of the pivot above it (a staircase)✓✓
Entries below each pivot are 0✓✓
Every pivot is 1—✓
Entries above each pivot are 0 as well—✓

So RREF is REF plus two extra demands: pivots normalised to 1, and the column cleared above each pivot as well as below.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Testing two matrices for REF

[[1,2,3], [0,1,4], [0,0,1]] — pivots sit in columns 1, 2, 3, each one further right than the last, and everything below each pivot is 0. Yes, this is in REF. (It is not RREF: there are non-zero entries above the pivots.)

[[1,2,3], [0,0,1], [0,1,0]] — row 2's pivot is in column 3, and row 3's pivot is in column 2, which is further left. The staircase goes backwards. No.

Scan the pivot columns top to bottom: if they do not strictly increase, it is not in echelon form, and you can stop there.

📘 DEFINITION
A matrix has many valid REFs — the answer depends on which row operations you chose — but exactly one RREF. The extra conditions pin it down completely, which is why RREF can be used to decide whether two matrices are row-equivalent.
🎯 EXAM TIP
Count the demands: REF has three, RREF has five. If a question shows a matrix with a pivot that is not 1, or a non-zero entry above a pivot, it is REF but not RREF.

Each row operation from the previous lesson can itself be written as a matrix. An elementary matrix is what you get by applying one row operation to the identity matrix — and multiplying by it on the left performs that same operation on any matrix.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — three elementary matrices (3×3)

Each one is the identity matrix with a single row operation applied to it. Multiply on the left and it performs that operation on whatever it multiplies:

OperationElementary matrixWhere the change sits
R₁ ↔ R₂ — swap rows 1 and 2010100001rows 1 and 2 of I have traded places
5R₂ — multiply row 2 by 5100050001the 1 in position (2,2) has become a 5
R₃ + 2R₁ — add 2 × row 1 to row 3100010201a 2 sits in position (3,1): row 3 borrows from row 1

Compare each with the identity 100010001 — exactly one thing has changed in each.

Every elementary matrix is invertible, and its inverse is the matrix of the reversing operation: swapping twice returns you to the start, multiplying by 5 is undone by multiplying by 1/5, and adding 2R₁ is undone by subtracting it. That fact is what makes the next result work.

The Invertible Matrix Theorem

Because Gaussian elimination is a sequence of elementary matrices, a square matrix reduces to the identity exactly when it is invertible. That links every idea in this chapter into one theorem, and the exam treats the statements as interchangeable.

For a square matrix A, these all say the same thing
A is invertible — A−1 exists
det(A) ≠ 0
A row-reduces to the identity matrix
A·x = b has exactly one solution for every b
A·x = 0 has only the trivial solution x = 0
The rows of A are linearly independent
The columns of A are linearly independent
A has a pivot in every row and every column

The practical value is that you may check whichever condition is cheapest. For a 2×2, computing ad − bc is fastest. For a larger matrix, row-reducing and looking for a zero row is usually quicker than computing a determinant by hand.

And the negations are equally interchangeable: if any one fails, all of them fail. A singular matrix has determinant zero, does not reduce to the identity, has dependent rows, and gives a system with either no solution or infinitely many.

Finding an inverse by row reduction

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the augmented method
1.
Write [A | I] — the matrix beside an identity of the same size.
2.
Row-reduce until the left half becomes the identity.
3.
Whatever the right half has become is A⁻¹.
4.
If the left half cannot reach the identity — a zero row appears — then A is singular and has no inverse.

The reason this works is the elementary-matrix view: the operations that turn A into I are exactly the operations that turn I into A−1, because they encode the same sequence of steps.

📘 DEFINITION

Elementary matrix: the identity with one row operation applied

Invertible Matrix Theorem: a list of equivalent conditions for a square matrix to be invertible

Linearly independent: no row (or column) is a combination of the others

Trivial solution: the all-zero solution to A·x = 0

[A | I] method: row-reducing A to I while the attached identity becomes A⁻¹

Rank: the number of pivots; a square matrix is invertible exactly when its rank equals its size

★ ON THE OA

A matrix is invertible ⇔ det ≠ 0 ⇔ it row-reduces to the identity ⇔ A·x = b has a unique solution. For a 2×2, A⁻¹ = (1/det)·d−b−ca. Any one of those statements failing means all of them fail.

💡 WHY IT MATTERS

This theorem is why the chapter hangs together. Determinants, row reduction and solving systems are three routes to the same question — does this matrix undo itself — and recognising them as one question is what makes the exam items fast.

The invertible matrix theorem

For a square matrix these conditions are all equivalent — establish any one and you have all of them. That is what makes the theorem useful: you get to pick whichever is easiest to check.

📊 FIGURE — six ways of saying one thing

📘 DEFINITION

An elementary matrix is what you get by applying one row operation to I. Multiplying by it on the left performs that operation, so row-reducing A to I is the same as writing Ek…E₂E₁A = I — which means A⁻¹ = Ek…E₂E₁.

That is exactly the Gauss–Jordan method for inverting: augment A with I, reduce the left half to I, and whatever the right half becomes is A⁻¹.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For a homogeneous system Ax = 0 the zero vector is always a solution, so it can never be inconsistent. The only question is whether it has only that one — and the answer is yes exactly when A is invertible.

An elementary matrix is one row operation, frozen

Take the identity matrix. Perform exactly one row operation on it. What you are left with is an elementary matrix — and multiplying any matrix by it on the left performs that same operation on that matrix. The row operation and the matrix are two ways of writing one thing.

Here is the matrix everything below acts on — a haulier’s cost table, three depots by three routes:

Read the position of the odd entry and you can read the operation. A 2 in position (3,1) means “row 3 gains 2 × row 1” — the row it changes is the row index, the row it borrows from is the column index. Rows first, columns second, exactly as in section 1.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why E · A does the operation — check one entry

Take E₃ = 100010201 and A = 12301892415204528. Entry (3,1) of the product is row 3 of E₃ dotted with column 1 of A:

100010201·12301892415204528→2·12 + 0·9 + 1·20 = 24 + 20 = 44

The 2 pulls in twice the first entry of column 1, the 1 keeps the third entry, and the 0 discards the middle. That is “row 3 + 2 × row 1” written as arithmetic. Row 1 of E₃ is [1, 0, 0], which copies row 1 of A through unchanged — which is why the other two rows are untouched.

Every elementary matrix is invertible — undo the operation

Each of the three operations can be reversed, so each elementary matrix has an inverse, and that inverse is just the elementary matrix of the reversing operation.

A swap is its own inverse — do it twice and you are back where you started. The other two just flip the sign or take the reciprocal of the single off-identity entry.

Inverting a matrix by row reduction: the [A │ I] method

If a sequence of row operations turns A into I, then that same sequence — the same elementary matrices, in the same order — turns I into A⁻¹. So write them side by side and reduce both halves at once.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — invert the print shop matrix by row reduction

A = 8532. Augment it with the 2 × 2 identity:

startR₁R₂85│1032│01left half A, right half I
R₁ − 2R₂R₁R₂21│1−232│01shrink the leading 8
R₂ − R₁R₁R₂21│1−211│−13
R₁ − R₂R₁R₂10│2−511│−13
R₂ − R₁R₁R₂10│2−501│−38left half is now I

The left half has become the identity, so the right half is the inverse:

A⁻¹ =2−5−38

Which matches the formula answer from the previous section, (1/1)·2−5−38. Verify:

8532·2−5−38=1001I ✓

For a 2 × 2 the formula is faster. For a 3 × 3 or bigger there is no formula worth memorising, and this is the method.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — what failure looks like

The singular matrix from the previous section, augmented with I:

startR₁R₂1525│10915│01
5R₂ − 3R₁R₁R₂1525│1000│−35a row of zeros on the left

The left half can never become the identity, because row 2 is now all zeros there and no legal operation will put a pivot back. The matrix is singular — and sure enough det = 15·15 − 25·9 = 0. The two conditions failed together, which is the theorem below in miniature.

The Invertible Matrix Theorem

Because elimination is nothing but a chain of elementary matrices, Ek…E₂E₁A = I whenever the reduction succeeds — which makes A⁻¹ = Ek…E₂E₁. That single fact ties every idea in this chapter together. For a square matrix A, the following statements are all the same statement:

If A is invertible, all of these are trueIf A is singular, all of these are true instead
A⁻¹ existsA⁻¹ does not exist
det A ≠ 0det A = 0
A row-reduces to Irow reduction leaves a row of zeros
A has a pivot in every row and every columnat least one column has no pivot
A·x = b has exactly one solution, for every bA·x = b has no solution, or infinitely many
A·x = 0 has only the trivial solution x = 0A·x = 0 has non-zero solutions too
the rows are linearly independentsome row is a combination of the others
the columns are linearly independentsome column is a combination of the others
rank A = n (full rank)rank A < n
📊 FIGURE — one question, two prices — pick the cheaper test

The practical value is that you may check whichever condition is cheapest. For a 2 × 2, ad − bc takes five seconds. For a 4 × 4, row-reducing and watching for a zero row is far quicker than expanding a determinant by hand. And the negations are equally interchangeable — if any one condition fails, every one of them fails.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — using the theorem instead of computing

“The 3 × 3 matrix M row-reduces to a form whose bottom row is all zeros. What is det M, and how many solutions does M·x = b have?”

No arithmetic is needed. A zero row means M does not reduce to I, so M is singular; therefore det M = 0, and M·x = b has either no solution or infinitely many — never exactly one. Which of the two it is depends on b, and only further reduction of the augmented matrix will say.

“A·x = 0 has a non-zero solution. Is A invertible?” No. A homogeneous system always has the trivial solution x = 0; having a second one puts you in the singular column of the table above.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Multiplying on the wrong side. E·A performs a row operation. A·E performs a column operation, which is a different thing entirely. Row operations always come from multiplying on the left — the same side the inverse goes on when you solve A·x = b.

Assuming the theorem covers non-square matrices. Every statement in it begins “for a square matrix”. A 3 × 4 matrix has no determinant and no inverse, whatever its entries are, so none of the equivalences apply to it.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Learn the theorem as two columns, not nine facts. Given any one statement, you can supply the other eight. Exam items nearly always hand you one condition and ask for another: “det = 0, so how many solutions?”, “reduces to I, so is it invertible?”, “A·x = 0 has only the trivial solution, so what is the rank?”

Remember the one asymmetry: A·x = 0 can never be inconsistent, because x = 0 always works. So for a homogeneous system the only question is whether that trivial solution is the only one — and the answer is yes exactly when A is invertible.

What an elementary matrix actually does

📘 DEFINITION
An elementary matrix E is what you get by performing one row operation on the identity matrix I. Its whole point is this: multiplying on the left, the effect of EA is to perform that same row operation on A. A row operation and a matrix multiplication are the same act.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Building E for \"add 2 × row 1 to row 2\"
  1. Start from the identity: I₂ = [[1, 0], [0, 1]].
  2. Carry out the operation on the identity: row 2 becomes row 2 + 2 × row 1, so [0, 1] becomes [2, 1].
  3. That gives E = [[1, 0], [2, 1]].
  4. Now EA does that operation to any A. The 2 sits at position (2,1) — row 2 borrowing from row 1.

The same recipe covers the other two kinds. For scaling — multiply row 2 by 5 — scale row 2 of I: [[1, 0], [0, 5]]. To swap rows 1 and 2, swap them in I: [[0, 1], [1, 0]]. Read the operation, do it to I, and you have E.

The Invertible Matrix Theorem, in the form it is asked

If A is invertible……then
its RREF isthe identity Iₙ
its determinant isnon-zero
its rows/columns arelinearly independent
Ax = b hasexactly one solution for every b

Every line is an \"if and only if\", so each one read backwards is also true — which is how the contrapositive version gets asked: if row-reducing A produces a row of zeros, the RREF cannot be the identity, so A is singular — not invertible. A zero row means one row was a combination of the others, carrying no independent information.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why row-reducing [A | I] hands you the inverse
  1. Reducing A to I is a chain of row operations, so it is a chain of elementary matrices: Eₖ…E₂E₁A = I.
  2. By the definition of an inverse, that product Eₖ…E₂E₁ is A⁻¹.
  3. So applying the very same steps to the identity gives Eₖ…E₂E₁I = A⁻¹.
  4. Which is why you write [A | I], reduce until the left side is I, and read A⁻¹ off the right.

The augmented-matrix trick is not a coincidence to memorise — it is this identity.

🎯 EXAM TIP
\"EA does what?\" → performs that row operation on A. \"How do I build E?\" → do the operation to the identity. \"Row of zeros?\" → singular.

A sequence is an ordered list of numbers, and it is formally a function whose domain is the positive integers: the input is the position n, and the output is the term an. Seeing it that way explains why sequences sit in the same course as functions and relations rather than in calculus.

An arithmetic sequence is one where each term is the previous term plus a fixed common difference d. That single constant determines everything about it.

📐 Arithmetic sequence formulas
Common difference
d = aₙ − aₙ₋₁ (the same for every consecutive pair)
nth term (explicit)
aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d
Recursive form
aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d, with a₁ given
Sum of n terms
Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2

The (n − 1) in the explicit formula is where marks are lost. Getting from the 1st term to the nth takes n − 1 steps, not n — you are already standing on the first term. So the 10th term of a sequence starting at 3 with d = 5 is 3 + 9(5) = 48, not 3 + 10(5).

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — find the 20th term of 4, 7, 10, 13, …
1.
Find d: 7 − 4 = 3. Check it holds throughout: 10 − 7 = 3 ✓.
2.
Identify a₁ = 4 and n = 20.
3.
Apply the formula: a₂₀ = 4 + (20 − 1)(3) = 4 + 57.
4.
a₂₀ = 61.

The sum formula, and where it comes from

The sum Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2 is worth understanding rather than memorising, because the reasoning reappears in 6.3. Pair the first term with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on: every pair has the same total a₁ + aₙ, and there are n/2 such pairs. Multiplying gives the formula.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — sum the first 20 terms of 4, 7, 10, …
1.
From above, a₁ = 4 and a₂₀ = 61.
2.
Apply the sum formula: S₂₀ = 20(4 + 61)/2.
3.
= 20(65)/2 = 10 × 65.
4.
S₂₀ = 650.

If the last term is not given, compute it first with the nth-term formula — the sum formula needs both ends. That two-step order is the shape of nearly every arithmetic-series exam question.

Recognising the type from a word problem

Sequence questions are usually dressed as situations, and the phrase that identifies the type is about how the quantity changes. \"Increases by 5 each year\", \"adds 200 every month\" and \"the difference is constant\" are all arithmetic. \"Grows by 5 per cent\", \"doubles\", \"halves\" and \"the ratio is constant\" are all geometric. Percentage change is always geometric, because a percentage is a multiplier.

After identifying the type, the second decision is whether the question wants a term or a sum. \"How much in year 10\" is a term; \"how much altogether over 10 years\" is a sum. Answering one when the question asked the other is a common and completely avoidable loss.

Finally, watch the indexing. If the problem says \"in the first year\", that is a₁, and year 10 is a₁₀ with n = 10. If it says \"after 10 years\" starting from a value at year 0, the starting value is a₀ and everything shifts by one.

📘 DEFINITION

Sequence: an ordered list of numbers; a function on the positive integers

Term (aₙ): the value at position n

Arithmetic sequence: consecutive terms differ by a constant

Common difference (d): the constant added to get the next term; can be negative

Explicit formula: gives aₙ directly from n

Recursive formula: gives aₙ from the previous term, plus a starting value

Series: the sum of the terms of a sequence

Partial sum (Sₙ): the sum of the first n terms

★ ON THE OA

An arithmetic sequence has a constant common difference d. The nth term is aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d and the sum of n terms is Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2. The (n − 1) is the part most often written as n by mistake.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Confirm the difference is constant before using any formula. If a₂ − a₁ and a₃ − a₂ differ, the sequence is not arithmetic and these formulas give a confidently wrong answer.

Arithmetic sequences are straight lines

📊 FIGURE — 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20 plotted

A constant difference d makes the plot linear with slope d — an arithmetic sequence is a linear function restricted to the positive integers. A geometric sequence would curve.

QuantityFormulaFor a₁ = 2, d = 3
nth termaₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)da₁₀ = 2 + 27 = 29
Sum of first nSₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2S₁₀ = 10(2 + 29)/2 = 155
Equivalent sum formSₙ = n[2a₁ + (n − 1)d]/2S₁₀ = 10[4 + 27]/2 = 155
Common differenced = aₙ − aₙ₋₁any consecutive pair: 5 − 2 = 3
🎯 EXAM TIP

Always test your formula at n = 1 — it must return a₁. Writing a₁ + nd instead of a₁ + (n − 1)d gives 5 instead of 2 and fails immediately. That one check catches the most frequent error in the whole unit.

📊 FIGURE — an arithmetic sequence is a constant-size step repeated

Read the picture rather than the formula. You stand on the first term, then take steps of size d. Reaching the 5th dot took four steps — that single observation is the whole content of the \"n − 1\" that costs marks on the exam.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — charging points — the 12th quarter and the running total

A city installed 380 public charging points in the first quarter of its rollout, and in every quarter after that it installed 145 more than in the quarter before. How many go in during quarter 12, and how many have been installed in total after 12 quarters?

  1. Identify the pattern: each quarter adds a fixed extra amount, so this is arithmetic with a₁ = 380 and d = 145.
  2. Quarter 12 is 11 steps past quarter 1 (12 − 1 = 11).
  3. a₁₂ = a₁ + (n − 1)d = 380 + 11(145) = 380 + 1,595.
  4. a₁₂ = 1,975 charging points installed during quarter 12.
  5. Total uses the sum formula, which needs both ends: S₁₂ = n(a₁ + a₁₂)/2 = 12(380 + 1,975)/2.
  6. = 12(2,355)/2 = 6 × 2,355 = 14,130.
Answer: 1,975 in quarter 12; 14,130 installed in total.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a theatre with widening rows

A theatre has 26 seats in the front row, and every row behind it has 3 more seats than the row in front. How many seats are in row 18, and how many seats do rows 1 through 18 hold altogether?

  1. a₁ = 26, d = 3, n = 18.
  2. a₁₈ = 26 + (18 − 1)(3) = 26 + 17(3) = 26 + 51.
  3. a₁₈ = 77 seats in row 18.
  4. S₁₈ = 18(26 + 77)/2 = 18(103)/2 = 9 × 103.
  5. S₁₈ = 927 seats in the first eighteen rows.

Sanity check: 18 rows averaging (26 + 77)/2 = 51.5 seats gives 18 × 51.5 = 927. The sum formula is \"number of terms × average of the two ends\".

Answer: Row 18 has 77 seats; the block holds 927.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Two errors account for most lost marks here. (1) Using n instead of n − 1. Row 18 is 26 + 17(3) = 77, not 26 + 18(3) = 80. (2) Using the sum formula without the last term. Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2 needs both ends, so if the question only gives you a₁ and d you must compute aₙ first. There is no shortcut past that two-step order.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a question asks how many terms there are rather than what a term equals, rearrange: n = (aₙ − a₁)/d + 1. Seats 12, 19, 26, …, 96 in a row: n = (96 − 12)/7 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13 seats. Forgetting the \"+ 1\" is the classic off-by-one, and it is the same \"you are already standing on the first term\" idea in a different disguise.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Recovering a₁ from a later term

An arithmetic sequence has a₇ = 38 and d = 5. Find a₁.

  1. aₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)d, so 38 = a₁ + 6(5).
  2. 38 = a₁ + 30.
  3. a₁ = 8.

The usual slip is using n instead of n − 1: a₇ is six steps after a₁, not seven.

A geometric sequence multiplies instead of adding: each term is the previous one times a fixed common ratio r. The change from + to × changes the behaviour completely — arithmetic sequences grow steadily, geometric ones explode or collapse.

📐 Geometric sequence formulas
Common ratio
r = aₙ / aₙ₋₁ (the same for every consecutive pair)
nth term
aₙ = a₁ · r^(n−1)
Recursive form
aₙ = r · aₙ₋₁, with a₁ given
Sum of n terms
Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), r ≠ 1
Infinite sum
S = a₁/(1 − r), only when |r| < 1

The exponent is n − 1 for the same reason as before: the first term has been multiplied by r zero times. And note the two conditions attached to the sums — r ≠ 1 in the finite formula, because the denominator would be zero, and |r| < 1 for the infinite one.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — find the 8th term of 3, 6, 12, 24, …
1.
Find r: 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Confirm: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 ✓.
2.
a₁ = 3, n = 8.
3.
a₈ = 3 · 2⁷ = 3 × 128.
4.
a₈ = 384.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — sum the first 8 terms
1.
Apply Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1): S₈ = 3(2⁸ − 1)/(2 − 1).
2.
= 3(256 − 1)/1 = 3 × 255.
3.
S₈ = 765.

Why |r| < 1 changes everything

When the ratio is between −1 and 1, each term is smaller than the last, and the terms shrink toward zero fast enough that an infinite number of them still add up to a finite total. That is the geometric series result, and it is one of the more surprising facts in the course.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an infinite geometric sum
1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + …      a₁ = 1,  r = 1/2\n\n|r| = 1/2 < 1, so the infinite sum converges:\n\nS = a₁/(1 − r) = 1/(1 − 1/2) = 1/(1/2) = 2\n\nAdding infinitely many positive numbers gives exactly 2.

If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink, so the sum grows without bound and the series diverges — there is no total to find. Checking |r| < 1 before applying the infinite formula is the whole test, and a question offering an answer for r = 2 is checking whether you skipped it.

Sequence typeRuleGrowth
Arithmeticadd d each steplinear — a straight line
Geometric, |r| > 1multiply by rexponential — accelerating
Geometric, |r| < 1multiply by rdecaying toward zero
📘 DEFINITION

Geometric sequence: consecutive terms have a constant ratio

Common ratio (r): the constant multiplier; found by dividing consecutive terms

Geometric series: the sum of a geometric sequence

Convergent series: one whose infinite sum approaches a finite value

Divergent series: one whose sum grows without bound

Exponential growth / decay: the behaviour when |r| > 1 and |r| < 1

★ ON THE OA

A geometric sequence has a constant common ratio r. The nth term is aₙ = a₁ · r^(n−1), and the finite sum is Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1). The infinite sum a₁/(1 − r) exists only when |r| < 1.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Tell the two sequence types apart by testing both: subtract consecutive terms and divide consecutive terms. Whichever gives a constant names the sequence — and if neither does, it is neither.

Adding a step versus multiplying by a ratio

📊 FIGURE — Arithmetic vs. geometric growth, plotted
Arithmetic sequences add the same difference each step (d = +3): the dots march in a straight line. Geometric sequences multiply by the same ratio (r = ×2): the dots curve upward explosively. Recognizing which pattern you are looking at tells you which formula family to use.
ArithmeticGeometric
What changes each termadd a common difference dmultiply by a common ratio r
nth termaₙ = a₁ + (n − 1)daₙ = a₁ · rn−1
Sum of first nSₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)
Infinite sumnever converges (unless d = 0)a₁/(1 − r), and only when |r| < 1
Shape when plotteda straight linea curve — explodes or decays

The (n − 1) in both formulas is where marks go. The first term has already happened, so getting to the nth term takes n − 1 steps, not n. Substituting n = 1 into a formula you have written is the check: it must return a₁.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a₁ = 5, d = 3 — find a₁₀ and S₁₀

a₁₀ = 5 + (10 − 1)(3) = 5 + 27 = 32.

S₁₀ = 10(5 + 32)/2 = 10(37)/2 = 185.

Check: with n = 1, a₁ = 5 + 0 = 5 ✓.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a₁ = 8, r = ½ — find the infinite sum

|r| = 0.5 < 1, so it converges. S = a₁/(1 − r) = 8/(1 − 0.5) = 8/0.5 = 16.

Had r been 2, the terms would grow without bound and there would be no sum at all — checking |r| < 1 before using the formula is the whole question in disguise.

📊 FIGURE — geometric growth: the multiplier, not the gap, stays fixed

The bars make the difference visible. In an arithmetic sequence the bars would climb by the same height each time; here each bar is three times the one before, so the early terms look almost flat and the last one runs off the top of the page. Any phrase like \"doubles\", \"grows 6% a year\", \"loses 15% of its value\" or \"halves\" is a multiplier, and therefore geometric.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — how far a rumour spreads, and how many people have heard it

On day 1 a rumour reaches 7 people. Each day the number of new people who hear it is three times the previous day. How many hear it on day 6, and how many people have heard it in total over the six days?

  1. Constant multiplier → geometric, with a₁ = 7 and r = 3.
  2. a₆ = a₁r⁶⁻¹ = 7 · 3⁵. Note the exponent is 5, not 6 — the same \"already standing on term 1\" idea as before.
  3. 3⁵ = 243, so a₆ = 7 × 243 = 1,701 new people on day 6.
  4. Total: Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) = 7(3⁶ − 1)/(3 − 1).
  5. 3⁶ = 729, so S₆ = 7(728)/2 = 7 × 364.
  6. S₆ = 2,548 people have heard it in total.

Check by adding: 7 + 21 + 63 + 189 + 567 + 1,701 = 2,548. ✓

Answer: 1,701 on day 6; 2,548 people in total.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — depreciation — a multiplier smaller than 1

A packaging machine is bought for $42,000 and loses 15% of its value each year. What is it worth after 5 years?

  1. \"Loses 15%\" means it keeps 85%, so r = 0.85, not −0.15. This is the single most common slip in depreciation questions.
  2. Set the purchase price as the value at year 0, so value after n years = 42,000 · (0.85)ⁿ.
  3. After 5 years: 42,000 × 0.85⁵.
  4. 0.85⁵ = 0.4437053125.
  5. 42,000 × 0.4437053125 = $18,635.62 (to the nearest cent).

If instead you index the purchase price as a₁, then year 5 is a₆ = 42,000 · 0.85⁵ — the same arithmetic. Decide which convention you are using and stay with it.

Answer: About $18,635.62.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Percentage change is not the ratio. \"Grows 6% a year\" gives r = 1.06, and \"falls 15% a year\" gives r = 0.85. Students who use r = 0.06 or r = −0.15 get answers that collapse to nearly nothing. Second trap: the exponent in aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹ is n − 1, so a₆ uses r⁵. Third: the sum formula is a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), where the exponent is n — the two formulas deliberately differ, and swapping them is a guaranteed wrong answer.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Test the type in one move: compute both aₙ − aₙ₋₁ and aₙ ÷ aₙ₋₁ for two consecutive pairs. Whichever one comes out the same twice tells you the type. For 7, 21, 63: the differences are 14 and 42 (not constant) but the ratios are 3 and 3 (constant) → geometric.

Classifying a sequence, and compounding

Given a list of terms, run two checks in order:

  1. Differences between consecutive terms. Constant → arithmetic. For 3, 7, 11, 15 the differences are 4, 4, 4 → arithmetic.
  2. If not, ratios. Constant → geometric. For 2, 4, 8, 16 the differences are 2, 4, 8 (not constant) but the ratios are 2, 2, 2 → geometric.

The second case is exactly the trap: the differences of 2, 4, 8 are 2 and 4, which is not constant, so \"not arithmetic\" is not the same as \"no pattern\". Always check ratios before concluding.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Compound interest is a geometric sequence

$2,400 at 6% compounded annually. What is the balance after 10 years?

  1. Each year multiplies by 1.06, so this is geometric with a₁ = 2400 and r = 1.06.
  2. Balance after n years = 2400 × 1.06n.
  3. 1.06¹⁰ ≈ 1.790847.
  4. 2400 × 1.790847 ≈ 4298.03 → $4,298.

Note the exponent is 10, not 9: the deposit is made at time 0 and earns interest ten times. Compare that with the aₙ = a₁rⁿ⁻¹ term formula, where the exponent is n − 1 because a₁ is itself the first term.

Sigma notation is compact instruction for a sum. Every part of it tells you something specific, and reading it correctly is most of the work.

        n\n       ___\n       \\\n        >    aᵢ          \"sum of aᵢ, for i running from 1 to n\"\n       /__\n       i = 1\n\n  i      the INDEX — the counter\n  i = 1  the LOWER bound — where it starts\n  n      the UPPER bound — where it stops (INCLUSIVE)\n  aᵢ     the TERM — what to add at each step

The upper bound is inclusive, which is the detail most often missed. Σ from i = 1 to 4 has four terms, and in general the number of terms is upper − lower + 1. A sum from 3 to 7 has five terms, not four.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — expand and evaluate Σ (i = 1 to 4) of 2i
1.
Substitute each index value in turn: i = 1, 2, 3, 4.
2.
Terms: 2(1) + 2(2) + 2(3) + 2(4).
3.
= 2 + 4 + 6 + 8.
4.
= 20.

The formulas to memorise

📐 Standard summation formulas
Constant
Σ (i = 1 to n) c = n · c
First n integers
Σ (i = 1 to n) i = n(n + 1)/2
First n squares
Σ (i = 1 to n) i² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
First n cubes
Σ (i = 1 to n) i³ = [n(n + 1)/2]²
Pulling out a constant
Σ c·aᵢ = c · Σ aᵢ
Splitting a sum
Σ (aᵢ + bᵢ) = Σ aᵢ + Σ bᵢ

The constant rule is the one people over-think. Σ (i = 1 to 7) of 2 does not involve i at all — you are adding the number 2, seven times, so the answer is 14. The index just counts how many times.

The first n integers formula is the one proved by induction in 7.3, and it is the workhorse: 1 + 2 + … + 100 = 100(101)/2 = 5050 without adding anything.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — evaluate Σ (i = 1 to 5) of (3i + 2)
1.
Split the sum: Σ 3i + Σ 2.
2.
Pull the constant out of the first: 3 · Σ i, and use the formula: 3 · 5(6)/2 = 3 × 15 = 45.
3.
The second is a constant summed five times: 5 × 2 = 10.
4.
Total: 55. Check by expanding: 5 + 8 + 11 + 14 + 17 = 55 ✓.

When the lower bound is not 1, do not improvise. Compute the sum from 1 to the upper bound, then subtract the sum from 1 to just below the lower bound — Σ(3 to 7) = Σ(1 to 7) − Σ(1 to 2).

📘 DEFINITION

Sigma notation (Σ): compact notation for a sum

Index: the counter variable, usually i or k

Lower / upper bound: the first and last index values; both inclusive

Number of terms: upper − lower + 1

Linearity: constants factor out and sums split across addition

Closed form: a formula giving the sum without adding term by term

★ ON THE OA

Sigma notation sums the terms between its bounds, and both bounds are inclusive. Memorise Σ i = n(n + 1)/2 and Σ i² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6. A constant summed from 1 to n gives n·c — the index does not appear in the answer.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

The number of terms is upper − lower + 1, not upper − lower. Forgetting the +1 is the single most common sigma error and it shifts every subsequent calculation.

Reading sigma notation

📊 FIGURE — every part of a summation, named
FormulaResult
Σ from i=1 to n of 1n
Σ from i=1 to n of in(n + 1)/2
Σ from i=1 to n of i²n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6

Σ from i=0 to n of ri(rn+1 − 1)/(r − 1), for r ≠ 1
📘 DEFINITION

Two rules let you break any polynomial sum into the table above:

Σ(aᵢ + bᵢ) = Σaᵢ + Σbᵢ — a sum splits.
Σ(c·aᵢ) = c·Σaᵢ — a constant factor comes out front.

And a constant with no i in it is not free: Σ from i=1 to n of c = n·c, because it is added n times.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — evaluate Σ from i=1 to 10 of (2i + 3)

Split it: Σ2i + Σ3 = 2·Σi + 10·3.

Σ from 1 to 10 of i = 10(11)/2 = 55, so 2(55) = 110. And the constant contributes 10 × 3 = 30.

Total = 110 + 30 = 140.

Sanity-check by treating it as arithmetic: the terms run 5, 7, …, 23, which is 10 terms averaging 14 → 140 ✓.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The number of terms is upper − lower + 1, not upper − lower. Summing from i = 0 to n gives n + 1 terms, and forgetting the +1 is where the geometric-series formula gets misremembered.

📊 FIGURE — every part of Σ notation, named

Sigma notation is only an instruction: substitute each value of the index, then add. Everything else is bookkeeping. Three closed forms turn that bookkeeping into one line:

SumClosed formExample
Σk=1..n cn·cΣk=1..40 12 = 480
Σk=1..n kn(n + 1)/2Σk=1..40 k = 820
Σk=1..n k²n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6Σk=1..25 k² = 5,525
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — total quarterly bonus paid by a firm

A firm pays each of its 40 sales staff a bonus of $12 base plus $7 per rank position, where the staff member ranked k gets 7k + 12 dollars. The total bonus bill is Σk=140 (7k + 12). Find it.

  1. Split the sum across the plus sign: Σ(7k + 12) = Σ7k + Σ12.
  2. Pull the constant 7 out of the first piece: Σ7k = 7·Σk.
  3. Σk=1..40 k = 40(41)/2 = 820, so the first piece is 7 × 820 = 5,740.
  4. The second piece is a constant added 40 times: 12 × 40 = 480.
  5. Total = 5,740 + 480 = $6,220.
Answer: $6,220.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a sum that does not start at k = 1

A quality lab logs k² defective units in week k. Find the total defects across weeks 6 through 25, that is Σk=625 k².

  1. The closed form only works from k = 1, so build the answer as a difference: Σ6..25 = Σ1..25 − Σ1..5.
  2. Σ1..25 k² = 25(26)(51)/6 = 33,150/6 = 5,525.
  3. Σ1..5 k² = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 = 55.
  4. Subtract: 5,525 − 55 = 5,470.

Notice the cut-off: you subtract everything up to k = 5, not up to k = 6, because week 6 belongs to the answer.

Answer: 5,470 defective units.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Do not distribute a constant across a squared sum. Σ(3k)² is 9·Σk², not 3·Σk². And Σk² is not (Σk)²: for n = 25 the first is 5,525 and the second is 820² = 672,400 — different by a factor of over a hundred. Finally, when the index starts above 1, subtract the terms strictly before the start.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Count the terms before you compute. A sum from k = 6 to k = 25 has 25 − 6 + 1 = 20 terms, not 19. That off-by-one is the same one from arithmetic sequences and it shows up in the constant piece: Σk=6..25 9 = 9 × 20 = 180.

Partial ranges, and translating a word problem

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Summing 4 + 5 + 6 + … + 12

The formula Sₙ = n(n+1)/2 adds up from 1, so subtract the part you do not want.

  1. Sum 1 … 12 = 12 × 13 / 2 = 78.
  2. Sum 1 … 3 = 3 × 4 / 2 = 6.
  3. Subtract: 78 − 6 = 72.

Take the sum up to the top of your range and remove the sum up to just below the bottom. Subtracting S₄ instead of S₃ would wrongly delete the 4 you meant to keep.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Turning words into sigma notation

A gym charges member k a fee of 20 + 4k dollars, for members 1 through 25.

  1. The term is the fee for one member: (20 + 4k).
  2. The index runs over the members: k = 1 to 25.
  3. So the total is Σk=125 (20 + 4k).
  4. Split it: 25 × 20 + 4 × (1 + 2 + … + 25) = 500 + 4 × 325 = 500 + 1300 = 1,800.
