A sequence has infinitely many terms, so the natural question is what happens to them in the long run. The limit of a sequence is the value the terms approach as n grows without bound. If such a value exists the sequence converges; if not, it diverges.

SequenceTermsBehaviour
aₙ = 1/n1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, …converges to 0
aₙ = n1, 2, 3, 4, …diverges — grows without bound
aₙ = (−1)ⁿ−1, 1, −1, 1, …diverges — oscillates, settles nowhere
aₙ = (n + 1)/n2, 1.5, 1.33, 1.25, …converges to 1
aₙ = (1/2)ⁿ1/2, 1/4, 1/8, …converges to 0

The third row is worth pausing on. The terms of (−1)ⁿ stay small and never approach any single value — they bounce between two. Divergence does not require growing to infinity; it only requires the absence of a limit.

Evaluating limits of rational sequences

For a ratio of polynomials, the outcome is decided entirely by the highest power in each part. The reliable method is to divide every term by the highest power of n in the denominator, after which every term of the form c/nk goes to 0.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — find the limit of (3n² + 2n) / (5n² − 1)
1.
Highest power in the denominator: n².
2.
Divide every term by n²: (3 + 2/n) / (5 − 1/n²).
3.
As n → ∞, both 2/n and 1/n² go to 0.
4.
The limit is 3/5. So the sequence converges to 0.6.

That gives a shortcut worth having. Comparing the degree of the numerator with the degree of the denominator settles it: equal degrees give the ratio of the leading coefficients, a smaller numerator degree gives 0, and a larger numerator degree diverges.

ComparisonLimit
numerator degree < denominator degree0
degrees equalratio of leading coefficients
numerator degree > denominator degreediverges

Geometric sequences and monotonicity

For aₙ = rn, the limit is 0 when |r| < 1, is 1 when r = 1, and diverges otherwise. That is the same |r| < 1 condition as the infinite geometric sum in 6.2, and it is not a coincidence: a series can only converge if its terms shrink toward zero.

Two descriptive terms appear in questions. A sequence is monotonic if it always increases or always decreases, and bounded if its terms stay within fixed limits. A sequence that is both monotonic and bounded must converge — it is heading in one direction and cannot escape, so it has to settle.

📘 DEFINITION

Limit of a sequence: the value the terms approach as n grows without bound

Converges: the terms approach a single finite value

Diverges: no limit exists — the terms grow without bound or oscillate

Monotonic: always increasing or always decreasing

Bounded: all terms lie within fixed upper and lower limits

Oscillating sequence: one that alternates without settling

Leading coefficient: the coefficient of the highest power in a polynomial

★ ON THE OA

A sequence converges when its terms approach one finite value and diverges otherwise — including when it oscillates. For a ratio of polynomials, compare degrees: smaller on top gives 0, equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients, larger on top diverges.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For any limit as n → ∞, treat c/n, c/n² and rⁿ with |r| < 1 as going to zero. Nearly every sequence limit in this course reduces to spotting those.

Convergence, precisely

📘 DEFINITION

aₙ → L means: for every tolerance ε > 0, there is an index N such that every term after N is within ε of L.

Read it as a challenge and a response. Someone names a band however narrow; you must be able to name a point past which the sequence never leaves it.

📊 FIGURE — a sequence settling into the ε-band around L
SequenceBehaviourLimit
aₙ = 1/nconverges0
aₙ = (3n + 1)/(n + 2)converges — divide top and bottom by n3
aₙ = rⁿ with |r| < 1converges0
aₙ = rⁿ with |r| > 1diverges to ±∞none
aₙ = (−1)ⁿoscillates — bounded but not convergentnone
aₙ = ndivergesnone

For a ratio of polynomials, the limit is decided by the highest powers: divide every term by the largest power of n and read off what survives. (3n + 1)/(n + 2) becomes (3 + 1/n)/(1 + 2/n) → 3/1 = 3.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Bounded does not mean convergent. (−1)ⁿ never leaves [−1, 1] and still has no limit, because it never settles. What is true is the monotone convergence theorem: a sequence that is both bounded and monotonic must converge.

📊 FIGURE — convergence: the terms settle into any band you draw around L

\"Converges to L\" means: name any tolerance you like, however small, and from some point onward every term of the sequence is within that tolerance of L. The green band is the tolerance; the sequence enters it and never leaves. If no single number L works, the sequence diverges — either to infinity, or by oscillating.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — average cost per parcel

A courier has fixed costs of $9,500 per month plus $240 of variable cost per parcel. The average cost per parcel when n parcels are shipped is aₙ = (9,500 + 240n)/n. What does the average cost approach as volume grows?

  1. Split the fraction: aₙ = 9,500/n + 240n/n = 240 + 9,500/n.
  2. As n grows, 9,500/n gets arbitrarily small: at n = 100 it is 95, at n = 1,000 it is 9.50, at n = 100,000 it is 0.095.
  3. So the sequence approaches 240 + 0.
  4. lim aₙ = 240. The average never actually reaches $240, but it gets as close as you please.

The general rule this illustrates: for a ratio of polynomials, compare the highest powers. Same degree → the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients. Bigger degree on the bottom → limit 0. Bigger degree on the top → diverges.

Answer: The average cost converges to $240 per parcel.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two look-alike sequences, only one of which converges

A sensor is calibrated two ways. Reading A on day n is aₙ = 3 + (−1)ⁿ/n. Reading B on day n is bₙ = 180 + 45(−1)ⁿ. Which readings settle down?

  1. List A: a₁ = 2, a₂ = 3.5, a₃ = 2.667, a₄ = 3.25, a₅ = 2.8, a₆ = 3.167. The values bounce, but the size of the bounce is 1/n, which shrinks to 0.
  2. So aₙ − 3 = (−1)ⁿ/n, and |aₙ − 3| = 1/n → 0. Reading A converges to 3.
  3. List B: b₁ = 135, b₂ = 225, b₃ = 135, b₄ = 225, … The bounce is always 45; it never shrinks.
  4. No single L can have every later term near it — half the terms sit at 135 and half at 225. Reading B diverges by oscillation.
Answer: A converges to 3; B diverges, even though B is bounded.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Alternating does not mean divergent, and bounded does not mean convergent. Reading A above alternates yet converges, because the swing shrinks. Reading B is trapped between 135 and 225 forever yet diverges, because the swing does not shrink. The question is never \"does it wobble?\" — it is \"does the wobble die out?\"

🎯 EXAM TIP

For a quotient of polynomials, do not plug in large numbers — divide top and bottom by the highest power of n on the bottom. For aₙ = (6n² + 40n)/(3n² + 500), divide through by n²: (6 + 40/n)/(3 + 500/n²) → 6/3 = 2. It takes one line and never goes wrong.

Two techniques for sequence limits

Ratio of polynomials. Compare the highest powers of n. If the top and bottom have the same degree the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients; if the bottom wins the limit is 0; if the top wins it diverges. Dividing every term by the highest power of n in the denominator makes this fall out.

Linearity. Limits respect sums and constant multiples, so the limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, and lim(c·aₙ) = c·lim aₙ. That is what lets you break a messy expression into pieces and take each limit separately.

A series is what you get by adding a sequence's terms. The distinction matters because they behave differently: the sequence 1, 1/2, 1/3, … converges to 0, while the series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverges. Terms shrinking to zero is necessary for a series to converge, and it is not sufficient.

The bridge between the two is the partial sum Sn — the total of the first n terms. Partial sums form a sequence of their own, and the whole theory of series is the statement that a series converges exactly when its sequence of partial sums converges.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — partial sums of 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + …
S₁ = 1/2                       = 0.5\nS₂ = 1/2 + 1/4                 = 0.75\nS₃ = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8           = 0.875\nS₄ = …                         = 0.9375\nS₅ =                           = 0.96875\n\nThe partial sums climb toward 1 and never pass it,\nso the series converges to 1.

The two series with formulas

📐 Finite sum formulas
Arithmetic
Sₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2
Geometric
Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), r ≠ 1
Infinite geometric
S = a₁/(1 − r), only when |r| < 1
First n integers
Σ i = n(n + 1)/2
First n squares
Σ i² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6

Only arithmetic and geometric series have simple closed forms, and that is why they dominate exam questions. For anything else the task is not to compute the sum but to decide whether it converges — which is 6.6 and 6.7.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a savings problem — deposit £100, then 5% more each month, for 12 months
1.
Recognise the type: each term is the previous one times 1.05, so it is geometric with a₁ = 100 and r = 1.05.
2.
Twelve terms, so n = 12.
3.
S₁₂ = 100(1.05¹² − 1)/(1.05 − 1).
4.
1.05¹² ≈ 1.7959, so S₁₂ ≈ 100(0.7959)/0.05.
5.
≈ £1,591.71.

The first step is the one that decides the answer. Identify whether the terms are being added to or multiplied by a constant before reaching for a formula, because using the arithmetic formula on a geometric series produces a plausible number that is simply wrong.

Telescoping series

One more type is worth recognising because it appears without warning. In a telescoping series, consecutive terms cancel, leaving only the ends. For Σ (1/n − 1/(n+1)) from 1 to N, everything in the middle cancels and the sum collapses to 1 − 1/(N+1) — which converges to 1.

📘 DEFINITION

Series: the sum of the terms of a sequence

Partial sum (Sₙ): the sum of the first n terms

Convergent series: one whose partial sums approach a finite limit

Divergent series: one whose partial sums do not settle

Finite series: a sum with a fixed number of terms

Telescoping series: one in which consecutive terms cancel, leaving only the ends

★ ON THE OA

A series is the sum of a sequence. The partial sum is the total of the first n terms, and a series converges exactly when its partial sums converge. Only arithmetic and geometric series have simple closed-form sums — identify which before applying a formula.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Terms approaching zero does not guarantee convergence. The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … has terms going to zero and still diverges — which is exactly why the tests in 6.7 exist.

A series is the limit of its partial sums

📘 DEFINITION

The nth partial sum Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ. The series is the limit of the sequence S₁, S₂, S₃, … — so a series is a sequence question in disguise.

📊 FIGURE — adding 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 + … as lengths on a line
SeriesSₙ formulaConverges?
ArithmeticSₙ = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2never, unless d = 0
Geometric, finiteSₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r)—
Geometric, infiniteS = a₁/(1 − r)only when |r| < 1
Telescopingmost terms cancel in pairsdepends what is left
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a telescoping series: Σ from n=1 to ∞ of 1/(n(n+1))

Split the term: 1/(n(n+1)) = 1/n − 1/(n+1).

So Sₙ = (1 − ½) + (½ − ⅓) + (⅓ − ¼) + … + (1/n − 1/(n+1)). Every interior term cancels with its neighbour, leaving Sₙ = 1 − 1/(n+1).

As n → ∞ that goes to 1. Telescoping questions are always solved by writing out three or four terms and watching what survives at the two ends.

📊 FIGURE — a series is the running total of a sequence

A sequence is the list; a series is what you get when you add the list up. The nth partial sum Sₙ stops after n terms, and the picture shows the key relationship: Sn = Sn−1 + an. Every partial sum is a finite number, even when the infinite series that they build toward diverges.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a delivery route that adds seven stops a week

A courier handled 18 deliveries in week 1 and 7 more each week after that. How many deliveries in total across the first 30 weeks?

  1. Arithmetic with a₁ = 18, d = 7, n = 30.
  2. The sum formula needs the last term, so first: a₃₀ = 18 + (30 − 1)(7) = 18 + 203 = 221.
  3. S₃₀ = n(a₁ + a₃₀)/2 = 30(18 + 221)/2.
  4. = 30(239)/2 = 15 × 239.
  5. S₃₀ = 3,585 deliveries.
Answer: 3,585 deliveries in 30 weeks.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a geometric partial sum

A social post is shared 3 times in hour 1, and the number of shares is 4 times the previous hour thereafter. What is the total number of shares over the first 8 hours?

  1. Geometric with a₁ = 3, r = 4, n = 8.
  2. Sₙ = a₁(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) = 3(4⁸ − 1)/(4 − 1).
  3. 4⁸ = 65,536, so the numerator is 3(65,535).
  4. Divide by r − 1 = 3: the 3s cancel, leaving 65,535.
  5. S₈ = 65,535 shares.

The exponent here is n, not n − 1. Compare with the nth-term formula a₈ = 3·4⁷ = 49,152, which does use n − 1. Two formulas, two different exponents — write both on your scratch sheet before you start.

Answer: 65,535 shares.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Sₙ is the total of n terms, not the nth term. A question asking \"how many deliveries in week 30?\" wants a₃₀ = 221; one asking \"how many deliveries in the first 30 weeks?\" wants S₃₀ = 3,585. Read for the words in total, altogether and cumulative. Second trap: dividing by r − 1 when r < 1 gives a negative denominator, so use a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) instead and keep everything positive.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Both sum formulas can be checked instantly on small n. For the geometric one, S₂ should equal a₁ + a₁r = 3 + 12 = 15, and the formula gives 3(4² − 1)/3 = 15. ✓ If your formula fails at n = 2 you have mis-remembered it, and you have caught it in ten seconds.

Partial sums, and picking the formula

The \"series sum\" up to n and the \"nth partial sum\" are the same calculation under two names: Sₙ = a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ. A series is the sequence of these partial sums, which is why an infinite sum is defined as their limit.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Choosing between the arithmetic and geometric formula

A repayment pays $640 in month 1 and 5% less each month. Total over 24 months?

  1. \"5% less than the month before\" is multiplication by 0.95 — a constant ratio, so it is geometric, not arithmetic.
  2. a₁ = 640, r = 0.95, n = 24.
  3. Sₙ = a₁(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) = 640(1 − 0.95²⁴)/(1 − 0.95).
  4. That comes to about $9,063.

The tell is always the same: a constant difference means arithmetic, a constant percentage or ratio means geometric.

An infinite series asks you to add endlessly many terms, and the surprise is that it sometimes has a finite answer. The definition makes this precise: the series converges to S when its partial sums approach S, and diverges when they do not.

Two named series carry most of the exam weight, and they are worth knowing as a contrasting pair because they look similar and behave oppositely.

SeriesTermsBehaviourWhy
Geometric, |r| < 11 + 1/2 + 1/4 + …converges to a₁/(1 − r)terms shrink geometrically — fast
Harmonic1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + …divergesterms shrink, but far too slowly

The harmonic series is the standard counterexample to the intuition that shrinking terms must add to something finite. Grouping shows why: 1/3 + 1/4 is more than 1/2, 1/5 + … + 1/8 is more than 1/2, the next eight terms exceed 1/2 again, and so on forever. Infinitely many half-units add to infinity, however slowly.

The p-series

The harmonic series generalises. A p-series is Σ 1/np, and the whole family is settled by one comparison.

Σ 1/np converges when p > 1, diverges when p ≤ 1

SeriespResult
1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + …p = 1diverges — the harmonic series
1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + …p = 2converges
1 + 1/√2 + 1/√3 + …p = 1/2diverges
1 + 1/8 + 1/27 + …p = 3converges

The boundary sits exactly at p = 1, and it is inclusive on the diverging side: p = 1 itself diverges. Anything strictly above 1 converges, however slightly — p = 1.001 converges.

Alternating series

A series whose signs alternate, like 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + …, is easier to converge because each term partly cancels the last. The alternating series test says it converges if the absolute values decrease monotonically and approach zero.

That gives a striking result: the alternating harmonic series converges even though the plain harmonic series diverges. Same terms, alternating signs, opposite outcome — which is why the sign pattern must be checked before applying any test.

Why the harmonic series is the case to remember

It is worth being able to reproduce the grouping argument, because it is the reason a whole intuition fails. Group the terms as 1 + 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) + (1/5 + … + 1/8) + (1/9 + … + 1/16) + …. Each bracket contains terms all at least as large as the smallest one in it, and there are enough of them that every bracket totals more than 1/2.

Since there are infinitely many brackets, the sum exceeds 1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 + …, which grows without bound. The series therefore diverges — slowly. It takes over ten thousand terms to pass 10, and more terms than there are atoms in the observable universe to pass 100, which is why the divergence is so counter-intuitive.

Keep the contrast with Σ 1/n² in mind as the pair to reason from. Both have terms going to zero; one diverges and one converges, and the only difference is how fast the terms shrink. That is precisely what the p-series boundary at p = 1 is measuring.

Absolute and conditional convergence

An alternating series that converges divides into two cases, and the distinction is examined by name. Take the series and replace every term with its absolute value. If that version also converges, the original is absolutely convergent. If the absolute version diverges while the original converges, it is conditionally convergent.

The alternating harmonic series is the standard example of the second: 1 − 1/2 + 1/3 − 1/4 + … converges, but stripping the signs gives the harmonic series, which diverges. So it converges conditionally — it needs the alternation to do so.

📘 DEFINITION

Infinite series: the sum of infinitely many terms

Converges to S: the partial sums approach the finite value S

Harmonic series: Σ 1/n — diverges despite its terms going to zero

p-series: Σ 1/nᵖ — converges when p > 1, diverges when p ≤ 1

Alternating series: one whose terms alternate in sign

Alternating series test: converges if the absolute values decrease to zero

★ ON THE OA

A p-series Σ 1/nᵖ converges when p > 1 and diverges when p ≤ 1. The harmonic series (p = 1) diverges. A geometric series converges when |r| < 1. Those three facts answer most convergence questions on their own.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Identify the family before reaching for a test. If it is geometric, check |r|. If it is 1/nᵖ, check p against 1. Only when it is neither do you need the tests in the next lesson.

What convergence actually means

📘 DEFINITION

An infinite series converges when its sequence of partial sums Sₙ approaches a finite limit. The series is the limit of the partial sums — nothing is ever \"added infinitely many times\".

📊 FIGURE — the partial sums of a geometric series with r = ½
SeriesConverges whenSum
Geometric Σ a·rⁿ|r| < 1a/(1 − r)
p-series Σ 1/n^pp > 1no simple closed form
Harmonic Σ 1/nnever — diverges—
Any series whose terms do not → 0neverdivergence test
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The divergence test is one-directional. If the terms do not approach 0 the series definitely diverges. If they do approach 0, that proves nothing — the harmonic series 1 + ½ + ⅓ + ¼ + … has terms going to 0 and still diverges to infinity. Treating \"terms → 0\" as proof of convergence is the classic error this section is testing.

📊 FIGURE — the geometric test: everything depends on |r|

An infinite series is the limit of its partial sums. For a geometric series the answer is decided entirely by the ratio: if |r| < 1 the pieces shrink fast enough that the running total settles on a₁/(1 − r); otherwise no finite total exists. The bar above is the proof by picture — each new piece fills half of what is left, so the leftover gap shrinks to nothing but never overshoots.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — total distance travelled by a bouncing ball

A ball is dropped from 240 cm and each bounce returns it to 60% of its previous height. What total vertical distance does it travel before coming to rest?

  1. The first drop is a one-off: 240 cm down.
  2. After that, each bounce is travelled twice — up to a height, then back down.
  3. The bounce heights are 240(0.6) = 144, then 144(0.6) = 86.4, and so on: geometric with a₁ = 144 and r = 0.6.
  4. Sum of the bounce heights: 144/(1 − 0.6) = 144/0.4 = 360 cm.
  5. Each of those is travelled up and down, so double it: 2 × 360 = 720 cm.
  6. Total = 240 + 720 = 960 cm.
Answer: 960 cm, or 9.6 metres.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — turning a repeating decimal into a fraction

A measurement is recorded as 0.727272… Express it as an exact fraction.

  1. Write it as a sum: 0.72 + 0.0072 + 0.000072 + …
  2. Each term is the previous one divided by 100, so it is geometric with a₁ = 0.72 and r = 0.01.
  3. |r| = 0.01 < 1, so the series converges and S = a₁/(1 − r).
  4. S = 0.72 / 0.99 = 72/99.
  5. Divide top and bottom by 9: 8/11.

Check: 8 ÷ 11 = 0.727272… ✓

Answer: 0.727272… = 8/11 exactly.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

a₁ in S = a₁/(1 − r) is the first term of the series you are actually summing — not the number the problem opens with. In the bouncing-ball problem the drop of 240 is not part of the geometric series; the series starts at 144. Students who write 240/(1 − 0.6) = 600 have summed the wrong series. Second trap: this formula is for infinite geometric series only. The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + … has terms going to 0 and still diverges.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Terms going to zero is necessary but not sufficient for convergence. If the terms do not go to zero the series definitely diverges (that is the nth-term test, and it is a free mark). If they do go to zero you have learned nothing yet and must use another test.

What each test can and cannot tell you

If aₙ → 0, the divergence test is inconclusive — it says nothing at all. The harmonic series 1 + ½ + ⅓ + … has terms going to 0 and still diverges, while 1 + ¼ + ⅑ + … also has terms going to 0 and converges. Same signal, opposite outcomes, so the signal cannot decide.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The walk that totals exactly 1 mile

Walk ½ mile, then ¼, then ⅛, for ever.

  1. Geometric with a₁ = ½ and r = ½.
  2. |r| < 1, so it converges to a₁/(1 − r).
  3. (½)/(1 − ½) = (½)/(½) = 1 mile.

Infinitely many steps, a finite total — each step is half of what remains, so the distance is approached but never overshot.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Identifying a₁ when the first payment happens now

A machine is serviced immediately at $2,400, and every service after costs 0.8 of the one before, for ever.

  1. The immediate $2,400 is a₁ — this is the step to get right.
  2. r = 0.8, and |r| < 1, so the total is a₁/(1 − r).
  3. 2400/(1 − 0.8) = 2400/0.2 = $12,000.

If the first service were a year later, a₁ would instead be 2400 × 0.8. Read carefully whether the first payment is included.

When a series is neither geometric nor a p-series, convergence has to be decided by a test. Three appear in this course, and using them in the right order saves most of the work.

1. The divergence test — always first

If the terms do not approach zero, the series definitely diverges. Compute lim an before anything else, because it is cheap and it settles many questions immediately.

If limn→∞ an ≠ 0, the series diverges.

The critical restriction is that this test only ever proves divergence. If the limit is zero, the test says nothing at all and you must try something else — the harmonic series has terms going to zero and diverges anyway. Concluding convergence from a zero limit is the standard error, and it has a name: the converse of the test is false.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the divergence test in use
Σ n/(2n + 1)      lim = 1/2 ≠ 0   ->  DIVERGES ✓ (settled)\n\nΣ 1/n             lim = 0         ->  test is INCONCLUSIVE\n                                      (it happens to diverge, but not\n                                       because of this test)

2. The p-series and geometric checks

If the terms do go to zero, look for a recognisable family next. A geometric series converges when |r| < 1; a p-series Σ 1/np converges when p > 1. Between them these cover a large share of exam items with no calculation at all.

3. The integral test

For a series whose terms come from a function that is positive, continuous and decreasing, the series and the corresponding improper integral converge or diverge together.

Σ f(n) and ∫1∞ f(x) dx share the same fate.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — use the integral test on Σ 1/n²
1.
Check the conditions: f(x) = 1/x² is positive, continuous and decreasing on [1, ∞). ✓
2.
Evaluate the integral: ∫₁∞ x⁻² dx = [−1/x]₁∞.
3.
= (0) − (−1) = 1 — a finite value.
4.
The integral converges, so the series converges. (It agrees with the p-series rule, p = 2 > 1.)

Note that the integral's value is not the sum of the series. The test compares behaviour, not totals — it tells you the series converges, not what it converges to.

Order to work inTestCan prove
1stDivergence testdivergence only
2ndGeometric / p-serieseither — instantly, if it fits
3rdIntegral testeither, when the conditions hold
—Alternating series testconvergence of an alternating series
📘 DEFINITION

Divergence test: if the terms do not approach 0, the series diverges; otherwise inconclusive

Inconclusive: the test gives no information and another must be used

Integral test: a series and its improper integral converge or diverge together

Improper integral: an integral with an infinite bound

Conditions for the integral test: the function must be positive, continuous and decreasing

p-series test: Σ 1/nᵖ converges exactly when p > 1

★ ON THE OA

Run the divergence test first: terms not going to zero means it diverges. But a limit of zero proves nothing — that is the trap. Then check for a geometric or p-series. Only after that reach for the integral test, and only when the function is positive, continuous and decreasing.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

\"The terms go to zero, so it converges\" is false, and it is the most commonly tested misconception in this chapter. The harmonic series is the counterexample to quote.

Which test, in which order

Run the cheap check first. The divergence test costs one limit and settles a large share of exam questions outright.

📊 FIGURE — the order to try the tests in
TestConverges whenDiverges when
Divergence (nth term)never concludes convergencelim aₙ ≠ 0
Geometric Σarⁿ|r| < 1|r| ≥ 1
p-series Σ1/n^pp > 1p ≤ 1
Integral test∫f(x)dx converges∫f(x)dx diverges
Ratio testlim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| < 1lim > 1 (= 1 is inconclusive)
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The harmonic series Σ1/n is the p-series with p = 1, so it diverges — even though its terms go to 0 and it grows agonisingly slowly. It is the standard counterexample to \"terms → 0 means it converges\", and it appears on nearly every exam that covers this topic.

The integral test requires the function to be positive, continuous and decreasing on the interval. Skipping that check is a real error, not a formality — the test is not valid otherwise.

📊 FIGURE — the integral test, drawn: rectangles versus the curve

Three tests cover almost everything the exam asks. Use them in this order, because each is cheaper than the next:

TestWhen it appliesWhat it says
nth-term (divergence) testalways — try it firstIf lim aₙ ≠ 0 the series diverges. If lim aₙ = 0 it tells you nothing.
p-seriesterms of the form 1/npConverges if p > 1, diverges if p ≤ 1. The harmonic series is p = 1, the boundary case, and it diverges.
Integral testaₙ = f(n) with f positive, continuous, decreasingThe series and ∫₁∞ f(x) dx do the same thing — both converge or both diverge.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a queue that never clears — the nth-term test

At a call centre, the fraction of calls still waiting after n minutes is modelled by aₙ = n/(4n + 9). Does Σ aₙ converge?

  1. Try the cheapest test first: what is lim aₙ?
  2. Divide top and bottom by n: aₙ = 1/(4 + 9/n).
  3. As n grows, 9/n → 0, so aₙ → 1/4.
  4. The limit is 1/4, which is not zero.
  5. By the nth-term test the series diverges. (Intuitively: you keep adding roughly a quarter, forever.)
Answer: Diverges, by the nth-term test.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two decay models — p decides everything

A signal-loss model gives Σ 1/n1.5; a competing model gives Σ 1/√n. Which total is finite?

  1. Both are p-series, so read off p in each case.
  2. First model: 1/n1.5 has p = 1.5 > 1 → converges (its total is about 2.612).
  3. Second model: 1/√n = 1/n0.5 has p = 0.5 ≤ 1 → diverges.
  4. Confirm the second with the integral test: ∫₁∞ x−1/2 dx = [2√x]₁∞ = ∞, so the series diverges too.

Both sets of terms go to zero. Only the speed differs, and p is the measure of that speed.

Answer: Σ 1/n^1.5 converges; Σ 1/√n diverges.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

The nth-term test can never prove convergence. \"The terms go to 0, therefore it converges\" is the single most common false statement in this unit, and Σ 1/n is the standing counterexample. Second trap: a square root is a fractional power. 1/√n means p = 1/2, which is below the cut-off, so it diverges — a lot of students see the root and guess \"converges\".

🎯 EXAM TIP

Memorise the boundary rather than the rule: p = 1 is the harmonic series, and it diverges. Anything with a bigger exponent converges; anything with a smaller one diverges. If you can recall which way the boundary case falls, you can reconstruct the whole p-series rule under exam pressure.

One-directional tests

The divergence (nth-term) test is one-directional: it can only ever prove divergence. If lim aₙ ≠ 0 the series diverges, full stop. If lim aₙ = 0 you have learned nothing and must try another test.

Put the other way round, \"terms → 0\" is necessary but not sufficient for convergence: every convergent series has it, but having it does not make a series converge.

The p-series result — Σ 1/np converges exactly when p > 1 — is not a separate fact to memorise. It comes from the integral test: the series and ∫₁∞ x−p dx converge or diverge together, and that integral is finite precisely when p > 1.

A graph is a set of vertices together with a set of edges joining pairs of them — written G = (V, E). It is the most general structure in this course, and everything from road networks to social networks to the relations of Unit 6 is one.

In fact a graph is a relation: the edge set is a subset of V × V, which is the definition from 3.3. An undirected graph corresponds to a symmetric relation, and a digraph to any relation at all.

TypeMeaning
Undirectededges have no direction — {a, b} is the same edge as {b, a}
Directed (digraph)edges have a direction — (a, b) is not (b, a)
Weightedeach edge carries a number: distance, cost, capacity
Simpleno loops and no repeated edges
Multigraphrepeated edges between the same pair are allowed
Complete (Kn)every pair of vertices is joined
Bipartitevertices split into two groups, edges only between groups

Degree and the handshaking lemma

The degree of a vertex is the number of edges meeting it, with a loop counting twice. Summing the degrees over the whole graph counts every edge exactly twice — once from each end — which gives the result the exam asks for by name.

Handshaking lemma: Σ deg(v) = 2 · |E|

Two consequences follow, and both are examined. The sum of all degrees is always even. And the number of vertices with odd degree is always even — because the odd degrees must pair up to keep the total even.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a graph has 5 vertices with degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 — how many edges?
1.
Sum the degrees: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12.
2.
Apply the lemma: 2|E| = 12.
3.
|E| = 6 edges. Note the two odd degrees — an even count, as required.

The lemma also rules things out instantly. A graph with degrees 3, 3, 3 is impossible, because three odd degrees cannot sum to an even number — so a question offering that degree sequence is testing whether you checked.

Complete graphs and edge counts

In a complete graph Kn every pair of vertices is joined, so the number of edges is the number of ways to choose two vertices from n.

|E(Kn)| = n(n − 1)/2

K₄ has 4(3)/2 = 6 edges and every vertex has degree 3. That formula is also the counting result \"n choose 2\", which is where it comes from.

📘 DEFINITION

Graph G = (V, E): a set of vertices and a set of edges joining pairs of them

Vertex (node): a point of the graph

Edge: a connection between two vertices

Degree deg(v): the number of edges meeting a vertex; a loop counts twice

Handshaking lemma: the degrees sum to twice the number of edges

Adjacent: two vertices joined by an edge

Complete graph Kₙ: every pair joined; n(n − 1)/2 edges

Bipartite graph: vertices split into two sets with edges only between them

Simple graph: no loops, no repeated edges

★ ON THE OA

A graph is vertices plus edges, and the degree of a vertex is its edge count. The handshaking lemma says the degrees sum to 2 × |E|, so the number of odd-degree vertices is always even. A complete graph Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges.

🎯 EXAM TIP

When a question gives a degree sequence, add it up first. An odd total is impossible, and an odd number of odd degrees is impossible — either check can eliminate options before any real work.

Degree and the handshake theorem

📊 FIGURE — A graph, its degrees, and the handshake theorem
The degree of a vertex is the number of edge-ends touching it. Summing every degree counts each edge twice, so Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. Here the degrees 2+3+2+2+1 = 10 = 2 · 5 edges — a quick sanity check you can run on any exam graph.
📘 DEFINITION

Handshake theorem: the sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges, because every edge contributes 1 to each of its two endpoints.

Σ deg(v) = 2|E|

Two consequences the exam leans on. First, the number of odd-degree vertices is always even — an odd count is impossible, so a question offering one is offering an impossible graph. Second, given the degree sum you get the edge count for free by halving it.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a graph has degree sequence 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 — how many edges?

Sum = 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 12. Edges = 12 / 2 = 6.

Check the parity rule: two vertices have odd degree, which is an even count ✓. Had the sequence been 3, 2, 2, 2, 2 the sum would be 11 — odd, so no such graph exists, and that is the answer to \"which of these degree sequences is impossible\".

GraphVerticesEdgesEvery degree
Complete Kₙnn(n−1)/2n − 1
Cycle Cₙnn2
Path Pₙnn − 12, except 1 at the two ends
Treenn − 1varies
Complete bipartite Km,nm + nm × nn on one side, m on the other
📊 FIGURE — the handshake theorem, counted on a route map

The degree of a vertex is the number of edge-ends meeting it. Add up all the degrees and every edge gets counted twice — once at each endpoint — which is the whole content of the handshake theorem: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|. Two consequences fall straight out of it, and both are exam favourites.

📘 DEFINITION

Handshake Theorem. In any undirected graph, the sum of the degrees equals twice the number of edges. Corollary 1: the degree sum is always even. Corollary 2: the number of vertices of odd degree is always even — odd degrees can only occur in pairs.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — how many routes does the network have?

A regional airline serves six airports whose degrees are 4, 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2. How many routes are in the network?

  1. Add the degrees: 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 16.
  2. By the handshake theorem this equals 2|E|, so 2|E| = 16.
  3. |E| = 16 / 2 = 8 routes.
  4. Sanity check: 16 is even, as it must be, and exactly two airports (the two of degree 3) have odd degree — an even count, as required.
Answer: 8 routes.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a network that cannot exist

A planner claims to have built a six-site fibre network with degrees 5, 4, 3, 2, 2 and 1. Is that possible?

  1. Add the degrees: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 17.
  2. The handshake theorem says the sum must equal 2|E|, which is even for every graph.
  3. 17 is odd, so no graph has this degree sequence.
  4. The second corollary confirms it independently: the odd degrees here are 5, 3 and 1 — three of them, and the count of odd-degree vertices must be even.
  5. Verdict: impossible, and no amount of redrawing will fix it.

Also worth knowing: a simple graph on n vertices has a maximum degree of n − 1, since a vertex can join each of the others at most once. A claimed degree of 6 among six sites would be impossible for that separate reason.

Answer: Impossible — the degree sum is odd.
🎯 EXAM TIP

For the complete graph Kn, every one of the n vertices joins all n − 1 others, so |E| = n(n − 1)/2 = C(n, 2). A nine-city network where every pair has a direct route has 9(8)/2 = 36 routes, and every city has degree 8. Expect this to be asked as \"if every pair of offices needs a dedicated line, how many lines?\"

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

A loop adds 2 to a vertex's degree, not 1, because both of its ends attach to the same vertex. Second trap: degree counts edge-ends, not neighbours. In a multigraph with two parallel routes between the same pair of cities, each city gains 2 degree from that pair although it has only one neighbour there.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Solving for n from an edge count

The complete graph Kₙ has 15 edges. What is n?

  1. Kₙ has n(n − 1)/2 edges — every pair joined once.
  2. Set n(n − 1)/2 = 15, so n(n − 1) = 30.
  3. Consecutive integers multiplying to 30: 6 × 5.
  4. n = 6.

The hypercube Qₖ has 2k vertices, one for each k-bit string, and joins two whenever they differ in exactly one bit. Each vertex therefore has k neighbours — one per bit you could flip — so Qₖ is k-regular. Q₄ is 4-regular.

A drawing is fine for six vertices and useless for six thousand, so graphs are stored in one of two standard forms. The choice is a genuine trade-off, and the exam asks which suits a given situation.

The adjacency matrix

An adjacency matrix is a |V| × |V| grid with a 1 at position (i, j) when an edge joins vertex i to vertex j, and 0 otherwise.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — a small undirected graph
Edges: A–B, A–C, B–C, C–D
ABCDABCD0110101011010010
Symmetric across the diagonal, because the graph is undirected.
Row sums are the degrees: A=2, B=2, C=3, D=1.

Three properties fall out of that example and each is a question in its own right. For an undirected graph the matrix is symmetric. The row sum gives the degree of that vertex. And the main diagonal is all zeros unless the graph has loops.

For a directed graph the symmetry disappears: entry (i, j) records an edge from i to j only. Row sums then give out-degree and column sums give in-degree.

The adjacency list

An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, only the vertices it is joined to.

A: B, C\nB: A, C\nC: A, B, D\nD: C

It records exactly the same graph in far less space when edges are scarce. That is the trade.

Adjacency matrixAdjacency list
Spacealways |V|² entriesproportional to |V| + |E|
\"Is there an edge i–j?\"instant — one lookupscan vertex i's list
\"List all neighbours of i\"scan a whole row of |V| entriesinstant — read the list
Best fordense graphs, many edgessparse graphs, few edges

A graph is dense when it has close to the maximum n(n − 1)/2 edges and sparse when it has far fewer. A social network is sparse — you know a few hundred people, not a few billion — which is why real systems use adjacency lists.

One further use of the matrix carries over from 3.5: the k-th power of an adjacency matrix counts walks of length exactly k between each pair of vertices, which is how reachability questions are answered computationally.

📘 DEFINITION

Adjacency matrix: a |V| × |V| grid with 1 where an edge exists

Adjacency list: each vertex paired with the list of its neighbours

Symmetric matrix: what an undirected graph always produces

Row sum: the degree of that vertex, in an undirected graph

Dense graph: a graph with close to the maximum number of edges

Sparse graph: a graph with far fewer edges than the maximum

Incidence matrix: an alternative form with vertices as rows and edges as columns

★ ON THE OA

Two representations: an adjacency matrix (|V| × |V|, entry 1 if an edge exists, symmetric for undirected graphs) and an adjacency list (each vertex lists its neighbours, better for sparse graphs).

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

In an undirected graph, one edge appears twice in the matrix — at (i, j) and (j, i). Counting the 1s and reporting that as the edge count doubles the answer; divide by two.

Picture, matrix, list

📊 FIGURE — one graph written three ways
RepresentationSpaceBest atWeak at
Adjacency matrixO(n²) always\"is there an edge u–v?\" in O(1)wastes space on sparse graphs
Adjacency listO(n + m)walking a vertex's neighboursedge lookup costs O(deg v)
Edge listO(m)algorithms that sort edges, e.g. Kruskalno fast neighbour lookup

For an undirected graph the matrix is always symmetric, and the diagonal is 0 unless the graph has self-loops. For a directed graph it need not be symmetric — that asymmetry is exactly the direction information.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Row sums of an undirected adjacency matrix are the degrees. So the handshake theorem reappears here as \"the sum of all matrix entries equals 2|E|\" — a fast way to count edges from a matrix without listing them.

📊 FIGURE — one graph, two representations

The same network as an adjacency matrix

The adjacency matrix puts a 1 in row i, column j when i and j are joined. In an undirected graph the matrix is always symmetric, and the degree of a vertex is the sum of its row — or equivalently of its column, since the two are identical.

C₁C₂C₃C₄C₅R₁R₂R₃R₄R₅0111010001100101010101010ROW 1 tinted, read ACROSS: Library joins Gym, Hall and Lab → deg(Library) = 3C₁C₂C₃C₄C₅R₁R₂R₃R₄R₅0111010001100101010101010COLUMN 1 tinted, read DOWN: exactly the same three 1s, because walkways run both ways
row i = the neighbours of vertex icolumn i = the same neighbours (undirected ⇒ symmetric)

Order of the labels: R₁/C₁ = Library, R₂/C₂ = Gym, R₃/C₃ = Hall, R₄/C₄ = Lab, R₅/C₅ = Café.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — reading everything off the matrix

From the matrix above, find (a) the degree of the Lab, (b) the total number of walkways, and (c) whether the Gym connects directly to the Hall.

  1. (a) The Lab is R₄. Read row 4 across: 1, 0, 1, 0, 1. Add them: deg(Lab) = 3 — it joins the Library, the Hall and the Café.
  2. (b) Add every entry in the matrix: rows sum to 3 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 12.
  3. Each walkway appears twice in a symmetric matrix (once as (i, j) and once as (j, i)), so |E| = 12 / 2 = 6 walkways.
  4. (c) The Gym is index 2 and the Hall is index 3, so look at row 2, column 3. The entry is 0, so there is no direct walkway between them — you must pass through the Library, the Lab or the Café.
Answer: (a) 3. (b) 6 walkways. (c) No.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — when the network is one-way

A campus shuttle runs one-way loops, so the graph is directed: the matrix records a 1 in row i, column j only when a shuttle runs from i to j. Suppose the Café row reads 0, 1, 0, 0, 0 and the Café column reads 0, 0, 0, 1, 0. Interpret both.

  1. The row lists departures. Row Café = (0, 1, 0, 0, 0) means exactly one shuttle leaves the Café, and it goes to the Gym. So the out-degree of the Café is 1.
  2. The column lists arrivals. Column Café = (0, 0, 0, 1, 0) means exactly one shuttle arrives at the Café, and it comes from the Lab. So the in-degree of the Café is 1.
  3. The matrix is no longer symmetric, and that asymmetry is the one-way information.
  4. General rule for directed graphs: row sum = out-degree, column sum = in-degree, and the sum of all out-degrees equals the sum of all in-degrees equals the number of arcs.
Answer: Row = out (departures); column = in (arrivals).
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Do not halve the entry count in a directed graph. For an undirected graph the number of edges is (sum of all entries)/2, but for a directed graph each arc appears once, so the number of arcs is simply the sum of the entries. Halving is a habit that quietly produces answers exactly twice too small. Second trap: a loop at vertex v puts a 1 at (v, v), and by convention it contributes 2 to deg(v) in an undirected graph even though it is one matrix entry.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Choose the representation to suit the question. \"Are A and B adjacent?\" is one matrix lookup and is instant. \"List everything reachable from A\" is one line of the adjacency list and avoids scanning zeros. For a sparse network — most real ones — the list is far smaller: this campus needs 25 matrix entries but only 12 list entries.

Two graphs drawn differently can be the same graph. Isomorphic graphs have identical structure and differ only in how their vertices are labelled or positioned — formally, there is a bijection between the vertex sets that preserves adjacency.

\"Preserves adjacency\" is the load-bearing phrase: if two vertices are joined in the first graph, their partners must be joined in the second, and if they are not joined, their partners must not be.

The necessary conditions

Checking every possible relabelling is impractical, so the practical method is to look for a reason the graphs cannot match. Three properties must agree.

InvariantMust matchIf it differs
Number of vertices|V₁| = |V₂|not isomorphic — done
Number of edges|E₁| = |E₂|not isomorphic — done
Degree sequencethe sorted list of degrees is identicalnot isomorphic — done
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — eliminating a pair quickly
G1: degrees 3, 3, 2, 2       sorted: [3, 3, 2, 2]\nG2: degrees 3, 2, 2, 2       sorted: [3, 2, 2, 2]\n\nDifferent degree sequences  ->  NOT isomorphic.\nNo further work needed.

The critical qualification is that these conditions are necessary but not sufficient. Two graphs can agree on all three and still fail to be isomorphic, because the degrees can be arranged differently — one graph might join its two degree-3 vertices to each other while the other does not.

So matching invariants never proves isomorphism. To prove it you must exhibit the actual mapping and verify every edge; to disprove it, a single mismatched invariant is enough. That asymmetry is the same one as ∀ and counterexamples in 1.3.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — exhibit an isomorphism
1.
Confirm the invariants agree: same vertex count, edge count and degree sequence.
2.
Match vertices by degree — a degree-3 vertex can only map to a degree-3 vertex.
3.
Write the proposed bijection explicitly, e.g. A→1, B→2, C→3, D→4.
4.
Check every edge: for each edge in the first graph, confirm the mapped pair is an edge in the second.
5.
Check no extra edges exist in the second graph. Both directions must hold.

Other invariants can settle harder cases: the number of cycles of each length, whether the graph is connected, and the number of components. Any structural property that does not depend on labels is fair game.

What isomorphism is actually asserting

Two isomorphic graphs are the same graph drawn differently — same structure, different labels or positions. This matters because a drawing carries information the graph does not: where vertices sit on the page, whether edges cross, how long they look. None of that is part of the graph, which is only a set of vertices and a set of pairs.

So a question showing two very different-looking pictures may well be showing one graph twice. Straightening the edges or moving a vertex changes nothing, and the invariants are exactly the properties that survive such redrawing — which is why they are the right tool.

A practical checking order

Compare vertex counts, then edge counts, then degree sequences, and stop at the first mismatch. If all three agree, look at how the high-degree vertices connect to each other — whether the two degree-3 vertices are adjacent is a structural fact that a degree sequence cannot capture, and it settles most of the remaining cases.

Writing a degree sequence

A degree sequence is conventionally written in non-increasing order — largest first — so that two graphs can be compared term by term. A graph with degrees 2, 3, 1, 3 has degree sequence (3, 3, 2, 1). Sorting is what makes the comparison meaningful, since the labels are arbitrary.

📘 DEFINITION

Isomorphic graphs: graphs related by an adjacency-preserving bijection of their vertices

Graph invariant: a property unchanged by relabelling

Degree sequence: the sorted list of all vertex degrees

Necessary condition: must hold, but does not by itself guarantee the result

Sufficient condition: guarantees the result

Bijection: a one-to-one and onto mapping — from 3.2

★ ON THE OA

Two graphs are isomorphic if a vertex bijection preserves adjacency — same structure, relabelled. The necessary conditions are the same vertex count, edge count and degree sequence — but these can all match and the graphs still not be isomorphic.

🎯 EXAM TIP

To disprove isomorphism, find one differing invariant and stop. To prove it, you must give the mapping and check every edge — there is no shortcut in that direction.

Two pictures of one graph

📘 DEFINITION

Two graphs are isomorphic when a relabelling of the vertices turns one into the other — same structure, different drawing. The bijection must preserve adjacency: u–v is an edge exactly when f(u)–f(v) is.

📊 FIGURE — the same cycle drawn two ways

Position on the page means nothing. Crossing lines mean nothing. Only which vertices are joined counts.

Invariant — must match if isomorphicEnough on its own to PROVE isomorphism?
Number of verticesNo
Number of edgesNo
Degree sequenceNo
Number of cycles of each lengthNo
ConnectednessNo
An explicit vertex mapping that preserves every edgeYes
🎯 EXAM TIP

Invariants are for disproving. If two graphs differ in any invariant they cannot be isomorphic, and that settles the question instantly. If every invariant matches you have proved nothing — you must exhibit the actual mapping. Matching degree sequences is the classic trap: two graphs can share one and still be different.

📊 FIGURE — same counts, same degrees — and still not the same graph

Two graphs are isomorphic when there is a one-to-one relabelling of the vertices of one onto the other that turns every edge into an edge and every non-edge into a non-edge. Position on the page is irrelevant: G and H above look nothing alike and are the same graph.

InvariantMust match if isomorphic?Why it is useful
Number of verticesyesfirst thing to count
Number of edgesyessecond thing to count
Degree sequence (sorted)yescheap and rules out most pairs
Connected / how many componentsyescatches the two-triangles case
Length of the shortest cycleyescatches C₆ versus two triangles
Drawn shape, crossings, labelsnothese are artefacts of the picture
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — proving two graphs ARE isomorphic

G has vertices A–F with edges AB, BC, CD, DE, EF, FA. H has vertices P, Q, R, S, T, U with edges PR, RT, TQ, QS, SU, UP. Show they are isomorphic.

  1. Check the cheap invariants first: both have 6 vertices, 6 edges, and every vertex has degree 2. Nothing rules them out.
  2. Both are single cycles, so write each one as a cycle in order. G: A–B–C–D–E–F–A. H: P–R–T–Q–S–U–P.
  3. Now match them position by position around the cycle:
  4. A→P, B→R, C→T, D→Q, E→S, F→U.
  5. Verify every edge: AB→PR ✓, BC→RT ✓, CD→TQ ✓, DE→QS ✓, EF→SU ✓, FA→UP ✓.
  6. All six edges of G map to the six edges of H, and the map is a bijection, so G ≅ H.

To prove isomorphism you must exhibit the mapping. Matching invariants is never a proof on its own — it only fails to disprove.

Answer: The bijection A→P, B→R, C→T, D→Q, E→S, F→U works.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — proving two graphs are NOT isomorphic

G is the 6-cycle above. K consists of two separate triangles VWX and YZM. Both have 6 vertices, 6 edges, and every vertex of degree 2. Are they isomorphic?

  1. Every count matches, so the easy invariants are useless here — you must find a structural one.
  2. Connectivity: G is connected — you can walk from A to any other vertex. K is not: there is no path from V to Y.
  3. Connectivity is preserved by isomorphism (a relabelling cannot create or destroy a path), so G ≇ K.
  4. A second independent argument: the shortest cycle in K has length 3, while the shortest cycle in G has length 6. Cycle lengths are preserved too.

One invariant that differs is enough. You never need to check all of them, and you certainly never need to try all 720 possible relabellings.

Answer: Not isomorphic — K is disconnected and contains 3-cycles.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Matching degree sequences do not prove isomorphism. This is the single most common wrong answer in the topic, and the two-triangles example is the standard counterexample. Degree sequences are a screening tool: if they differ, stop, the graphs are not isomorphic; if they agree, you have learned nothing and must look at structure.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Work in this order and you will be fast and correct: (1) compare |V|, (2) compare |E|, (3) compare sorted degree sequences, (4) compare number of components, (5) compare shortest cycle length. If any differ, you are done — not isomorphic. Only if all agree do you go hunting for an explicit bijection, and start by matching up the highest-degree vertices.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Matching invariants does not prove isomorphism. Two graphs having the same vertex count, edge count and degree sequence is not guaranteed to make them isomorphic — those tests can only ever prove graphs are not isomorphic. To prove that they are, you must exhibit an explicit bijection and check every edge maps to an edge.

Moving through a graph has three names, and the exam distinguishes them precisely by what is allowed to repeat.

TermRepeated vertices?Repeated edges?Closed?
Walkallowedallowedeither
Trailallowednot allowedeither
Pathnot allowednot allowedno
Cycle (circuit)only the start = endnot allowedyes

So a walk is the loosest notion — wander anywhere, revisit anything. A path is the strictest for an open route: no vertex twice. A cycle is a closed path, returning to where it began without repeating anything else. The length of any of these is its number of edges, not vertices.

Connectivity

A graph is connected when there is a path between every pair of vertices. When it is not, it falls into connected components — maximal pieces that are internally connected and joined to nothing outside.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — components
Vertices: A B C D E\nEdges:   A–B, B–C, D–E\n\nA–B–C is one component;  D–E is another.\nThe graph is DISCONNECTED with 2 components.\nThere is no path from A to D.

For directed graphs the idea splits in two. A digraph is strongly connected when a directed path runs between every ordered pair, and weakly connected when it would be connected if you ignored the directions. A one-way street system can easily be weakly but not strongly connected.

Euler and Hamilton

Two classical questions ask for a route that covers everything, and the difference between them is what \"everything\" means.

EulerHamilton
Must use everyedge exactly oncevertex exactly once
Path exists whenexactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degreeno simple criterion known
Circuit exists whenevery vertex has even degreeno simple criterion known
Also requiresthe graph is connectedthe graph is connected

The Euler condition is one of the most quotable results in the course, and it comes straight from the handshaking argument: every time a route passes through a vertex it uses two edges, one in and one out, so an odd-degree vertex can only be a start or an end. With two odd vertices you must start at one and finish at the other; with none you can return to where you began.

The contrast is instructive. Euler routes are decided by a two-second degree count. Hamilton routes have no such test — deciding whether one exists is NP-complete, which is why the exam asks for the Euler criterion and only asks you to find a Hamilton path by inspection on tiny graphs.

Two more terms the questions use

A trail sits between a walk and a path: edges may not repeat, but vertices may. That is what makes a circuit a closed trail rather than a closed path — an Euler circuit revisits vertices freely while using each edge once.

An isolated vertex is one with degree 0 — no edges at all. It forms a connected component by itself, so a graph containing one cannot be connected unless it is the only vertex.

📘 DEFINITION

Walk: any sequence of adjacent vertices; repeats allowed

Trail: a walk with no repeated edge

Path: a walk with no repeated vertex

Cycle / circuit: a closed path returning to its start

Length: the number of edges in a walk or path

Connected graph: a path exists between every pair of vertices

Connected component: a maximal connected piece of a graph

Euler path / circuit: uses every edge exactly once; open or closed

Hamilton path / circuit: visits every vertex exactly once

Strongly connected: in a digraph, a directed path exists between every ordered pair

★ ON THE OA

A walk allows repeats; a path repeats no vertex; a cycle is a closed path. A graph is connected when a path joins every pair. An Euler path exists exactly when 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree — and an Euler circuit when all degrees are even.

⚠ COMMON MISTAKE

Euler is about edges, Hamilton is about vertices. Mixing them up is the standard error, and the degree criterion applies only to Euler.

Walks, trails, paths, circuits, cycles

📊 FIGURE — a cycle highlighted inside a larger graph
TermMay repeat vertices?May repeat edges?Closed?
WalkYesYesEither
TrailYesNoEither
PathNoNoNo
CircuitYesNoYes
CycleNo (except the shared start/end)NoYes

Length is the number of edges, not vertices. The highlighted cycle passes 5 vertex-slots but has length 4, and that off-by-one is the most common wrong answer.

📘 DEFINITION

A graph is connected when a path exists between every pair of vertices. If not, it splits into connected components.

An Euler circuit uses every edge exactly once and exists iff the graph is connected and every vertex has even degree. An Euler path (open) exists iff exactly two vertices have odd degree.

A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once, and has no simple test — deciding it is NP-complete. Euler is about edges and easy; Hamilton is about vertices and hard.

📊 FIGURE — walk, trail, path, circuit, cycle — each one adds a restriction

The five words above are nested: every path is a trail, and every trail is a walk. Each step adds one prohibition — first \"do not reuse an edge\", then \"do not reuse a vertex\" — and a question that uses the wrong word is asking a different question.

Counting routes with the adjacency matrix

Powers of the adjacency matrix count walks, because walks are the version with no restrictions — and that is exactly why they are the countable one. Entry (i, j) of Ak is the number of walks of length exactly k from i to j.

C₁C₂C₃C₄C₅R₁R₂R₃R₄R₅0111010001100101010101010A — the walkway network. R₁/C₁ = Library, R₂/C₂ = Gym, R₃/C₃ = Hall, R₄/C₄ = Lab, R₅/C₅ = Café. Row 1 tinted.C₁C₂C₃C₄C₅R₁R₂R₃R₄R₅3011202120112111213020102A² — the tinted row and column meet at entry (1, 5) = 2: two walks of length 2 from the Library to the Café.
row 1 = start at the Librarycolumn 5 = finish at the Caféwhere they meet = the answer
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — two-step routes across campus

Using the matrices above, find the number of Library → Café routes that pass through exactly one other building, and name them.

  1. That is a walk of length 2, so read entry (row 1, column 5) of A².
  2. The entry is 2.
  3. To name them, redo the dot product by hand: row 1 of A across is (0, 1, 1, 1, 0); column 5 of A down is (0, 1, 0, 1, 0).
  4. Multiply position by position: 0·0 + 1·1 + 1·0 + 1·1 + 0·0 = 0 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 2.
  5. The contributing positions are 2 and 4, which are the Gym and the Lab.
  6. The two routes are Library → Gym → Café and Library → Lab → Café.

The diagonal of A² is worth a glance too: entry (1, 1) = 3 = deg(Library), because a length-2 walk from a vertex back to itself is \"out along an edge and straight back\".

Answer: 2 routes: via the Gym and via the Lab.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — cut vertices and bridges in a delivery network

A delivery network joins depots N–O, O–P, P–N (a triangle) and O–Q, with Q attached only to O. Which vertices and edges are critical?

  1. A cut vertex is one whose removal disconnects the graph. Remove O: N and P remain joined by the edge NP, but Q is now isolated. So O is a cut vertex.
  2. Remove N: O, P and Q remain connected through O. Not a cut vertex. Same for P and for Q.
  3. A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph. Remove OQ: Q is stranded, so OQ is a bridge.
  4. Remove NO instead: N is still reachable as N–P–O. Not a bridge. Likewise OP and NP are not bridges.
  5. General rule visible here: an edge on a cycle is never a bridge, because the rest of the cycle provides a detour.
Answer: O is the only cut vertex; OQ is the only bridge.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Ak counts walks, not paths. Some of the walks it counts revisit vertices, so a large entry does not mean many genuinely distinct routes. Second trap: \"connected\" is about vertices, not edges. A graph with a hundred edges can still be disconnected if one vertex sits alone; and a graph is connected exactly when there is a path between every pair.

🎯 EXAM TIP

To decide \"can I get from A to B at all?\", do not compute powers one at a time — the answer is yes exactly when a nonzero entry appears somewhere in A + A² + … + An−1, where n is the number of vertices. No path ever needs more than n − 1 edges, because a longer one would have to revisit a vertex.

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. That one sentence forces a surprising number of consequences, and the exam tests them as separate facts even though they all follow from the definition.

📐 Properties of a tree with n vertices
Edge count
exactly n − 1 edges
Uniqueness
exactly one path between any two vertices
Fragility
removing any edge disconnects it
Saturation
adding any edge creates a cycle
Equivalence
connected + acyclic ⇔ connected with n − 1 edges ⇔ acyclic with n − 1 edges

The last line is worth reading carefully: any two of connected, acyclic and n − 1 edges imply the third. So a question giving you two of them has already told you it is a tree.

The n − 1 count is the fact most often asked. A tree with 10 vertices has 9 edges — no more, no fewer — which also means a graph with 10 vertices and 12 edges cannot possibly be a tree.

Rooted trees

Designating one vertex as the root imposes a hierarchy and brings a family vocabulary that questions use directly.

TermMeans
Rootthe designated top vertex; the only one with no parent
Parentthe vertex immediately above
Childa vertex immediately below
Leafa vertex with no children
Internal vertexany vertex that is not a leaf
Depth / levelthe distance from the root; the root is at level 0
Heightthe depth of the deepest leaf
Subtreea vertex together with all its descendants

Binary trees

A binary tree allows each vertex at most two children, conventionally left and right. Two counting facts about them are examined.

A binary tree of height h has at most 2h+1 − 1 vertices and at most 2h leaves.

A tree achieving those maxima is full at every level. The reason to care is efficiency: n items stored in a balanced binary tree give a height of about log₂n, so a search that descends from the root touches about 20 vertices for a million items — the same logarithmic behaviour as binary search.

A binary search tree adds an ordering rule: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the vertex, everything in the right subtree is larger. That rule is what makes the inorder traversal in the next lesson produce sorted output.

The equivalent definitions, and why they are equivalent

A tree can be characterised in several ways that sound different and describe the same object. Connected and acyclic. Connected with n − 1 edges. Acyclic with n − 1 edges. Exactly one path between every pair. Minimally connected — remove any edge and it breaks. Maximally acyclic — add any edge and a cycle appears.

The reason they coincide is a counting argument. A connected graph needs at least n − 1 edges to reach every vertex, and any graph with more than n − 1 edges must contain a cycle. So n − 1 is exactly the boundary where connectivity is achieved and cycles have not yet appeared — which is what a tree is.

For exam purposes that means any two of the three properties give you the third for free, and a question stating two of them has already told you the answer without saying \"tree\".

The rest of the family vocabulary

Two vertices with the same parent are siblings. Everything reachable downward from a vertex is its set of descendants, and everything on the path back up to the root is its ancestors. A vertex's subtree is that vertex together with all of its descendants.

📘 DEFINITION

Tree: a connected acyclic graph

Forest: a graph with no cycles that may be disconnected — a set of trees

Root: the designated top vertex of a rooted tree

Leaf: a vertex with no children

Internal vertex: a vertex with at least one child

Depth / level: distance from the root

Height: the greatest depth in the tree

Binary tree: each vertex has at most two children

Binary search tree: a binary tree ordered so left < vertex < right

★ ON THE OA

A tree is connected and acyclic. A tree with n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges and a unique path between any two vertices. Adding any edge creates a cycle; removing any edge disconnects it.

🎯 EXAM TIP

Count edges first when asked whether a graph is a tree. If the count is not exactly n − 1, the answer is no and nothing else needs checking.

Tree anatomy, and the three traversals

📘 DEFINITION

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. Three facts follow and all three are examinable: a tree on n vertices has exactly n − 1 edges; there is exactly one path between any two vertices; and adding any edge creates a cycle while removing any edge disconnects it.

📊 FIGURE — one binary search tree, read three ways
TraversalOrder of workReading the tree aboveUsed for
Preordernode, left, rightF B A D C E G I Hcopying a tree; prefix notation
Inorderleft, node, rightA B C D E F G H Ia BST comes out sorted
Postorderleft, right, nodeA C E D B H I G Fdeleting a tree; postfix notation

The name tells you when the node itself is visited — pre before its children, in between them, post after both. Inorder on a binary search tree is the one to remember: it always comes out in sorted order, which is the answer to a whole family of questions.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — why is inorder sorted here?

Because a BST stores everything smaller than a node in its left subtree and everything larger in its right. Visiting left, then the node, then right therefore emits every smaller value first, then the node, then every larger one — recursively, all the way down. The output A B C D E F G H I is alphabetical, which is the check.

📊 FIGURE — rooted-tree vocabulary on an org chart
📘 DEFINITION

A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. Four statements about a graph on n vertices are equivalent, and any one of them can be used as the definition: (1) it is connected and acyclic; (2) it is connected with exactly n − 1 edges; (3) it is acyclic with exactly n − 1 edges; (4) there is exactly one path between every pair of vertices.

That last one is the most useful in practice. In an org chart there is exactly one chain of command between any two people; in a road network with a cycle there would be a detour, and a tree has no detours anywhere. Two immediate consequences: adding any edge to a tree creates exactly one cycle, and removing any edge disconnects it — so every edge of a tree is a bridge.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — counting edges, leaves and reporting lines

A company has 10 staff arranged in the org chart above. (a) How many reporting lines are there? (b) How many people are leaves? (c) What is the height of the tree, and what does it mean?

  1. (a) A tree on n vertices has n − 1 edges, so 10 people give 9 reporting lines. No counting of the picture is required.
  2. (b) A leaf is a vertex with no children: Warehouse, Audit, Rider and UI. That is 4 leaves — the staff with nobody reporting to them.
  3. (c) The height is the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. CEO → Ops → Delivery → Rider is 3 edges, and nothing is longer, so the height is 3.
  4. In organisational terms the height is the number of management layers between the CEO and the most distant employee.
Answer: (a) 9. (b) 4 leaves. (c) Height 3.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — sizing a full m-ary tree

A decision system is a full binary tree (every internal node has exactly 2 children) with 25 internal nodes. (a) How many nodes in total? (b) How many leaves? (c) Repeat for a full 3-ary tree with 17 internal nodes.

  1. The formula for a full m-ary tree with i internal nodes is n = m·i + 1. The \"+ 1\" is the root, which is nobody's child.
  2. (a) m = 2, i = 25: n = 2(25) + 1 = 51 nodes.
  3. (b) Leaves are the nodes that are not internal: l = n − i = 51 − 25 = 26 leaves.
  4. (c) m = 3, i = 17: n = 3(17) + 1 = 52 nodes, and l = 52 − 17 = 35 leaves.
  5. Check with the direct leaf formula l = (m − 1)i + 1: for (c) that is 2(17) + 1 = 35 ✓.

The reasoning behind n = m·i + 1: every node except the root is somebody's child, and the i internal nodes contribute m children each, so the number of non-root nodes is m·i.

Answer: (a) 51. (b) 26. (c) 52 nodes and 35 leaves.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Height is measured in edges, not in nodes. A root-to-leaf chain of 4 boxes has height 3. Some sources count levels instead, so read the question — but the standard convention here is edges, and level numbering starts the root at level 0. Second trap: \"n − 1 edges\" only characterises a tree together with connectivity or acyclicity. A graph with 10 vertices and 9 edges made of a triangle plus a separate 7-vertex tree has the right edge count and is not a tree.

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a question gives you a number of vertices and asks for edges in a tree, the answer is n − 1 with no work required. Going the other way: a connected graph with more than n − 1 edges must contain a cycle, and the number of edges you would have to remove to reach a spanning tree is exactly |E| − (n − 1).

A traversal visits every vertex of a tree in a defined order. For binary trees there are three, and they differ only in when the root is visited relative to its subtrees — which is exactly what their names encode.

TraversalOrderRoot is visited
PreorderRoot, Left, Rightfirst — \"pre\"
InorderLeft, Root, Rightin the middle — \"in\"
PostorderLeft, Right, Rootlast — \"post\"

The prefix names the position of Root in the sequence, and Left always comes before Right in all three. Once you have that, the three orders need no separate memorisation.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — all three on one tree
            F\n          /   \\\n         B     G\n        / \\     \\\n       A   D     I\n          / \\   /\n         C   E H\n\nPreorder  (Root,Left,Right):  F B A D C E G I H\nInorder   (Left,Root,Right):  A B C D E F G H I    <- sorted!\nPostorder (Left,Right,Root):  A C E D B H I G F

The inorder line is not a coincidence. This is a binary search tree, and the ordering rule — left subtree smaller, right subtree larger — means visiting left, then root, then right produces the values in ascending order. That is the standard exam use of inorder traversal, and it is worth recognising on sight.

How to trace one by hand

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — the reliable method for preorder
1.
Start at the root. Write it down (preorder visits Root first).
2.
Move to the entire left subtree and apply the same rule to it, recursively.
3.
When the left subtree is exhausted, do the same for the right subtree.
4.
The recursion is the method — treat each subtree as a smaller tree of the same kind.

Under exam pressure the reliable technique is to work one subtree at a time and write the partial sequence, rather than trying to hold the whole traversal in your head. The recursive structure means a mistake in one subtree does not corrupt the others.

Where each one is used

TraversalTypical use
Preordercopying a tree; producing prefix notation from an expression tree
Inorderreading a BST in sorted order; producing infix notation
Postorderdeleting a tree safely — children before parent; producing postfix notation

Postorder's use for deletion is a good illustration of why the order matters: you cannot free a parent before its children, or you lose the pointers to them. Applied to an expression tree, the same three traversals produce prefix, infix and postfix notation — which is how a compiler converts an expression into a form a stack machine can evaluate.

Descendants, and one classic application

The three traversals can be restated in terms of descendants, which is how questions often word them: preorder visits a vertex before its descendants, postorder visits it after its descendants, and inorder visits it between the left and right ones. Preorder is the natural choice for printing an outline or copying a structure, because the parent must exist before its children are placed.

The classic application of binary trees is Huffman coding, the compression scheme where frequent characters get short codes. Its codes are built by walking the tree, which gives them the prefix-free property: no code is a prefix of another, so a stream of bits can be decoded unambiguously with no separators.

📘 DEFINITION

Traversal: visiting every vertex of a tree in a defined order

Preorder: Root, Left, Right

Inorder: Left, Root, Right — gives sorted output for a BST

Postorder: Left, Right, Root

Expression tree: a tree with operators at internal vertices and operands at leaves

Prefix / infix / postfix: the notations produced by pre-, in- and postorder traversal

Breadth-first traversal: visiting level by level, using a queue

★ ON THE OA

The three binary-tree traversals are preorder (Root, Left, Right), inorder (Left, Root, Right — yields sorted order for a BST) and postorder (Left, Right, Root). The position of \"Root\" in the name tells you the order.

🎯 EXAM TIP

If a question gives a traversal sequence and asks which type it is, check whether it is sorted — sorted output on a search tree means inorder, and that single observation answers it.

Traversals are notations

The three traversal orders are not arbitrary — each one is a way of writing the expression a tree stores. Operators sit at internal nodes, operands at leaves.

📊 FIGURE — (3 × 4) + (9 − 2) as a tree, read three ways
TraversalOrderProducesUsed by
Preordernode, left, rightprefix (Polish)Lisp; copying a tree
Inorderleft, node, rightinfix — how humans write itprinting a BST in sorted order
Postorderleft, right, nodepostfix (reverse Polish)stack machines; freeing a tree
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — evaluate the postfix 3 4 × 9 2 − +

Push operands; when an operator arrives, pop two, apply, push the result.

3 → [3]. 4 → [3, 4]. × → pop 4 and 3, push 12 → [12].
9 → [12, 9]. 2 → [12, 9, 2]. − → pop 2 and 9, push 7 → [12, 7].
+ → pop 7 and 12, push 19 → [19].

No brackets were needed anywhere. That is the whole reason postfix exists.

📊 FIGURE — the three depth-first traversal orders on one tree

All three depth-first traversals visit the left subtree before the right one. The only thing that changes is when the node itself is recorded: before its subtrees (pre), between them (in), or after both (post). Say the word out loud — \"pre-order records the node pre-viously\" — and the ordering follows.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — all three traversals of a score tree

Exam scores are inserted into a binary search tree in the order 58, 34, 71, 26, 47, 65, 89 (smaller goes left, larger goes right). List the preorder, inorder and postorder traversals.

  1. First build the tree. 58 is the root. 34 < 58 so it goes left; 71 > 58 so it goes right. 26 < 58 and < 34 so it is 34's left child; 47 < 58 but > 34 so it is 34's right child. 65 > 58 but < 71 so it is 71's left child; 89 > 71 so it is 71's right child.
  2. Preorder (node, left, right): record 58, then do the whole left subtree — 34, then 26, then 47 — then the right subtree — 71, then 65, then 89.
  3. → 58, 34, 26, 47, 71, 65, 89.
  4. Inorder (left, node, right): finish 34's left subtree first (26), then 34, then 47, then the root 58, then 65, then 71, then 89.
  5. → 26, 34, 47, 58, 65, 71, 89.
  6. Postorder (left, right, node): 26 and 47 before 34; then 65 and 89 before 71; then the root last.
  7. → 26, 47, 34, 65, 89, 71, 58.

Two structural checks you get for free: preorder always starts with the root, postorder always ends with the root, and inorder on a BST is sorted. If any of those fails, the traversal is wrong.

Answer: Listed above; the inorder output 26, 34, 47, 58, 65, 71, 89 is sorted, confirming the tree.
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — an expression tree and postfix notation

An invoicing formula (12 + 5) × (30 − 18) is stored as an expression tree: the root is ×, its left child is + with children 12 and 5, and its right child is − with children 30 and 18. Give the postorder traversal, evaluate it, and give the preorder traversal.

  1. Postorder visits both children before the operator: 12, 5, +, then 30, 18, −, then the root ×.
  2. → 12 5 + 30 18 − ×, which is exactly postfix (reverse Polish) notation.
  3. Evaluate it with a stack: push 12, push 5; the + pops both and pushes 17.
  4. Push 30, push 18; the − pops both and pushes 30 − 18 = 12.
  5. The × pops 17 and 12 and pushes 17 × 12 = 204.
  6. Preorder puts each operator first: × + 12 5 − 30 18, which is prefix (Polish) notation.

This is why the traversals matter outside the exam: postorder is how a compiler emits stack-machine code, and inorder (with brackets) is how the expression is printed back for a human.

Answer: Postorder 12 5 + 30 18 − × evaluates to 204; preorder is × + 12 5 − 30 18.
⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

Inorder does not mean \"the order they were inserted\". It means the node is recorded in between its two subtrees, and on a BST that produces sorted output — which is usually nothing like the insertion order. Second trap: subtraction and division are not commutative, so in postfix the operands must stay in order: 30 18 − is 12, while 18 30 − is −12.

🎯 EXAM TIP

For a fast, reliable traversal by hand, draw a loop around the whole tree starting at the root and travelling anticlockwise, hugging the outline. Each node is passed three times: record it on the left pass for preorder, the bottom pass for inorder, and the right pass for postorder. One drawing then gives all three answers.

Variable-length codes. To compress text, give the frequent characters the shorter codes and the rare ones the longer ones — that is the entire idea behind Huffman coding, and it is why the total shrinks even though some characters cost more than before.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The giveaway distinguishing the traversals is the position of the root: pre-order visits it first (root, left, right), in-order in the middle (left, root, right), post-order last (left, right, root). Find the root in the output and you have identified the traversal.
